// บทความ · Laplace Transform

# การแปลงลาปลาซ (Laplace Transform) คืออะไร ใช้ทำอะไร

การแปลงลาปลาซคือเครื่องมือที่เปลี่ยนสมการเชิงอนุพันธ์ซึ่งแก้ยาก ให้เป็นสมการพีชคณิตซึ่งแก้ง่าย แล้วแปลงคำตอบกลับมาเป็นฟังก์ชันของเวลา บทความนี้อธิบายแนวคิด นิยาม และตัวอย่างวงจร RC ที่คำนวณตามได้ทุกบรรทัด

สรุปใน 30 วินาที

- นิยาม $F(s)=\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=\int_0^{\infty} f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$

- การหาอนุพันธ์ในโดเมนเวลา กลายเป็นการคูณด้วย $s$ ในโดเมน $s$

- ขั้นตอน: แปลง → แก้สมการพีชคณิต → แปลงกลับ

- ตำแหน่งโพลของ $F(s)$ บอกความเสถียรของระบบโดยไม่ต้องแก้สมการ

## แนวคิด: ทำไมต้องแปลง

สมมติวงจรหรือระบบกลไกหนึ่งอธิบายด้วยสมการเชิงอนุพันธ์ เช่น $y' + 3y = 6$ การแก้ตรง ๆ ต้องใช้ตัวประกอบอินทิเกรตหรือเดาคำตอบ แต่ถ้าเราย้ายสมการไปอยู่ในโดเมน $s$ อนุพันธ์จะหายไป เหลือเพียงการคูณและการบวก แก้เสร็จแล้วค่อยย้ายกลับ

เปรียบเทียบกับการใช้ลอการิทึมคูณเลขใหญ่ในสมัยก่อน: เปลี่ยนการคูณเป็นการบวก คำนวณให้เสร็จ แล้วเปลี่ยนกลับ ลาปลาซทำเช่นเดียวกันกับการหาอนุพันธ์และอินทิกรัล

## นิยามของการแปลงลาปลาซ

สำหรับฟังก์ชัน $f(t)$ ที่กำหนดสำหรับ $t \ge 0$ การแปลงลาปลาซด้านเดียวคือ

$$F(s) = \mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_0^{\infty} f(t)\,e^{-st}\,dt, \qquad s = \sigma + j\omega$$

ตัวคูณ $e^{-st}$ ทำหน้าที่เหมือนตัวกรอง: $f(t)$ ที่โตช้ากว่าเอกซ์โพเนนเชียลจะทำให้อินทิกรัลลู่เข้า ตัวอย่างพื้นฐานที่สุดคือ

$$\mathcal{L}\{e^{-at}\} = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+a)t}\,dt = \frac{1}{s+a}, \qquad \operatorname{Re}(s) > -a$$

จากสูตรนี้ ถ้า $a=0$ จะได้ $\mathcal{L}\{u(t)\}=1/s$ ส่วนสูตรอื่นที่ใช้บ่อยรวมไว้ใน ตารางการแปลงลาปลาซ แล้ว

## กุญแจสำคัญ: อนุพันธ์กลายเป็นการคูณ

เมื่ออินทิเกรตทีละส่วน จะได้สมบัติที่ทำให้ลาปลาซมีประโยชน์ที่สุด

$$\mathcal{L}\{y'(t)\} = sY(s) - y(0), \qquad \mathcal{L}\{y''(t)\} = s^2Y(s) - s\,y(0) - y'(0)$$

สังเกตว่าเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้น $y(0)$, $y'(0)$ ถูกใส่เข้าไปในสมการตั้งแต่ต้น ไม่ต้องหาค่าคงที่ทีหลังเหมือนวิธีแก้สมการเชิงอนุพันธ์แบบดั้งเดิม

## ขั้นตอนแก้สมการด้วยลาปลาซ 3 ขั้น

- แปลง ทั้งสองข้างของสมการเชิงอนุพันธ์ไปเป็นโดเมน $s$ โดยใส่เงื่อนไขเริ่มต้น

- แก้ หา $Y(s)$ ด้วยพีชคณิต

- แปลงกลับ เป็น $y(t)$ ด้วยเศษส่วนย่อยและตาราง (ดู วิธี Inverse Laplace ด้วยเศษส่วนย่อย)

## ตัวอย่างที่ 1: แก้ y′ + 3y = 6 เมื่อ y(0) = 0

- แปลงสมการ

$$sY(s) - 0 + 3Y(s) = \frac{6}{s}$$

- แก้หา $Y(s)$

$$Y(s)\,(s+3) = \frac{6}{s} \;\Rightarrow\; Y(s) = \frac{6}{s(s+3)}$$

- แยกเศษส่วนย่อย

$$\frac{6}{s(s+3)} = \frac{2}{s} - \frac{2}{s+3}$$

- แปลงกลับด้วย $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{1/s\}=1$ และ $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{1/(s+3)\}=e^{-3t}$

$$y(t) = 2 - 2e^{-3t}, \quad t \ge 0$$

ตรวจคำตอบ: $y' = 6e^{-3t}$ ดังนั้น $y' + 3y = 6e^{-3t} + 6 - 6e^{-3t} = 6$ ✓ และ $y(0)=2-2=0$ ✓

## ตัวอย่างที่ 2: วงจร RC รับแรงดันขั้นบันได 5 V

ตัวต้านทาน $R = 1\,\text{k}\Omega$ ต่ออนุกรมกับตัวเก็บประจุ $C = 100\,\mu\text{F}$ ป้อนแรงดัน $v_{in}(t) = 5\,u(t)$ โวลต์ ตัวเก็บประจุเริ่มต้นว่าง ค่าคงที่เวลา $\tau = RC = 1000 \times 100\times10^{-6} = 0.1$ วินาที

- สมการวงจร $RC\,\dfrac{dv_c}{dt} + v_c = v_{in}$ แปลงเป็นโดเมน $s$ ด้วย $v_c(0)=0$

$$(RCs + 1)V_c(s) = \frac{5}{s} \;\Rightarrow\; V_c(s) = \frac{5}{s(0.1s+1)} = \frac{50}{s(s+10)}$$

- เศษส่วนย่อย

$$\frac{50}{s(s+10)} = \frac{5}{s} - \frac{5}{s+10}$$

- แปลงกลับ

$$v_c(t) = 5\left(1 - e^{-10t}\right)\ \text{V}$$

ที่ $t = \tau = 0.1$ s แรงดันคร่อมตัวเก็บประจุ $= 5(1 - e^{-1}) \approx 3.16$ V (ประมาณ 63.2 % ของ 5 V) ตรงกับนิยามของค่าคงที่เวลา โพลอยู่ที่ $s=-10 = -1/\tau$

## ลาปลาซใช้ทำอะไรในงานวิศวกรรม

- วิเคราะห์วงจรไฟฟ้า RC, RL, RLC ที่มีสวิตช์หรือแหล่งจ่ายขั้นบันได ได้ทั้งผลตอบสนองชั่วครู่และสภาวะคงตัว

- ฟังก์ชันถ่ายโอน $G(s)=Y(s)/U(s)$ ใช้อธิบายระบบเชิงเส้นไม่แปรตามเวลาทุกชนิด ตั้งแต่มอเตอร์ถึงตัวกรอง

- ความเสถียร ถ้าโพลทุกตัวอยู่ซีกซ้ายของระนาบ $s$ ระบบเสถียร (ใช้ต่อในเกณฑ์ Routh–Hurwitz และรูทโลคัส)

- ระบบควบคุม ออกแบบตัวควบคุม PID ชดเชย และวิเคราะห์ผลตอบสนองความถี่

## ข้อผิดพลาดที่พบบ่อย

- ลืมเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้นตอนแปลงอนุพันธ์ ทำให้คำตอบผิดทั้งข้อ

- ลืมว่าลาปลาซด้านเดียวสนใจเฉพาะ $t \ge 0$ คำตอบที่ได้จึงต้องเขียนกำกับว่า $t \ge 0$ หรือคูณ $u(t)$

- สับสนระหว่าง $s$ กับ $\omega$ ในโดเมนเวลาไม่ต้องมี $j$ แต่ในโดเมน $s$ ความถี่แกว่งอยู่ที่ส่วนจินตภาพของโพล

## เรียนต่อในคลังความรู้

- การแปลงลาปลาซ: นิยาม ตารางคู่การแปลงพร้อม ROC

- คุณสมบัติของการแปลงลาปลาซครบทุกข้อ

- แก้สมการเชิงอนุพันธ์อันดับหนึ่งและสองด้วยลาปลาซ (มีตัวแก้โต้ตอบ)

- แล็บระบบอันดับหนึ่ง: ค่าคงที่เวลาของ RC และ RL

## คำถามที่พบบ่อย

การแปลงลาปลาซกับการแปลงฟูเรียร์ต่างกันอย่างไร?
ลาปลาซใช้ตัวแปรเชิงซ้อน $s = \sigma + j\omega$ จึงจัดการกับสัญญาณที่โตขึ้นหรือลดลงแบบเอกซ์โพเนนเชียลและเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้นได้ ส่วนฟูเรียร์ใช้เฉพาะ $j\omega$ ถ้าบริเวณลู่เข้า (ROC) รวมแกน $j\omega$ การแปลงฟูเรียร์คือลาปลาซที่แทน $s = j\omega$

ลาปลาซด้านเดียว (unilateral) คืออะไร ทำไมอินทิเกรตจาก 0?
ในงานวงจรและระบบควบคุมเรามักสนใจเหตุการณ์ตั้งแต่ $t = 0$ เป็นต้นไป และใส่ผลของสภาวะก่อนหน้าไว้ในเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้น ลาปลาซด้านเดียวจึงอินทิเกรตจาก 0 ไปถึงอนันต์ ส่วนแบบสองด้านอินทิเกรตจาก $-\infty$ ใช้ในวิชาสัญญาณและระบบเมื่อต้องวิเคราะห์ ROC อย่างเต็มรูปแบบ

ต้องแปลงกลับเป็นฟังก์ชันของเวลาเสมอไหม?
ไม่เสมอไป ถ้าต้องการแค่ความเสถียรหรือรูปแบบการตอบสนอง ดูตำแหน่งโพลของ $F(s)$ ก็บอกได้เลย แต่ถ้าต้องการค่า $y(t)$ ที่เวลาใดเวลาหนึ่งต้องทำการแปลงกลับ ซึ่งมักใช้วิธีเศษส่วนย่อยร่วมกับตาราง

ตัวแปร s มีหน่วยหรือความหมายอย่างไร?
$s$ มีหน่วยเป็นความถี่ (1/วินาที) ส่วนจริง $\sigma$ บอกอัตราการโตหรือลดแบบเอกซ์โพเนนเชียล ส่วนจินตภาพ $\omega$ คือความถี่การแกว่ง เช่น โพลที่ $s = -10$ หมายถึงสัญญาณลดลงแบบ $e^{-10t}$

## FAQ

**การแปลงลาปลาซกับการแปลงฟูเรียร์ต่างกันอย่างไร?**
ลาปลาซใช้ตัวแปรเชิงซ้อน $s = \sigma + j\omega$ จึงจัดการกับสัญญาณที่โตขึ้นหรือลดลงแบบเอกซ์โพเนนเชียลและเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้นได้ ส่วนฟูเรียร์ใช้เฉพาะ $j\omega$ ถ้าบริเวณลู่เข้า (ROC) รวมแกน $j\omega$ การแปลงฟูเรียร์คือลาปลาซที่แทน $s = j\omega$

**ลาปลาซด้านเดียว (unilateral) คืออะไร ทำไมอินทิเกรตจาก 0?**
ในงานวงจรและระบบควบคุมเรามักสนใจเหตุการณ์ตั้งแต่ $t = 0$ เป็นต้นไป และใส่ผลของสภาวะก่อนหน้าไว้ในเงื่อนไขเริ่มต้น ลาปลาซด้านเดียวจึงอินทิเกรตจาก 0 ไปถึงอนันต์ ส่วนแบบสองด้านอินทิเกรตจาก $-\infty$ ใช้ในวิชาสัญญาณและระบบเมื่อต้องวิเคราะห์ ROC อย่างเต็มรูปแบบ

**ต้องแปลงกลับเป็นฟังก์ชันของเวลาเสมอไหม?**
ไม่เสมอไป ถ้าต้องการแค่ความเสถียรหรือรูปแบบการตอบสนอง ดูตำแหน่งโพลของ $F(s)$ ก็บอกได้เลย แต่ถ้าต้องการค่า $y(t)$ ที่เวลาใดเวลาหนึ่งต้องทำการแปลงกลับ ซึ่งมักใช้วิธีเศษส่วนย่อยร่วมกับตาราง

**ตัวแปร s มีหน่วยหรือความหมายอย่างไร?**
$s$ มีหน่วยเป็นความถี่ (1/วินาที) ส่วนจริง $\sigma$ บอกอัตราการโตหรือลดแบบเอกซ์โพเนนเชียล ส่วนจินตภาพ $\omega$ คือความถี่การแกว่ง เช่น โพลที่ $s = -10$ หมายถึงสัญญาณลดลงแบบ $e^{-10t}$

# PID Controller คืออะไร: Kp Ki Kd ทำงานอย่างไร และจูนอย่างไร

Summary: ตัวควบคุม PID รวมสามเทอมคือสัดส่วน ปริพันธ์ และอนุพันธ์ของค่าผิดพลาด อธิบายผลของ Kp Ki Kd ตารางผลต่อการตอบสนอง ตัวอย่างจูนด้วย Ziegler–Nichols และปัญหาที่พบจริง

# PID Controller คืออะไร: Kp Ki Kd ทำงานอย่างไร และจูนอย่างไร

PID เป็นตัวควบคุมที่ใช้มากที่สุดในอุตสาหกรรม เพราะหลักการง่าย: ดูค่าผิดพลาดระหว่างค่าที่ต้องการกับค่าที่วัดได้ แล้วปรับสัญญาณควบคุมด้วยสามมุมมอง คือปัจจุบัน อดีต และอนาคตของค่าผิดพลาด

สรุปใน 30 วินาที

- $u(t)=K_pe(t)+K_i\int e\,dt+K_d\dfrac{de}{dt}$ โดย $e=r-y$

- P = ปัจจุบัน · I = อดีต (กำจัดค่าผิดพลาดคงตัว) · D = แนวโน้ม (ลดการเกินเป้า)

- จูนเริ่มต้นด้วย Ziegler–Nichols แล้วปรับละเอียดจากผลตอบสนองจริง

## สูตรและฟังก์ชันถ่ายโอนของ PID

ให้ $r(t)$ เป็นค่าที่ต้องการ $y(t)$ เป็นค่าที่วัดได้ และค่าผิดพลาด $e(t)=r(t)-y(t)$

$$u(t)=K_p\,e(t)+K_i\int_0^t e(\tau)\,d\tau+K_d\,\frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

ในโดเมน $s$ ได้ตัวควบคุมที่เขียนได้สองรูปเทียบเท่ากัน

$$C(s)=K_p+\frac{K_i}{s}+K_d s \;=\; K_p\left(1+\frac{1}{T_i s}+T_d s\right),\qquad K_i=\frac{K_p}{T_i},\; K_d=K_pT_d$$

รูปแรกใช้ในคู่มือซอฟต์แวร์หลายตัว รูปหลังพบในตำราและตัวควบคุมอุตสาหกรรม ต้องดูว่าอุปกรณ์ที่ใช้ตั้งค่าแบบไหน

## แต่ละเทอมทำอะไร

- P (สัดส่วน): ผิดพลาดมากสั่งแรง ผิดพลาดน้อยสั่งเบา เพิ่ม $K_p$ ทำให้เร็วขึ้น แต่ถ้ามากเกินไปจะแกว่งหรือไม่เสถียร และระบบส่วนใหญ่ยังเหลือค่าผิดพลาดคงตัวเมื่อมี P อย่างเดียว

- I (ปริพันธ์): ยังมีค่าผิดพลาดค้างอยู่ก็สะสมต่อไปจนสั่งแรงพอจะกำจัดมัน จึงทำให้ค่าผิดพลาดคงตัวต่อค่าคงที่เป็นศูนย์ แต่ทำให้ตอบสนองช้าลงและเกินเป้าได้

- D (อนุพันธ์): ดูอัตราการเปลี่ยนของค่าผิดพลาด ช่วยเบรกล่วงหน้า ลดการเกินเป้า แต่ขยายสัญญาณรบกวนความถี่สูง

### ผลของการเพิ่มแต่ละค่าต่อการตอบสนองขั้นบันได

| เพิ่ม | เวลาขึ้น | เกินเป้า | เวลาเข้าที่ | ค่าผิดพลาดคงตัว |

| $K_p$ | ลดลง | เพิ่มขึ้น | เปลี่ยนเล็กน้อย | ลดลง |

| $K_i$ | ลดลง | เพิ่มขึ้น | เพิ่มขึ้น | กำจัดได้ |

| $K_d$ | เปลี่ยนเล็กน้อย | ลดลง | ลดลง | ไม่เปลี่ยน |

ตารางนี้เป็นแนวโน้มทั่วไปของระบบอันดับต่ำ ค่าทั้งสามส่งผลต่อกัน จึงต้องจูนร่วมกัน ไม่ใช่ปรับทีละตัวแล้วเสร็จ

## จูนเริ่มต้นด้วย Ziegler–Nichols (วิธีวงปิด)

ตั้ง $K_i=K_d=0$ เพิ่ม $K_p$ ทีละน้อยจนระบบแกว่งสม่ำเสมอ บันทึกค่า $K_p$ ตอนนั้นเป็น $K_u$ (ultimate gain) และคาบการแกว่งเป็น $P_u$ แล้วอ่านค่าจากตาราง

| ชนิด | $K_p$ | $T_i$ | $T_d$ |

| P | $0.5K_u$ | – | – |

| PI | $0.45K_u$ | $P_u/1.2$ | – |

| PID | $0.6K_u$ | $P_u/2$ | $P_u/8$ |

ตัวอย่าง

### พบ $K_u=8$ และ $P_u=2$ วินาที

-
$$K_p=0.6\times8=4.8,\qquad T_i=\frac{2}{2}=1\ \text{s},\qquad T_d=\frac{2}{8}=0.25\ \text{s}$$

-
$$K_i=\frac{K_p}{T_i}=4.8,\qquad K_d=K_pT_d=4.8\times0.25=1.2$$

ค่าเริ่มต้น $K_p=4.8$, $K_i=4.8\ \text{s}^{-1}$, $K_d=1.2\ \text{s}$ วิธีนี้มักให้การเกินเป้าสูง ให้ใช้เป็นจุดเริ่มต้นแล้วลด $K_p$ หรือ $K_i$ ลงตามผลตอบสนองจริง

## ปัญหาที่พบจริง

- Integral windup: ตัวขับอิ่มตัวแต่เทอม I ยังสะสม ทำให้เกินเป้ามากเมื่อค่าผิดพลาดกลับเครื่องหมาย แก้ด้วย anti-windup เช่น หยุดสะสมเมื่ออิ่มตัว

- สัญญาณรบกวนในเทอม D: ใส่ตัวกรองความถี่ต่ำที่เทอมอนุพันธ์ และหาอนุพันธ์จากค่าที่วัด $y$ แทนค่าผิดพลาด $e$ เพื่อไม่ให้เกิดการกระชากเมื่อเปลี่ยนค่าเป้าหมายทันที

- ความหน่วงเวลา (dead time): ยิ่งมาก ยิ่งต้องลด $K_p$ และเทอม D ไม่ช่วยมากนัก

## เรียนต่อในคลังความรู้

- ตัวควบคุม PID: โครงสร้าง ผล และแล็บจำลองในเบราว์เซอร์

- การจูน PID: Ziegler–Nichols, Cohen–Coon และวิธีอื่น

- เสถียรภาพของระบบควบคุม

- ระบบควบคุมทั้งชุด: ป้อนกลับ รูทโลคัส โบด

## คำถามที่พบบ่อย

Kp Ki Kd แต่ละค่าทำหน้าที่อะไร?
Kp ตอบสนองต่อค่าผิดพลาดปัจจุบัน เพิ่มแล้วเร็วขึ้นแต่เสี่ยงเกินเป้า Ki สะสมค่าผิดพลาดในอดีต ช่วยกำจัดค่าผิดพลาดคงตัว Kd ดูแนวโน้มของค่าผิดพลาด ช่วยลดการเกินเป้าแต่ไวต่อสัญญาณรบกวน

ทำไมบางระบบใช้แค่ PI ไม่ใช้ PID?
เพราะเทอมอนุพันธ์ขยายสัญญาณรบกวนจากเซนเซอร์ วงควบคุมที่สัญญาณวัดมีสัญญาณรบกวนมาก เช่น อัตราการไหลและระดับของเหลว จึงมักใช้ PI ซึ่งเรียบง่ายและเพียงพอ ส่วนระบบที่ตอบสนองช้าและสัญญาณวัดสะอาดอาจได้ประโยชน์จากเทอม D

Integral windup คืออะไร?
เมื่อตัวขับ (วาล์ว มอเตอร์ ฮีตเตอร์) อิ่มตัวแล้ว แต่ค่าผิดพลาดยังไม่เป็นศูนย์ เทอมปริพันธ์จะสะสมค่าต่อไปเรื่อย ๆ พอค่าผิดพลาดกลับเครื่องหมายจึงใช้เวลานานกว่าจะคลาย ทำให้เกินเป้ามาก แก้ด้วย anti-windup เช่น หยุดสะสมเมื่ออิ่มตัว

Ziegler–Nichols ใช้ได้กับระบบทุกชนิดไหม?
ไม่ทุกชนิด วิธีวงปิดต้องปล่อยให้ระบบแกว่งต่อเนื่องที่ $K_u$ ซึ่งอาจอันตรายกับกระบวนการจริง และให้ผลเริ่มต้นที่มักแกว่งแรง ควรใช้เป็นจุดเริ่มต้นแล้วจูนละเอียดต่อ

# How to Find the Determinant and Inverse Matrix (2×2 and 3×3) with Examples

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/determinant-and-inverse-matrix/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: Learn to find 2×2 and 3×3 determinants by cofactors and the inverse matrix with the adjugate formula, with numeric examples checked by multiplying back, and the condition for a singular matrix.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Linear algebra

# How to Find the Determinant and Inverse Matrix (2×2 and 3×3) with Examples

The determinant tells you whether a matrix is invertible, and the inverse is used to solve systems of equations such as the currents in a multi-loop circuit. This article walks through the hand calculations with examples checked by multiplying back.

30-second summary

- 2×2: $\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc$

- 3×3: expand along the first row with cofactors (alternating signs $+\,-\,+$)

- Inverse: $A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}(A)$, which exists only when $\det A\ne0$

## The 2×2 determinant

$$\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc$$

Example: $\det\begin{pmatrix}4&7\\2&6\end{pmatrix}=4\cdot6-7\cdot2=24-14=10$

## The 3×3 determinant by cofactors

Expand along the first row: multiply each entry by the 2×2 determinant that remains when its row and column are removed, with alternating signs $+,-,+$.

$$\det A=a_{11}M_{11}-a_{12}M_{12}+a_{13}M_{13}$$

Example

### $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&-1&4\\1&2&5\end{pmatrix}$

-
$$\det A=2\begin{vmatrix}-1&4\\2&5\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}0&4\\1&5\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0&-1\\1&2\end{vmatrix}$$

-
$$=2(-5-8)-1(0-4)+3(0+1)=-26+4+3$$

$\det A=-19$ (not zero, so the inverse exists)

For 3×3 you can also use the Sarrus rule: copy the first two columns to the right, add the products along the three downward diagonals and subtract the products along the three upward diagonals. The result is the same.

## The 2×2 inverse (shortcut formula)

$$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$$

Swap $a$ and $d$, change the signs of $b$ and $c$, then divide by the determinant.

Example

### $N=\begin{pmatrix}4&7\\2&6\end{pmatrix}$

-
$$N^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}6&-7\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&-0.7\\-0.2&0.4\end{pmatrix}$$

- Check: the first row of $N$ times the first column of $N^{-1}$

$$4(0.6)+7(-0.2)=2.4-1.4=1$$

And $4(-0.7)+7(0.4)=0$, $2(0.6)+6(-0.2)=0$, $2(-0.7)+6(0.4)=1$, so $NN^{-1}=I$ ✓

## The 3×3 inverse with the adjugate

Steps: (1) find the cofactor matrix $C$; (2) swap rows and columns (transpose) to get $\operatorname{adj}(A)=C^{T}$; (3) divide by $\det A$.

Continuing the example $A$ above

### Find $A^{-1}$

- Cofactors $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}-13&4&1\\1&7&-3\\7&-8&-2\end{pmatrix}$$

- Transpose

$$\operatorname{adj}(A)=C^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}-13&1&7\\4&7&-8\\1&-3&-2\end{pmatrix}$$

- Divide by $\det A=-19$

$$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{19}\begin{pmatrix}13&-1&-7\\-4&-7&8\\-1&3&2\end{pmatrix}$$

Check: the first row of $A$ times the first column of $A^{-1}$: $\dfrac{1}{19}\big(2(13)+1(-4)+3(-1)\big)=\dfrac{19}{19}=1$ ✓ and the first row times the second column: $\dfrac{1}{19}\big(2(-1)+1(-7)+3(3)\big)=0$ ✓

## What it is used for

- Solving systems of equations: $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\Rightarrow\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, for example the loop currents in a multi-loop electric circuit.

- Checking for a unique solution: if $\det A\ne0$ the system has exactly one solution.

- Eigenvalues: found from $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, used in the stability analysis of state-space systems.

## Keep learning in the library

The full lessons are in Thai, with English technical terms and the same formulas.

- Determinants: properties, cofactors and row operations (in Thai)

- The inverse matrix, by both the adjugate and Gauss–Jordan (in Thai)

- Matrix lab: a calculator that shows the working step by step (in Thai)

- Applications in electric circuits and power systems (in Thai)

## Frequently asked questions

What does a zero determinant mean?
The matrix is singular and has no inverse, and the system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ does not have a unique solution: it has either no solution or infinitely many. The rows or columns of the matrix are linearly dependent.

Can the Sarrus rule be used for a 4×4 matrix?
No. The Sarrus rule (drawing diagonals) works only for 3×3. Larger matrices use cofactor expansion or row operations down to a triangular matrix.

Why do we divide by the determinant when finding the inverse?
Because $A\,\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)\,I$, so we must divide by $\det(A)$ to get the identity matrix. That is impossible when $\det(A)=0$.

Which method is preferred for finding an inverse in practice?
By hand, use the shortcut formula for 2×2, and the adjugate or row operations (Gauss–Jordan) for 3×3. In computer programs one usually solves $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ by factorisation without forming the inverse explicitly, for better accuracy.

# Dot Product vs Cross Product: Formulas, Meaning and Examples

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/dot-product-cross-product/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: Compare the dot product (scalar product) and cross product (vector product): formulas, geometric meaning, calculation from components, and how they are used for work, torque and angles.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Vectors

# Dot Product vs Cross Product: Formulas, Meaning and Examples

Two vectors can be multiplied in two ways. The first gives a number; the second gives a new vector. Both have clear physical meanings: the dot product is used for work and angles, while the cross product is used for torque and area.

30-second summary

- Dot: $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z$ → scalar

- Cross: $|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$ → vector perpendicular to both, direction by the right-hand rule

- Dot = 0 ⇒ perpendicular · Cross = 0 ⇒ parallel

## A short comparison

| | Dot product $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}$ | Cross product $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ |

| Result | Scalar | Vector (3D) |

| Formula with the angle | $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta$ | Magnitude $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$ |

| Formula with components | $a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z$ | Determinant with $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}$ |

| Geometric meaning | Projection of one vector onto the other × length | Area of the parallelogram the two vectors span |

| Swapping the order | Unchanged | Sign reverses |

| Equals zero when | Perpendicular | Parallel |

| Used to find | Work, angle, projection, real power | Torque, magnetic force, a perpendicular direction |

## Dot product (scalar product)

For $\mathbf{a}=(a_x,a_y,a_z)$ and $\mathbf{b}=(b_x,b_y,b_z)$, multiply the components along the same axis and add them.

$$\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z=|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta$$

So the angle between the vectors follows from $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|}$. A positive value means an acute angle, a negative value an obtuse angle.

Work example

### A 50 N force at 30° to a 4 m displacement

-
$$W=\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d}=|\mathbf{F}||\mathbf{d}|\cos\theta=50\times4\times\cos30^\circ$$

$W = 200\times0.866 \approx 173.2$ J (only the component of the force parallel to the displacement does work)

## Cross product (vector product)

The result is perpendicular to both $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, with direction given by the right-hand rule: point your fingers along $\mathbf{a}$ and curl them toward $\mathbf{b}$; your thumb points in the direction of $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$. With components it is calculated as follows.

$$\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\a_x&a_y&a_z\\b_x&b_y&b_z\end{vmatrix}=(a_yb_z-a_zb_y)\,\mathbf{i}-(a_xb_z-a_zb_x)\,\mathbf{j}+(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)\,\mathbf{k}$$

Torque example

### A 0.3 m wrench with a 100 N force perpendicular to the handle

-
$$\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F},\quad |\boldsymbol{\tau}|=rF\sin90^\circ=0.3\times100\times1$$

$|\boldsymbol{\tau}|=30$ N·m, with the torque direction along the axis of rotation of the nut. If the force is applied at a slant, the torque falls in proportion to $\sin\theta$.

## The same example, computed both ways

Let $\mathbf{a}=(2,3,1)$ and $\mathbf{b}=(1,-1,4)$.

- Dot product

$$\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=2(1)+3(-1)+1(4)=3$$

- Cross product

$$\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\big(3\cdot4-1\cdot(-1),\; 1\cdot1-2\cdot4,\; 2\cdot(-1)-3\cdot1\big)=(13,\,-7,\,-5)$$

- The angle between the vectors, with $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{14}$, $|\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{18}$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{18}}\approx0.189\;\Rightarrow\;\theta\approx79.1^\circ$$

- Check with the magnitude of the cross product, which must equal $|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\sin\theta$

$$|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=\sqrt{13^2+7^2+5^2}=\sqrt{243}\approx15.59$$

$\sqrt{14\times18}\,\sin79.1^\circ\approx15.87\times0.982\approx15.59$ ✓ and $\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})=2(13)+3(-7)+1(-5)=0$ ✓ (the cross product is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$)

## How it is used in electrical engineering

- Real power: treating the voltage and current phasors (RMS values) as vectors in a 2D plane, the real power $P=VI\cos\varphi$ is their dot product.

- Force on a conductor: $\mathbf{F}=I\,\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{B}$ and the Lorentz force $\mathbf{F}=q\,\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ are cross products.

- Motor torque: $\boldsymbol{\tau}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}$.

## Frequently asked questions

How do the results of the dot product and cross product differ?
The dot product gives a scalar (a single number). The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both vectors, with its direction given by the right-hand rule. The cross product is defined only for 3D vectors.

What does it mean if the dot product is zero?
The two vectors are perpendicular (when neither is the zero vector). For example, a force perpendicular to the motion does zero work.

What does it mean if the cross product is the zero vector?
The two vectors are parallel or lie along the same line, because $\sin\theta = 0$.

Why does the sign change when you swap the order of a cross product?
Because the direction of the result is set by the right-hand rule. Swapping the order, $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}$, reverses the direction, so $\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}=-\,\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$. The dot product is commutative.

# How to Find the Inverse Laplace Transform: 3 Partial-Fraction Cases with Examples

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/inverse-laplace-transform-partial-fractions/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: Invert the Laplace transform with partial fractions for distinct, repeated and complex poles, with checked examples and what to do when the numerator degree is too high.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Inverse Laplace Transform

# How to Find the Inverse Laplace Transform: 3 Partial-Fraction Cases with Examples

After solving an equation in the $s$ domain you get $Y(s)$ as a ratio of polynomials, and the final step is to convert back to $y(t)$. The standard method that works for almost every problem is to split into partial fractions and then use the table. This article divides the work into 3 cases according to the type of pole.

30-second summary

- Factor the denominator → identify the pole type → write the partial fractions → find the coefficients → use the table

- Distinct poles: use cover-up · repeated poles: include every power of $(s+p)^k$ · complex poles: complete the square

- If the numerator degree ≥ the denominator degree, do long division first

## The transform pairs you need

All three cases use this small set of pairs (the full set is in the Laplace transform table).

| $F(s)$ | $f(t)$, $t \ge 0$ |

| $\dfrac{1}{s}$ | $1$ |

| $\dfrac{1}{s+a}$ | $e^{-at}$ |

| $\dfrac{1}{(s+a)^2}$ | $t\,e^{-at}$ |

| $\dfrac{\omega}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $e^{-at}\sin\omega t$ |

| $\dfrac{s+a}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $e^{-at}\cos\omega t$ |

## Case 1: distinct poles (non-repeated real roots)

If $F(s)=\dfrac{N(s)}{(s+p_1)(s+p_2)}$, it can be written as $\dfrac{A}{s+p_1}+\dfrac{B}{s+p_2}$ where $A = \left[(s+p_1)F(s)\right]_{s=-p_1}$. This is the cover-up method: cover the factor you are interested in, then substitute the value of $s$ into what remains.

Example 1

### Find $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{3s+5}{(s+1)(s+2)}\right\}$

- Find $A$ at the pole $s=-1$: cover $(s+1)$ and substitute $s=-1$

$$A = \frac{3(-1)+5}{(-1)+2} = \frac{2}{1} = 2$$

- Find $B$ at the pole $s=-2$

$$B = \frac{3(-2)+5}{(-2)+1} = \frac{-1}{-1} = 1$$

- Use the table

$$F(s)=\frac{2}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} \;\Rightarrow\; f(t) = 2e^{-t} + e^{-2t}$$

Check: $\dfrac{2}{s+1}+\dfrac{1}{s+2} = \dfrac{2(s+2)+(s+1)}{(s+1)(s+2)} = \dfrac{3s+5}{(s+1)(s+2)}$ ✓

## Case 2: repeated poles

A pole repeated $k$ times needs a term for every power from 1 to $k$. For example $(s+1)^2$ must be written as $\dfrac{B}{s+1}+\dfrac{C}{(s+1)^2}$. If you write only the squared term, the coefficients cannot be matched. The coefficient of the highest power can be found by cover-up, and the remaining terms from derivatives.

$$\text{If } F(s)=\frac{G(s)}{(s+p)^2}: \quad C = G(-p), \quad B = \left.\frac{dG}{ds}\right|_{s=-p}$$

Example 2

### Find $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{1}{s(s+1)^2}\right\}$

- Write the partial-fraction form

$$\frac{1}{s(s+1)^2} = \frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{(s+1)^2}$$

- Distinct pole at $s=0$: $A = \dfrac{1}{(0+1)^2}=1$

- Repeated pole at $s=-1$: let $G(s)=1/s$, so $C=G(-1)=-1$ and $B=G'(-1)=-\dfrac{1}{s^2}\Big|_{s=-1}=-1$

- Use the table

$$F(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{(s+1)^2} \;\Rightarrow\; f(t)=1-e^{-t}-t\,e^{-t}$$

Check the initial value: $f(0)=1-1-0=0$, which matches the initial value theorem $\lim_{s\to\infty} sF(s)=\lim \dfrac{1}{(s+1)^2}=0$ ✓

## Case 3: complex poles (complete the square)

If the denominator is a quadratic that does not factor into real roots, do not split it into complex numbers. Complete the square to get $(s+a)^2+\omega^2$, then arrange the numerator as $(s+a)$ plus a constant. This matches the cosine and sine pairs with the factor $e^{-at}$.

Example 3

### Find $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{s+3}{s^2+2s+5}\right\}$

- Complete the square in the denominator: $s^2+2s+5=(s+1)^2+2^2$

- Arrange the numerator: $s+3=(s+1)+2$, then split

$$F(s)=\frac{s+1}{(s+1)^2+2^2}+\frac{2}{(s+1)^2+2^2}$$

- Use the table with $a=1$, $\omega=2$

$$f(t)=e^{-t}\cos 2t + e^{-t}\sin 2t = e^{-t}(\cos 2t+\sin 2t)$$

The poles are at $s=-1\pm j2$, so the response is an oscillation at 2 rad/s whose amplitude decays as $e^{-t}$. Because the poles are in the left half plane, the system is stable.

## When the numerator degree is too high

Partial fractions work only for proper fractions. If the numerator degree ≥ the denominator degree, do long division first. A constant quotient is an impulse $\delta(t)$, while a quotient that is a polynomial in $s$ corresponds to derivatives of the impulse, which usually indicates a model that differentiates its input in a physically unrealistic way. Check the problem again.

## Checklist before you hand in the answer

- Substitute $t=0$ and compare with the initial value theorem: $f(0^+)=\lim_{s\to\infty}sF(s)$.

- If all poles of $sF(s)$ are in the left half plane (a distinct pole at $s=0$ in $F(s)$ is fine), compare $f(\infty)$ with $\lim_{s\to0}sF(s)$.

- Add the partial fractions back together; you must recover the original numerator.

## Frequently asked questions

What if the numerator degree is greater than or equal to the denominator degree?
Do polynomial long division first so that a proper fraction remains (numerator degree less than denominator degree). For example, $\dfrac{s^2+1}{s(s+1)} = 1 + \dfrac{-s+1}{s(s+1)}$. The constant 1 becomes an impulse $\delta(t)$ in the time domain.

When does the cover-up method work?
It is the fastest way to find the coefficient of a distinct pole: multiply both sides by $(s+p)$ and substitute $s=-p$. For a repeated pole it works only for the coefficient of the highest-power term; the remaining terms need differentiation or equating coefficients.

Do complex poles always have to be split into partial fractions containing j?
No. For a quadratic with complex roots, complete the square so the denominator has the form $(s+a)^2+\omega^2$, then use the pairs for $e^{-at}\cos\omega t$ and $e^{-at}\sin\omega t$. The result is real from the start.

# Laplace Transform Table: The Most Commonly Used Pairs

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/laplace-transform-table/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: The 15 most common Laplace transform pairs and a table of properties (time shift, frequency shift, derivative, integral, convolution, initial and final value), with tips for remembering them.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Laplace Transform Table

# Laplace Transform Table: The Most Commonly Used Pairs

A summary of the transform pairs and properties used in almost every circuit and control problem. Every pair is the unilateral Laplace transform ($t \ge 0$), with tips so you do not have to memorise the whole table.

## Table of basic transform pairs

In the table, $a$ and $\omega$ are real constants, $n$ is a positive integer, and every time function is understood to be multiplied by $u(t)$.

| # | $f(t)$, $t \ge 0$ | $F(s)$ |

| 1 | $\delta(t)$ (unit impulse) | $1$ |

| 2 | $1$ or $u(t)$ | $\dfrac{1}{s}$ |

| 3 | $t$ | $\dfrac{1}{s^2}$ |

| 4 | $t^n$ | $\dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ |

| 5 | $e^{-at}$ | $\dfrac{1}{s+a}$ |

| 6 | $t\,e^{-at}$ | $\dfrac{1}{(s+a)^2}$ |

| 7 | $t^n e^{-at}$ | $\dfrac{n!}{(s+a)^{n+1}}$ |

| 8 | $\sin\omega t$ | $\dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |

| 9 | $\cos\omega t$ | $\dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |

| 10 | $e^{-at}\sin\omega t$ | $\dfrac{\omega}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}$ |

| 11 | $e^{-at}\cos\omega t$ | $\dfrac{s+a}{(s+a)^2+\omega^2}$ |

| 12 | $\sinh at$ | $\dfrac{a}{s^2-a^2}$ |

| 13 | $\cosh at$ | $\dfrac{s}{s^2-a^2}$ |

| 14 | $t\sin\omega t$ | $\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2}$ |

| 15 | $t\cos\omega t$ | $\dfrac{s^2-\omega^2}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2}$ |

## Table of commonly used properties

Let $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ and $\mathcal{L}\{g(t)\}=G(s)$.

| Property | Time domain | $s$ domain |

| Linearity | $af(t)+bg(t)$ | $aF(s)+bG(s)$ |

| Frequency shift (multiplying by an exponential) | $e^{-at}f(t)$ | $F(s+a)$ |

| Time shift (delay) | $f(t-T)\,u(t-T)$, $T>0$ | $e^{-sT}F(s)$ |

| First derivative | $f'(t)$ | $sF(s)-f(0)$ |

| Second derivative | $f''(t)$ | $s^2F(s)-sf(0)-f'(0)$ |

| Integral | $\displaystyle\int_0^t f(\tau)\,d\tau$ | $\dfrac{F(s)}{s}$ |

| Multiplication by $t$ | $t\,f(t)$ | $-\dfrac{dF}{ds}$ |

| Convolution | $(f*g)(t)$ | $F(s)\,G(s)$ |

| Initial value | $f(0^+)$ | $\displaystyle\lim_{s\to\infty}sF(s)$ |

| Final value | $f(\infty)$ | $\displaystyle\lim_{s\to0}sF(s)$ (when all poles of $sF$ are in the left half plane) |

## Tips for remembering the table without rote learning

- Three pairs are enough: $1/s$, $1/(s+a)$, $\omega/(s^2+\omega^2)$. The rest can be built from them.

- Seeing $(s+a)$ in place of $s$ means multiplying by $e^{-at}$ in the time domain. For example, replacing $s \to s+a$ in $\omega/(s^2+\omega^2)$ gives pair 10.

- Sine versus cosine: sine has $\omega$ in the numerator (since $\sin 0 = 0$ there is no $s$ term), while cosine has $s$ in the numerator (since $\cos 0 = 1$).

- Multiplying by $t$ means differentiating with respect to $s$ and changing the sign, for example $-\dfrac{d}{ds}\dfrac{1}{s+a}=\dfrac{1}{(s+a)^2}$ gives pair 6.

Using the tip

### Find $\mathcal{L}\{t\cos\omega t\}$ from pair 9

- Multiplying by $t$ means $-\dfrac{d}{ds}$

$$-\frac{d}{ds}\frac{s}{s^2+\omega^2} = -\frac{(s^2+\omega^2) - s(2s)}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2} = \frac{s^2-\omega^2}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2}$$

This matches pair 15 in the table ✓

## Frequently asked questions

When can the final value theorem be used?
$f(\infty)=\lim_{s\to0}sF(s)$ is valid only when all poles of $sF(s)$ lie in the left half of the $s$ plane. If there are poles on the imaginary axis or in the right half plane (for example a sine that oscillates forever) the formula gives a wrong answer.

Does this table apply for t less than 0?
No. This table is for the unilateral Laplace transform, which treats the function as zero for negative time. Every function in the table therefore has an implied factor of $u(t)$.

How do I remember the whole table?
Remember three main pairs first: $1/s$, $1/(s+a)$ and $\omega/(s^2+\omega^2)$. The rest follow from properties: multiplying by $e^{-at}$ replaces $s$ with $s+a$, and multiplying by $t$ means differentiating with respect to $s$ and changing the sign.

# PID Tuning: The Complete Guide from Step Test to Ziegler–Nichols, SIMC and Anti-Windup

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/pid-tuning-guide/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: A full PID tuning course in one article: identify the process with a step test, tune with Ziegler–Nichols, Cohen–Coon, SIMC or relay, compare the results by simulation, then fix windup and noise.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Guide · PID Academy · Control systems

# PID Tuning: The Complete Guide from Step Test to Ziegler–Nichols, SIMC and Anti-Windup

Tuning decides whether a PID loop runs quietly for ten years or rings every shift. This is the whole course in one article: how to read your controller's equation, how to measure the process, seven tuning methods with their formulas and limits, a simulated head-to-head comparison on one plant, the practical fixes that real loops need, and a troubleshooting table you can take to the plant floor. Every number is worked out and checked by simulation.

30-second summary

- Check the controller's equation first (ideal, series or parallel; seconds or minutes). The same numbers mean different things in different forms.

- One open-loop step test gives $K$, $L$, $T$. The ratio $L/T$ tells you how hard the loop is.

- Good default: SIMC with $\tau_c=L$: $K_p=\dfrac{T}{K(\tau_c+L)}$, $T_i=\min\big(T,\,4(\tau_c+L)\big)$. Ziegler–Nichols and Cohen–Coon are fast but leave thin margins.

- Real loops also need a filtered D term, anti-windup, sensible sample time and a check of valve stiction.

## 1. Decide what “well tuned” means

Tuning is choosing $K_p$, $T_i$ and $T_d$ so that the closed loop meets a specification. Before touching a number, write that specification down, because a loop cannot be best at everything at once. Four things compete:

- Setpoint tracking: rise time, overshoot and settling time after the setpoint moves.

- Disturbance rejection: how far the measurement is pushed by a load change and how fast it returns.

- Robustness: whether the loop stays well damped when the process gain, time constant or dead time drifts by 30–50%.

- Control effort: how much the valve, motor or heater moves, including noise. Excess movement wears actuators.

Aggressive tuning improves the first two and costs the last two. Most process loops are regulatory: the setpoint rarely moves and disturbances dominate, so integral action and disturbance rejection matter most. Motion-control loops are servo loops: the setpoint moves constantly and overshoot is the main enemy. If both matter, use setpoint weighting (section 13) to tune the two behaviours separately.

Rule of thumb. Start from a smooth, robust tuning and speed it up only if the process demands it. It is much easier to explain a slightly slow loop than an oscillating one.

## 2. Know the equation your controller really uses

The most common tuning mistake is entering correct numbers into the wrong form. Three forms are common.

| Form | Transfer function | Where you meet it |

| Ideal (ISA, standard) | $C(s)=K_c\left(1+\dfrac{1}{T_is}+T_ds\right)$ | Textbooks, most DCS and PLC function blocks |

| Parallel | $C(s)=K_p+\dfrac{K_i}{s}+K_ds$ | Many MATLAB/Python libraries, some drives and microcontroller code |

| Series (interacting) | $C(s)=K_c'\left(1+\dfrac{1}{T_i's}\right)(1+T_d's)$ | Older pneumatic and electronic controllers, some vendors |

Ideal and parallel convert directly: $K_p=K_c$, $K_i=K_c/T_i$, $K_d=K_cT_d$. The series form multiplies out to the ideal form with different numbers:

$$K_c=K_c'\left(1+\frac{T_d'}{T_i'}\right),\qquad T_i=T_i'+T_d',\qquad T_d=\frac{T_i'T_d'}{T_i'+T_d'}$$

When $T_d$ is small compared with $T_i$ the two forms nearly agree, but with strong derivative action they do not. Three more details change what a number means:

- Proportional band: some controllers ask for PB (%) instead of gain: $PB=100/K_c$ when input and output are both in percent of span.

- Integral units: $T_i$ may be in seconds or minutes, and some vendors use repeats per minute $=1/T_i$. A larger number then means more integral action, the opposite of $T_i$.

- Engineering units vs percent: if the controller works on percent of span, the process gain $K$ must be expressed in the same percent. A gain measured in °C per % must be divided by the span of the measurement before you use a rule.

Check before you enter. Read the manual's equation, confirm the time units, and confirm whether the output is direct or reverse acting. A reverse-acting controller on a direct-acting process turns negative feedback into positive feedback within seconds.

## 3. What P, I and D do to the response

Here is a short recap; the article “What is a PID controller?” has the longer story. With error $e=r-y$:

$$u(t)=K_p\left[e(t)+\frac{1}{T_i}\int_0^t e\,d\tau+T_d\frac{de}{dt}\right]$$

- P acts on the present error. For a process with gain $K$ and no integrator, a P-only loop settles with a permanent offset $e_{ss}=\dfrac{1}{1+KK_p}$ for a unit setpoint step.

- I acts on the accumulated error, so it removes that offset. Its price is phase lag: more integral action (smaller $T_i$) means a slower, more oscillatory loop.

- D acts on the trend. It adds phase lead and damping, but its gain grows in proportion to frequency, so it amplifies high-frequency noise.

| Raise | Rise time | Overshoot | Settling | Offset | Stability |

| $K_p$ | Shorter | Larger | Little change | Smaller | Worse |

| Integral action (smaller $T_i$) | Shorter | Larger | Longer | Removed | Worse |

| $T_d$ | Little change | Smaller | Shorter | No change | Better, up to a point |

Figure 1. P-only control of the example plant $G(s)=2e^{-2s}/(10s+1)$. The final value is $KK_p/(1+KK_p)$: 0.50, 0.75 and 0.857 for $K_p=0.5,\,1.5,\,3$, exactly as the formula predicts. At $K_p=K_u=4.25$ the loop oscillates continuously; this is the experiment behind the Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop method.

## 4. Classify the process before you tune

Every tuning rule assumes a process model. Nearly all industrial processes can be described well enough by one of two shapes:

- Self-regulating (FOPDT): “first order plus dead time”, $G(s)=\dfrac{Ke^{-Ls}}{Ts+1}$. After a step in the output the measurement settles to a new value. Temperature, flow, pressure in a vented volume, speed.

- Integrating: $G(s)=\dfrac{K'e^{-Ls}}{s}$. The measurement ramps for as long as the input is nonzero. Tank level with a pump, the position of a motor driven by velocity.

The three FOPDT numbers are the process gain $K$ (change in measurement per change in output), the dead time $L$ (also called delay or $\theta$) and the time constant $T$ (also $\tau$). Dead time is the enemy: no controller can react before the measurement moves, and every extra second of delay lowers the gain you can safely use. The ratio $L/T$ summarises how hard the loop is.

| $L/T$ | Character | What it means for tuning |

| below 0.1 | Lag-dominant | High gain is possible; integral action should be fast; derivative can help; SIMC limits $T_i$ to $4(\tau_c+L)$. |

| 0.1 to 0.5 | Balanced | The “textbook” case. PI is usually enough; PID gives modest gains. |

| 0.5 to 1 | Delay matters | Lower the gain; derivative adds little; expect slower loops. |

| above 1 | Delay-dominant | Use low gain and mostly integral action. Consider dead-time compensation (Smith predictor) or feedforward. |

The example plant used throughout this article is $K=2$ (°C per % of heater output), $L=2$ s, $T=10$ s, so $L/T=0.2$. The numbers are scaled so they are easy to follow; the method is the same for a furnace measured in minutes.

## 5. Measure the process with a step test

A step test (also called a bump test) is the single most valuable half hour you can spend on a loop. It turns guesswork into three numbers.

### Procedure

- Prepare. Put the loop in manual and wait until the measurement is steady. Make sure other loops and operators are not changing the process.

- Step the output by 5–10% of its range. The measurement change should be at least 5–10 times the noise band, but small enough to stay in the linear region and within safety limits.

- Record the measurement and the output at a sample time of about one twentieth of the expected $T$ or faster, until the measurement is flat again (about 4–5 $T$ after the dead time).

- Restore the output and, if you can, repeat in the other direction and at another operating point. A large difference tells you the process is nonlinear.

### Reading K, L and T

The process gain is $K=\Delta y/\Delta u$ in the same units the controller uses. For $L$ and $T$ there are two standard readings.

Figure 2. Simulated step test of the example plant with $\Delta u=10\%$. The tangent at the steepest point cuts the starting value at $t=L$ and the final value at $t=L+T$. The two circles mark 28.3% and 63.2% of the final change.

- Tangent (reaction-curve) method. Draw the tangent at the steepest point. $L$ is where it crosses the initial value; $T$ is the time it takes to rise from there to the final value. It is quick but sensitive to how you draw the line, particularly with noise.

- Two-point method (28.3% and 63.2%). For a first-order response with delay, $y$ reaches 28.3% of its final change at $t_{28}=L+0.333T$ and 63.2% at $t_{63}=L+T$. Subtracting gives $T=1.5\,(t_{63}-t_{28})$ and $L=t_{63}-T$. This is more repeatable than a hand-drawn tangent.

Example 1

### Reading the step test in Figure 2

The heater output is stepped by $\Delta u=10\%$. The temperature rises by $\Delta y=20\,^\circ\text{C}$. It reaches 28.3% of the change (5.7 °C) at $t_{28}=5.3$ s and 63.2% (12.6 °C) at $t_{63}=12.0$ s.

-
$$K=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u}=\frac{20}{10}=2\ ^\circ\text{C}/\%$$

-
$$T=1.5\,(t_{63}-t_{28})=1.5\,(12.0-5.3)=10.05\approx 10\ \text{s}$$

-
$$L=t_{63}-T=12.0-10.05=1.95\approx 2\ \text{s}$$

$K=2$, $L=2$ s, $T=10$ s, so $L/T=0.2$. The tangent construction in Figure 2 gives the same values.

### Integrating processes

If the measurement ramps instead of settling (a tank level), step the output and measure the slope after the dead time. Then $K'=\text{slope}/\Delta u$, and $L$ is the time from the step to the start of the steady ramp. The tuning rules for this case are in section 10.

## 6. Manual tuning: the procedure that always works

When you cannot run a clean step test, or you only need to refine a loop that already runs, tune by trial and error, but in a fixed order.

- Verify the loop first. Is the sensor reading sensible, does the valve move the right way, is the controller direct or reverse acting as required, is the output not already at a limit?

- Remove I and D. Set integral action off ($T_i$ at maximum) and $T_d=0$. Start with a low gain.

- Find the proportional gain. Make setpoint steps of 5–10%. Raise $K_p$ by factors of about 1.5–2 until the response begins to ring, then back off to roughly half. In practice this lands near $0.5K_u$.

- Add integral action. Begin with $T_i\approx T$ (or the time the measurement takes to reach 63% of its change). Shorten it step by step until the offset disappears in an acceptable time. Stop as soon as a slow, rolling overshoot appears.

- Add derivative only if needed. Try $T_d\approx 0.25$–$0.5\,L$, with its filter on. Increase until overshoot is acceptable and the output is not jittery.

- Test properly. Check a setpoint step and a disturbance (a load change or an output bump), at more than one operating point, and watch the controller output as well as the measurement.

| What you see | Probable cause | What to change |

| Fast ringing with short period, grows or persists | $K_p$ too high (or D too high with noise) | Lower $K_p$ by 30–50% |

| Slow rolling oscillation, period several times $T$ | Integral action too strong | Increase $T_i$ (or lower $K_i$) |

| Approaches setpoint very slowly and stops short | Gain too low, little integral action | Raise $K_p$; shorten $T_i$ |

| Large overshoot after a big setpoint change, controller output pinned at a limit | Integral windup | Enable anti-windup (section 13) |

| Output jumps wildly, measurement looks fine | D acting on noise | Filter D, lower $T_d$, or drop D |

| Sawtooth measurement with square-wave output | Valve stiction or backlash | Fix the valve (positioner); do not retune |

Manual tuning is slow for processes with long time constants, because each trial takes minutes or hours. That is when a model-based rule pays off.

## 7. Ziegler–Nichols closed-loop (ultimate gain) method

Published in 1942, this method needs no model. With $T_i$ at maximum and $T_d=0$, raise $K_p$ until the loop oscillates with constant amplitude. The gain at that point is the ultimate gain $K_u$ and the oscillation period is the ultimate period $P_u$. Then read the table.

| Controller | $K_p$ | $T_i$ | $T_d$ |

| P | $0.5K_u$ | – | – |

| PI | $0.45K_u$ | $P_u/1.2$ | – |

| PID | $0.6K_u$ | $P_u/2$ | $P_u/8$ |

| PI, Tyreus–Luyben | $K_u/3.2$ | $2.2P_u$ | – |

| PID, Tyreus–Luyben | $K_u/2.2$ | $2.2P_u$ | $P_u/6.3$ |

The classic rules aim for a quarter-amplitude decay ratio, in which each overshoot is a quarter of the previous one. That is fast but very oscillatory. The Tyreus–Luyben variant (1992) keeps $K_u$ and $P_u$ but is much gentler, and is a better default for chemical processes.

Example 2

### ZN closed-loop on the example plant

For $G(s)=2e^{-2s}/(10s+1)$, the phase reaches $-180^\circ$ at $\omega_u=0.844$ rad/s, where $|G|=0.2352$. So $K_u=1/0.2352=4.25$ and $P_u=2\pi/\omega_u=7.44$ s. (On the real plant you would find these values by experiment, as in Figure 1.)

-
$$K_p=0.6K_u=0.6\times4.25=2.55$$

-
$$T_i=\frac{P_u}{2}=3.72\ \text{s},\qquad T_d=\frac{P_u}{8}=0.93\ \text{s}$$

-
$$K_i=\frac{K_p}{T_i}=0.686\ \text{s}^{-1},\qquad K_d=K_pT_d=2.37$$

PID: $K_p=2.55$, $T_i=3.72$ s, $T_d=0.93$ s. Section 12 shows what this does to the real response: 56% overshoot.

Safety and limits. The experiment drives the process to the edge of stability. Do not run it on a boiler, reactor or anything that cannot tolerate sustained oscillation. It also needs enough phase lag: a pure first-order process with no dead time never reaches $-180^\circ$, so $K_u$ does not exist. On slow processes the test can take hours. The relay method in section 11 is a safer way to get $K_u$ and $P_u$.

## 8. Ziegler–Nichols open-loop (reaction-curve) method

The second ZN method uses the step test of section 5 instead of a stability experiment, and is safer. With $K$, $L$ and $T$ from the recording:

| Controller | $K_p$ | $T_i$ | $T_d$ |

| P | $\dfrac{T}{KL}$ | – | – |

| PI | $\dfrac{0.9\,T}{KL}$ | $3.33\,L$ | – |

| PID | $\dfrac{1.2\,T}{KL}$ | $2L$ | $0.5L$ |

Example 3

### ZN open-loop PID for $K=2,\ L=2\ \text{s},\ T=10\ \text{s}$

-
$$K_p=\frac{1.2\,T}{KL}=\frac{1.2\times10}{2\times2}=3.0$$

-
$$T_i=2L=4\ \text{s},\qquad T_d=0.5L=1\ \text{s}$$

$K_p=3.0$, $T_i=4$ s, $T_d=1$ s. Notice the formula: the gain is inversely proportional to $KL$, so a larger dead time or a larger process gain lowers the controller gain, which is exactly right.

The rule aims for quarter-amplitude decay on moderate-delay processes. It becomes poor when the dead time is very small compared with $T$ (the gain $T/(KL)$ grows without limit) or very large (the loop is then too aggressive).

## 9. Cohen–Coon

Cohen and Coon (1953) refined the step-test rules by adding terms that depend on the ratio $\tau=L/T$, so they cope better with a larger dead time than the ZN open-loop table. They still aim at quarter-amplitude decay. With $\tau=L/T$:

| Controller | $K_p$ | $T_i$ | $T_d$ |

| PI | $\dfrac{1}{K}\dfrac{T}{L}\left(0.9+\dfrac{\tau}{12}\right)$ | $L\,\dfrac{30+3\tau}{9+20\tau}$ | – |

| PID | $\dfrac{1}{K}\dfrac{T}{L}\left(\dfrac43+\dfrac{\tau}{4}\right)$ | $L\,\dfrac{32+6\tau}{13+8\tau}$ | $\dfrac{4L}{11+2\tau}$ |

Example 4

### Cohen–Coon PID for the same plant

Here $\tau=L/T=0.2$ and $T/(KL)=2.5$.

-
$$K_p=2.5\left(\tfrac43+\tfrac{0.2}{4}\right)=2.5\times1.3833=3.46$$

-
$$T_i=2\,\frac{32+1.2}{13+1.6}=4.55\ \text{s},\qquad T_d=\frac{8}{11+0.4}=0.70\ \text{s}$$

$K_p=3.46$, $T_i=4.55$ s, $T_d=0.70$ s. It is the most aggressive of the rules in this article (85% overshoot in section 12), so treat it as a starting point to be detuned.

## 10. IMC, lambda and SIMC: tune by choosing the speed

The earlier rules are fitted to a performance criterion. The internal model control (IMC) idea turns it around: decide how fast you want the closed loop to be and calculate the controller that gives exactly that. Ask for the response $\dfrac{y}{r}=\dfrac{e^{-Ls}}{\tau_cs+1}$, a first-order response with the unavoidable dead time. Approximating the delay as $e^{-Ls}\approx1-Ls$, the controller for a FOPDT process is a PI controller:

$$K_p=\frac{T}{K(\tau_c+L)},\qquad T_i=T \qquad\text{(IMC / lambda, with }\lambda=\tau_c\text{)}$$

Skogestad's SIMC rule (2003) modifies one number. For lag-dominant processes $T_i=T$ makes the loop slow to recover from a load disturbance, so SIMC caps it:

$$T_i=\min\big(T,\ 4(\tau_c+L)\big)$$

The single tuning knob $\tau_c$ is the desired closed-loop time constant. A practical recommendation is $\tau_c=L$: about as fast as the dead time allows. Larger values give smoother, more robust loops; values below $L$ buy little speed and cost a lot of robustness.

Example 5

### SIMC PI for $K=2,\ L=2\ \text{s},\ T=10\ \text{s}$

- With $\tau_c=L=2$ s:
$$K_p=\frac{10}{2\,(2+2)}=1.25,\qquad T_i=\min(10,\ 4\times4)=10\ \text{s}$$

- With $\tau_c=2L=4$ s (smoother):
$$K_p=\frac{10}{2\,(4+2)}=0.833,\qquad T_i=\min(10,\ 24)=10\ \text{s}$$

$K_p=1.25$, $T_i=10$ s for the tight setting; $K_p=0.83$, $T_i=10$ s for the smooth one. Computed exactly, the first has a gain margin of 3.14 and a phase margin of 61°.

### Other process shapes

- Integrating process $K'e^{-Ls}/s$ (tank level): $K_p=\dfrac{1}{K'(\tau_c+L)}$, $T_i=4(\tau_c+L)$.

- Second-order plus delay $\dfrac{Ke^{-Ls}}{(T_1s+1)(T_2s+1)}$: use the series form $K_c=\dfrac{T_1}{K(\tau_c+L)}$, $T_i=\min\big(T_1,4(\tau_c+L)\big)$, $T_d=T_2$ (convert to ideal form with the formulas of section 2).

- Lambda tuning is the same PI rule with $T_i=T$ always. It is popular in the paper and chemical industries because a large $\lambda$ gives smooth, non-interacting loops.

Because the response is specified rather than discovered, SIMC and lambda tuning fit well into a procedure: a model, a speed, a controller. That is why they are a good default.

## 11. Relay auto-tuning

The relay experiment of Åström and Hägglund (1984) finds $K_u$ and $P_u$ without taking the loop to the edge of stability. Replace the controller with a relay that switches the output between $u_0+d$ and $u_0-d$. Most processes then settle into a steady oscillation whose amplitude is limited by $d$. If the measurement oscillates with amplitude $a$, the describing-function approximation gives

$$K_u\approx\frac{4d}{\pi a},\qquad P_u=\text{measured period of the oscillation}$$

Then you apply the Ziegler–Nichols or Tyreus–Luyben table of section 7. This is how most commercial “auto-tune” buttons work.

Example 6

### Auto-tune of an oven

A relay of $d=5\%$ makes the oven temperature oscillate with amplitude $a=1.2\,^\circ\text{C}$ and period $P_u=7.5$ s.

-
$$K_u=\frac{4d}{\pi a}=\frac{4\times5}{\pi\times1.2}=5.31\ \%/^\circ\text{C}$$

- Tyreus–Luyben PI:
$$K_p=\frac{K_u}{3.2}=1.66,\qquad T_i=2.2P_u=16.5\ \text{s}$$

PI: $K_p=1.66\ \%/^\circ\text{C}$, $T_i=16.5$ s.

Practical points: use some hysteresis on the relay so measurement noise does not cause false switching; choose $d$ small enough that the oscillation is harmless but large enough to be clear of noise; and keep in mind that the approximation assumes the process filters out the harmonics of the square wave, which is true for most lag-type processes.

## 12. Head-to-head: the same plant, many rules

Each rule was applied to the plant $2e^{-2s}/(10s+1)$ and simulated: a unit setpoint step at $t=0$, then a load step of $-0.5$ at the process input at $t=70$ s. The D term acts on the measurement with a filter $T_d/10$. “Settling” is the time after which the response stays within 2%; IAE is the integrated absolute error (smaller is better), measured separately for the setpoint step and the load step.

| Rule | $K_p$ | $T_i$ (s) | $T_d$ (s) | Overshoot | Settling (s) | IAE setpoint | IAE load | Gain margin | Phase margin |

| ZN closed-loop PID | 2.55 | 3.72 | 0.93 | 56% | 19.1 | 5.50 | 0.90 | 1.63 | 40° |

| ZN closed-loop PI | 1.91 | 6.20 | – | 44% | 20.8 | 5.40 | 1.62 | 1.92 | 36° |

| ZN open-loop PID | 3.00 | 4.00 | 1.00 | 64% | 19.6 | 5.33 | 0.79 | 1.33 | 39° |

| Cohen–Coon PID | 3.46 | 4.55 | 0.70 | 85% | 24.2 | 6.08 | 0.79 | 1.31 | 27° |

| Tyreus–Luyben PI | 1.33 | 16.4 | – | 0% | 40.2 | 6.08 | 6.05 | 3.06 | 69° |

| Tyreus–Luyben PID | 1.93 | 16.4 | 1.18 | 0% | 13.7 | 4.22 | 4.16 | 1.76 | 75° |

| SIMC PI, $\tau_c=L$ | 1.25 | 10.0 | – | 4% | 12.1 | 4.34 | 3.99 | 3.14 | 61° |

| SIMC PI, $\tau_c=2L$ | 0.83 | 10.0 | – | 0% | 15.7 | 5.99 | 5.99 | 4.71 | 71° |

Figure 3. Closed-loop response of four of the rules on the same plant. The setpoint step is at $t=0$, the load disturbance at $t=70$ s. The orange and purple curves (ZN and Cohen–Coon) are fast but overshoot heavily; the blue and green curves (SIMC) are smooth.

### What the numbers say

- The ZN and Cohen–Coon PID rules reject the load four to five times better (IAE 0.8–0.9 versus 4.0 for SIMC) but overshoot by 56–85% and run with gain margins of 1.3–1.6, so a 30–60% rise in process gain would push them toward instability.

- The load-rejection difference is explained by one number, $K_i=K_p/T_i$. For a response with little overshoot, the area under the error after a load step of size $\Delta d$ is $\text{IAE}\approx\Delta d/K_i$. For SIMC: $K_i=1.25/10=0.125$ so $0.5/0.125=4.0$, matching the simulated 3.99. For ZN PID $K_i=0.686$, predicting 0.73 (the simulated 0.90 is higher because that response oscillates).

- SIMC with $\tau_c=L$ is the best all-rounder here: the fastest settling of every row (12.1 s), a setpoint error area (4.34) close to the best (4.22 for Tyreus–Luyben PID), only 4% overshoot, and a gain margin above 3. Its price is slower disturbance recovery, which you can buy back by choosing a smaller $T_i$ if the margins allow.

- Tyreus–Luyben PI is very slow on this plant because $T_i=16.4$ s exceeds the process time constant; adding D (the PID row) helps the setpoint response but narrows the gain margin to 1.76.

| Situation | Reasonable choice |

| You have a step test and want a smooth, safe loop | SIMC with $\tau_c=L$ (or $2L$ if the process varies) |

| You can only run experiments on the closed loop | Relay test, then Tyreus–Luyben (or ZN detuned) |

| Load disturbances dominate and some overshoot is acceptable | ZN open-loop, then detune $K_p$ by 20–30% |

| Level of a buffer tank | Integrating-process SIMC with a large $\tau_c$, or P-only/low-gain PI |

| Very long dead time ($L/T>1$) | Low-gain PI, then consider Smith predictor or feedforward |

| Process is nonlinear or varies | Tune at the worst operating point; use gain scheduling for the rest |

These results are for one plant. Different $L/T$ values change the picture, which is why you should always check a new tuning by simulation or a careful field test.

## 13. Practical fixes every real loop needs

### Filter the derivative and keep it off the setpoint

A pure derivative has infinite gain at high frequency. Use a first-order filter:

$$D(s)=\frac{K_pT_ds}{1+\dfrac{T_d}{N}s},\qquad N\approx 5\text{ to }20$$

so the high-frequency gain is limited to $K_pN$. Also apply the derivative to the measurement $y$, not the error $e$: a setpoint step then does not cause a huge “derivative kick” on the output. Most commercial controllers do this by default; check yours. If the signal is noisy, a first-order low-pass filter on the measurement is a better cure than a lower $N$.

### Setpoint weighting (two degrees of freedom)

The same $K_p$ that rejects disturbances makes the setpoint response overshoot. Weighting the proportional term of the setpoint, $u=K_p(b\,r-y)+\dots$ with $0If the actuator saturates (valve fully open, heater at 100%) while an error remains, the integral keeps growing. When the error finally reverses, the integral takes a long time to unwind and the measurement overshoots. Two common remedies:

- Clamping (conditional integration): stop integrating while the output is saturated and the error would push it further.

- Back-calculation: feed the saturation difference back into the integrator, $\dot I=K_ie+\dfrac{u_{sat}-u}{T_t}$. A common choice is $T_t\approx T_i$ for PI and $T_t=\sqrt{T_iT_d}$ for PID.

Figure 4. The same SIMC PI controller ($K_p=1.25$, $T_i=10$ s) with the actuator limited to $0\le u\le1$ and a setpoint step to 1.6. Without anti-windup the measurement overshoots by 19% and needs 57 s to settle; with back-calculation ($T_t=T_i$) the overshoot is 0.5% and it settles in 17.5 s.

### Bumpless transfer

When switching from manual to auto (or changing a setpoint source), initialise the integrator so that the output starts from its present value. Otherwise the output jumps and the process is bumped.

### Sample time

Digital controllers sample the measurement every $T_s$. As a rule of thumb, take $T_s$ at most one tenth of the time constant $T$, and no more than about half the dead time when $L$ is small. A zero-order hold also adds about $T_s/2$ of delay, so tune with $L_{eff}=L+T_s/2$. The lesson on digital control covers this in detail.

### When the hardware is the problem

- Stiction and backlash: a sticky valve sticks, then jumps. The result is a limit cycle (sawtooth measurement, square-wave output) that gets worse as you add integral action. Fix the valve or add a positioner; do not retune around it.

- Dead band and resolution: a coarse output (a few percent steps) or low-resolution input forces the loop to hunt. Reduce integral action or add a dead band in the controller.

- Nonlinearity: valve characteristics, pH curves and furnace gains change with the operating point. Tune at the most difficult point, or schedule the gain with the operating point.

- Saturation of your own range: if the output is saturated most of the time, no tuning will help; the loop is mis-sized.

## 14. Typical loop types and where to begin

Use these as qualitative starting points, then refine with a step test; plants differ widely.

| Loop | Typical character | Usual controller | Notes |

| Flow | Fast, small dead time, noisy signal | PI, low gain, no D | Filter the measurement; the valve is often the slowest element. |

| Pressure (gas) | Fast, often nearly integrating | PI, sometimes PID | Fast loops need fast sampling. |

| Level (buffer tank) | Integrating | P or low-gain PI | Averaging level control passes flow changes smoothly to the next unit; do not tune it tight. |

| Temperature | Slow, significant dead time | PI or PID | Large $T$ rewards D; large $L$ rewards patience. |

| Speed (motor) | Lag-dominant, fast | PI | Often inside a current loop; tune inner loops first. |

| Position | Integrating | P, PD or PID | Friction can need a little integral action and anti-windup. |

| pH, composition | Strongly nonlinear, long delay | PI with gain scheduling | Tune where the slope is steepest, then schedule. |

For cascade loops (temperature outer, flow or valve position inner) always tune the inner loop first and make it several times faster than the outer loop.

## 15. How to judge a tuning

Judge the loop with numbers, not by how the trend “feels”.

- Time-domain: overshoot, settling time (±2% or ±5%), peak deviation after a load step, and recovery time.

- Error integrals: IAE $=\int|e|\,dt$, ISE $=\int e^2dt$, ITAE $=\int t|e|\,dt$. Compare tunings on the same test; the lower the better. IAE for a load step is about $\Delta d/K_i$.

- Robustness: gain margin at least 2 (6 dB), phase margin 45–60° and peak sensitivity $M_s$ of 1.4–2. In the comparison table above, only the two SIMC rows and Tyreus–Luyben PI have both a gain margin above 2 and a phase margin above 45°.

- Control effort: look at the standard deviation or total variation of the output. Noise amplified by D shows up here first.

Quick robustness test in the field. Increase $K_p$ by 50% and run a setpoint step. If the loop stays stable and reasonably damped, you have real margin; if it rings badly, back the gain off. (On the example plant the ZN PID has a gain margin of only 1.63, so a 50% increase would leave it on the edge of instability.)

## 16. Troubleshooting guide

| Symptom | Check | Action |

| Loop runs away immediately after switching to auto | Direct/reverse action, sensor scaling, setpoint source | Fix action and scaling; initialise for bumpless transfer |

| Steady oscillation with period near $P_u$ | Is $K_p$ near $K_u$? | Halve $K_p$; verify with a 50% gain test |

| Slow oscillation, a few times $T$ | $T_i$ too small for the dead time | Double $T_i$ (or lower $K_p$ and $T_i$ together) |

| Never reaches setpoint, sits short | No integral action, or output clamped | Enable I; check output limits and mode |

| Reaches setpoint but crawls the last few percent | $T_i$ much too long | Shorten $T_i$ toward $T$ |

| Overshoots only after large moves | Windup | Anti-windup; limit the setpoint rate |

| Output noisy, valve chatters | D on noise, unfiltered measurement | Filter the measurement and D; lower $K_pN$ |

| Good at one load, bad at another | Nonlinear process | Tune at the hardest point or schedule the gain |

| Limit cycle that gets worse with more I | Valve stiction | Repair or add a positioner |

## 17. A repeatable tuning workflow

- Write the specification: tracking or regulation, allowed overshoot, allowed actuator movement.

- Check the hardware and the equation: sensor, valve, direct/reverse, form of the PID block, time units.

- Run a step test (section 5) and read $K$, $L$, $T$; compute $L/T$.

- Choose the rule: SIMC $\tau_c=L$ by default; a relay test if you cannot open the loop; Ziegler–Nichols only as a first guess.

- Convert to the controller's form and units (section 2).

- Add the practical items: D filter, anti-windup, output limits, sample time.

- Test a setpoint step, a disturbance and a 50% gain increase at the relevant operating points.

- Refine and document the final values, the date and the test results, so the next engineer does not start from zero.

## 18. Practice problems

Try each one on paper, then open the answer.

Problem 1

### Form conversion

A series-form controller has $K_c'=2$, $T_i'=10$ s, $T_d'=2$ s. Find the ideal-form values.

Show the answer

$$K_c=2\left(1+\frac{2}{10}\right)=2.4,\qquad T_i=10+2=12\ \text{s},\qquad T_d=\frac{10\times2}{12}=1.67\ \text{s}$$

Problem 2

### Ziegler–Nichols from an experiment

A closed-loop test gives $K_u=6$ and $P_u=4$ s. Find the ZN PID values and the parallel-form gains $K_i$ and $K_d$.

Show the answer

$$K_p=0.6\times6=3.6,\quad T_i=\frac{4}{2}=2\ \text{s},\quad T_d=\frac{4}{8}=0.5\ \text{s},\quad K_i=\frac{3.6}{2}=1.8\ \text{s}^{-1},\quad K_d=3.6\times0.5=1.8\ \text{s}$$

Problem 3

### SIMC for a delay-heavy process

A step test gives $K=0.5$, $L=3$ s, $T=12$ s. Find the SIMC PI values with $\tau_c=L$. What is $L/T$?

Show the answer

$$K_p=\frac{12}{0.5\,(3+3)}=4,\qquad T_i=\min(12,\ 4\times6)=12\ \text{s},\qquad \frac{L}{T}=0.25$$

Problem 4

### Estimating disturbance rejection

A PI loop has $K_p=2$ and $T_i=8$ s, with little overshoot. A load disturbance of 0.4 (in controller-output units) arrives. Estimate the IAE. How does it change if $T_i$ is halved?

Show the answer

$$K_i=\frac{2}{8}=0.25,\qquad \text{IAE}\approx\frac{0.4}{0.25}=1.6;\qquad T_i=4\Rightarrow K_i=0.5,\ \text{IAE}\approx0.8$$

Halving $T_i$ halves the error area, but it also lowers the margins, so check the response.

## Frequently asked questions

What is the fastest reliable way to tune a PID loop?
Run one open-loop step test, read the gain K, dead time L and time constant T from the recording, then apply the SIMC rule $K_p=T/(K(\tau_c+L))$, $T_i=\min(T,4(\tau_c+L))$ with $\tau_c=L$. It needs one experiment, has one knob, and gives a smooth response with a gain margin near 3.

Should I use Ziegler–Nichols?
Use it as a starting point when you have nothing else, and expect 40–80% overshoot and thin stability margins, because it was designed for a quarter-amplitude decay ratio. Most engineers detune it (lower $K_p$, larger $T_i$) or use SIMC or Tyreus–Luyben instead.

Do I always need the D term?
No. Most industrial loops run PI. Derivative action helps lag-dominant processes with clean measurements (temperature, some position and speed loops) and is of little use when dead time dominates or the signal is noisy. If you use it, always filter it.

How do I choose the integral time $T_i$?
For a self-regulating process a good first value is $T_i\approx T$ (the process time constant), limited to $4(\tau_c+L)$ when that is smaller. A $T_i$ that is too short gives slow, rolling oscillation; too long leaves the error hanging around. The load-disturbance error area is about $\Delta d/K_i$ with $K_i=K_p/T_i$.

What sample time should the controller use?
Roughly one tenth of the process time constant or smaller, and no more than about half the dead time when the dead time is small. Sampling adds about $T_s/2$ of extra delay, so slow sampling forces lower gains.

Why does my loop oscillate even with small gains?
Suspect the hardware first: valve stiction, backlash or a dead band produces a limit cycle that no gain setting removes, and a noisy or badly filtered measurement can do the same. Look at the controller output: a sawtooth in the measurement with a square-wave output is the classic sign of stiction.

What is integral windup and how do I stop it?
Windup is the integral term growing while the actuator is saturated, which causes large overshoot afterwards. Stop it with anti-windup: clamp the integrator, or use back-calculation $\dot I=K_ie+(u_{sat}-u)/T_t$. In the simulation in this guide, back-calculation cut the overshoot from 19% to 0.5%.

How can I tell whether a tuning is robust enough?
Aim for a gain margin of at least 2, a phase margin of 45–60° and a peak sensitivity $M_s$ of 1.4–2. A quick field check is to raise $K_p$ by 50% (or let the process gain double) and confirm that the response stays damped.

# How to Calculate the Size of a Power Factor Correction Capacitor (kvar) with an Example

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/power-factor-correction-capacitor-calculation/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: The formula Qc = P(tan φ1 − tan φ2) with a 100 kW, 400 V load corrected from PF 0.75 to 0.95 giving 55.3 kvar, microfarads per phase, a multiplier table and cautions about harmonics.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Power Factor Correction

# How to Calculate the Size of a Power Factor Correction Capacitor (kvar) with an Example

Correcting the PF means installing capacitors that supply the reactive power (kvar) to inductive loads, instead of drawing it from the grid. The size you need follows from a single formula and can be checked with the power triangle.

30-second summary

- $Q_c=P\,(\tan\varphi_1-\tan\varphi_2)$, where $\varphi_1$ is the angle before correction and $\varphi_2$ the target angle

- Real power P does not change; what falls is Q and S, so the current falls

- Choose the nearest standard size, and check harmonics before installing

## Where the formula comes from

From the power triangle, $Q=P\tan\varphi$. Before correction the load has $Q_1=P\tan\varphi_1$; after correction we want $Q_2=P\tan\varphi_2$. The capacitor must supply the difference.

$$Q_c=Q_1-Q_2=P\,(\tan\varphi_1-\tan\varphi_2),\qquad \varphi=\cos^{-1}(\text{PF})$$

Then find the capacitance per phase from $Q_c=3\,\omega C V^2$ for a delta connection, where $V$ is the line voltage and $\omega=2\pi f$.

## Example: a 100 kW, 400 V three-phase load, PF 0.75 → 0.95

- Find the angles and tangents before and after

$$\tan\varphi_1=\tan\!\big(\cos^{-1}0.75\big)=0.8819,\qquad \tan\varphi_2=\tan\!\big(\cos^{-1}0.95\big)=0.3287$$

- The reactive power to compensate

$$Q_c=100\times(0.8819-0.3287)\approx55.3\ \text{kvar}$$

- Line current before and after correction ($I=\dfrac{P}{\sqrt{3}\,V\,\text{PF}}$)

$$I_1=\frac{100000}{\sqrt{3}\,(400)(0.75)}\approx192.5\ \text{A},\qquad I_2=\frac{100000}{\sqrt{3}\,(400)(0.95)}\approx151.9\ \text{A}$$

- Capacitance per phase for a delta connection at 50 Hz

$$C=\frac{Q_c}{3\,\omega V^2}=\frac{55323}{3\,(2\pi\cdot50)(400)^2}\approx367\ \mu\text{F}$$

About 55.3 kvar of capacitors is needed. Choose the next standard size up, for example 60 kvar in several switched steps. The line current falls from 192.5 A to 151.9 A (about 21 % lower). If connected in wye, the capacitance per phase would be three times larger, about 1,101 µF.

## Multiplier table: Qc = P × k for a target PF of 0.95

Multiply the real power in kW by $k=\tan\varphi_1-\tan\varphi_2$ to get kvar directly.

| Original PF | $k$ | Example P = 100 kW |

| 0.70 | 0.692 | 69.2 kvar |

| 0.75 | 0.553 | 55.3 kvar |

| 0.80 | 0.421 | 42.1 kvar |

| 0.85 | 0.291 | 29.1 kvar |

| 0.90 | 0.156 | 15.6 kvar |

## Cautions before installing

- Use the measured P, not the motor nameplate power, because at light load the PF is lower and P is below the rating.

- Do not over-correct. If the capacitor is larger than the load's Q at light load, you get a leading PF and a higher voltage. Use an automatic bank that switches in steps.

- Harmonics: resonance between the capacitors and the system inductance can amplify harmonic currents. Measure THD, and choose a detuned type with reactors when there are many electronic loads.

- Voltage rating: choose capacitors with a voltage rating comfortably above the system voltage, as the manufacturer recommends.

## Frequently asked questions

What power factor should I correct to?
A common target is 0.95 or above, because it allows for light-load periods when a motor's PF drops, and it stops short of 1.0, which needs a lot more capacitance for only a small further reduction in current. An automatic installation that switches steps with the load prevents over-compensation into a leading PF.

Should capacitors be connected in delta or wye?
For the same kvar, a delta connection needs one third of the capacitance per phase of a wye connection (because the voltage across each unit is $\sqrt{3}$ times higher). Low-voltage capacitor banks are usually connected in delta.

What should I watch for after installing capacitors?
If the system has a lot of harmonics, the capacitors may resonate with the transformer inductance and amplify harmonic currents. Measure THD before installing, and use a capacitor bank in series with reactors (detuned) when necessary.

Which part of the electricity bill do capacitors reduce?
They reduce the PF penalty on the bill under the utility's criteria, and they reduce current in cables and transformers, which lowers losses. They do not reduce the kWh the load actually uses.

# What Is Power Factor? The cos φ Formula and the Relationship between kW, kVA and kvar

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/en/blog/power-factor-explained/
Updated: 2026-10-16
Summary: Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power. See the P Q S power triangle, a worked current calculation at PF 0.8 versus 1.0, lagging versus leading PF, and the effect of harmonics.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish
// Article · Power Factor

# What Is Power Factor? The cos φ Formula and the Relationship between kW, kVA and kvar

Power factor tells you how much of the electrical power supplied to a load is turned into real work. A low value means the cables and transformers carry current that does no work. This article explains it with the power triangle and numeric examples.

30-second summary

- $\text{PF}=\dfrac{P}{S}=\cos\varphi$ when voltage and current are sinusoidal

- P = real power (kW) · Q = reactive power (kvar) · S = apparent power (kVA), and $S^2=P^2+Q^2$

- Same real power but a low PF ⇒ the current rises by a factor of $1/\text{PF}$

## What is power factor

In an AC circuit, voltage and current do not necessarily rise and fall together. If they are out of phase by an angle $\varphi$, the power converted to real work is only a fraction of $V\times I$.

$$P = V I \cos\varphi, \qquad S = V I, \qquad \text{PF} = \frac{P}{S} = \cos\varphi$$

Here $V$ and $I$ are RMS values. A purely resistive load (a heater, an incandescent lamp) has $\varphi=0$ and PF = 1. Induction motors, transformers and iron-core ballasts contain coils, which make the current lag the voltage, so their PF is below 1.

## The P Q S power triangle

The three kinds of power are related as a right triangle.

| Power | Symbol · unit | Meaning | Formula |

| Real power | $P$ · W, kW | Power converted to work, heat, light or torque | $VI\cos\varphi$ |

| Reactive power | $Q$ · var, kvar | Power that shuttles back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric field in the load | $VI\sin\varphi$ |

| Apparent power | $S$ · VA, kVA | The burden that cables, transformers and generators must support | $VI=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$ |

For a balanced three-phase system, using line voltage and line current, $P=\sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L\cos\varphi$ and $S=\sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L$.

## Example: a 230 V, 10 A load with a lagging PF of 0.8

- Apparent power and real power

$$S=VI=230\times10=2300\ \text{VA},\qquad P=S\cos\varphi=2300\times0.8=1840\ \text{W}$$

- Reactive power from the power triangle

$$Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}=\sqrt{2300^2-1840^2}=1380\ \text{var}$$

- If the PF is corrected to 1.0 with the same real power, the current needed is

$$I'=\frac{P}{V}=\frac{1840}{230}=8\ \text{A}$$

- Compare the line loss $\propto I^2$

$$\left(\frac{10}{8}\right)^2=1.5625$$

At PF 0.8 the load draws 10 A, but at PF 1.0 only 8 A for the same 1840 W of work. The current differs by 25 % and the line loss is about 56 % higher (2300 : 1840 : 1380 is a 5 : 4 : 3 triangle).

## Lagging and leading PF

- Lagging: the current lags the voltage. Inductive loads (motors, transformers), which make up most of a factory's load.

- Leading: the current leads the voltage. Capacitive loads, or PF-correction capacitors installed beyond what is needed. A long unloaded cable has a similar effect.

A PF value alone does not say whether it is lagging or leading, so state it explicitly, for example "0.8 lagging".

## With harmonics: the true PF is lower than cos φ

Electronic loads such as switching power supplies and rectifiers draw non-sinusoidal current, which lowers the true PF even when the fundamental current is in phase with the voltage.

$$\text{PF}_{true}=\underbrace{\cos\varphi_1}_{\text{displacement}}\times\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\text{THD}_I^2}}$$

Example: $\cos\varphi_1=1$ and $\text{THD}_I=30\,\%$ give $\text{PF}_{true}=1/\sqrt{1.09}\approx0.958$. Installing PF-correction capacitors alone is therefore not enough, and may cause resonance with the harmonics, so THD must be considered as well.

## Frequently asked questions

What is a good power factor?
The closer to 1.0 the better. In Thai practice, customers in tariff classes that carry a penalty usually correct the PF to above 0.85 under the utility's criterion, and design for about 0.95 to allow for light-load periods. See the power factor and electricity bill page for the criteria.

What is the difference between lagging and leading PF?
Lagging means the current lags the voltage, caused by inductive loads such as motors and transformers. Leading means the current leads the voltage, caused by capacitive loads or by too many capacitors installed.

What harm does a low PF cause?
More current is needed for the same real power, so cables, transformers and breakers carry a heavier load, line losses ($I^2R$) and voltage drop increase, and some customer classes must pay a penalty.

How does true PF differ from cos φ?
cos φ is only the displacement PF of the fundamental frequency. If the current is distorted by harmonics, the true PF is $\text{PF}=\cos\varphi_1/\sqrt{1+\text{THD}_I^2}$, which is lower than cos φ.
