## Frequently asked questions

Which motors can be star–delta started?
Only motors whose delta voltage on the nameplate equals the supply line voltage. On a 400 V system that is a motor marked 400/690 V Δ/Y (usually 4 kW and above). A 230/400 V Δ/Y motor must run in star on 400 V and cannot be star–delta started.

Can the same equipment be used in Thailand and its neighbours?
In practice yes. Every country covered here uses 50 Hz three-phase four-wire systems with line voltages of 380–415 V (IEC 60038 nominal 230/400 V), so equipment rated 380–415 V 50 Hz fits all of them. Always measure the actual site voltage and check the local utility's rules.

What is the overload setting for a star–delta starter?
When the overload relay sits after the main contactor in the phase-current path (the most common arrangement) set it to 0.58 × the motor In, e.g. 8.5 A for a 14.6 A motor. If it sits in the line-current path before the split, set it to In.

When should I use a VFD instead of star–delta?
When you need variable speed, a soft start with high torque, energy savings on pumps and fans that often run below full flow (P ∝ n³), or when the starting voltage dip is a problem. If you only need to reduce the starting current of a light load at fixed speed, star–delta or a soft starter is cheaper.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# Applied Motor Control Circuits in Practice: Sequence Starting, Float-Switch Pumps, Pump Alternation, Pressure-Switch Compressors, Two-Speed Motors and Phase Protection Relays

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/applied-circuits/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: Contactor circuits used in real buildings and factories: timed sequence starting of conveyors, automatic water pumps with float switches or electrodes, Hand-Off-Auto selector switches, duty/standby pump alternation, air compressors with pressure switches, Dahlander two-speed motors, phase-failure, phase-reversal and voltage relays, and the formula for a pump's starts per hour.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.10 · AC Motor Control · Applied Circuits

# Applied Motor Control Circuits in Practice: Sequence Starting, Float-Switch Pumps, Pump Alternation, Pressure-Switch Compressors, Two-Speed Motors and Phase Protection Relays

Once you understand self-holding, interlocking and timers, almost every circuit in buildings and factories is just these three ideas combined with sensors. This page collects the circuits electricians meet most often, with the reason behind each point in the circuit.

In 30 seconds

- Sequence starting: a contact of the previous motor is placed in series in the circuit of the next one

- Float-switch pump: the differential between the on and off levels sets the number of starts, $N_{max} = Q_p/(4V)$

- Every position of Hand-Off-Auto must pass through the protective devices

- A phase protection relay pays off most on unstable supplies: it guards against phase loss, phase reversal and under/overvoltage

## Sequence starting (cascaded conveyors) Basic

Conveyors that feed one another must start from the discharge end back towards the feed end, and stop from the feed end towards the discharge end; otherwise material piles up on a stopped conveyor. The circuit uses an NO contact of the previous contactor (K1) in series in the circuit of the next (K2), plus a timer so that the next one starts by itself once the previous one has run for the set time — which also spreads out the starting currents so they do not occur together.

Figure 1 · K2 can pull in only while K1 is energised and timer K3T has timed out. If K1 stops or trips, K2 stops immediately (F2 and F4 are in series in the common path)

A1 Sequence interlock

$$K2 = K1 \cdot T_{K3T} \cdot \overline{S0} \qquad K1 = \overline{S0}\,(S1 + K1)$$

## Automatic water pump with a float switch and Hand-Off-Auto Basic

Figure 2 · The three-position selector switch has two contact sets: H feeds the coil directly, A feeds it through the float switch; both still pass through the overload

A tethered (cable) float switch changes state when it tilts up or down, so the differential between the on and off levels is set by the length of free cable. Systems that need a wide differential use two floats (upper and lower level) with a self-holding circuit, or an electrode-type level relay (e.g. probes E1 E2 E3) with built-in latching.

A2 Maximum starts per hour

$$t_{cycle} = \frac{V}{Q_p - q} + \frac{V}{q} \;\ge\; \frac{4V}{Q_p}\ \ (q = Q_p/2) \qquad N_{max} = \frac{Q_p}{4V}$$

Example A-1

### 18 m³/h pump, 5.5 kW motor, at most 10 starts per hour allowed

- A2: $V \ge Q_p/(4N) = 18/(4 \times 10) = 0.45$ m³ between the on and off levels

- Tank cross-section 1.5 m² → level differential $0.45/1.5 = 0.30$ m

- If a single float gives a differential of only 0.1 m, the pump could start up to 30 times per hour when demand is half the pump rate — a two-level float arrangement is needed

## Duty/standby pump alternation Intermediate

Building water supplies and pumping stations often have two pumps (duty/standby) that alternate each time a run command is given, so that running hours stay equal and the standby pump is always ready. The simplest way is an alternating relay, which swaps its output contact each time the run signal disappears. Worthwhile additions:

- High-high water level: call the second pump to assist (duty-assist)

- If the duty pump trips (F2 97-98 closes), the standby pump takes over automatically and an alarm is raised

- A separate hour meter for each pump, for maintenance planning

A3 Equal running hours

$$h_1 \approx h_2 \approx \frac{h_{total}}{2} \qquad \text{the standby pump must run at least every 1–2 weeks}$$

## Air compressor with a pressure switch Intermediate

A pressure switch has an NC contact that opens when the pressure reaches the cut-out value and closes when the pressure falls to the cut-in value; it is wired in series with the coil in the Auto position. A reciprocating compressor must start unloaded, so it has an unloader valve that vents the cylinder head when stopping. With star–delta starting it is even more important to check that the unloader works, because torque in star is low.

A4 Receiver size for compressor cycling

$$t_{off} = \frac{V_{tank}\,\Delta p}{p_0\,q_{use}} \qquad t_{on} = \frac{V_{tank}\,\Delta p}{p_0\,(Q_c - q_{use})}$$

$p_0$ = atmospheric pressure (absolute), Δp = pressure-switch differential · Fit an anti-short-cycle timer of 1–3 minutes after stopping to prevent the motor from starting more often than allowed.

## Dahlander two-speed motors Advanced

A Dahlander motor has a single winding that can be connected two ways, giving pole numbers in a 2:1 ratio, e.g. 4/2 poles (1500/3000 rpm). Low speed is connected in Δ and high speed in YY (two halves in parallel, connected in star). Three contactors are used: K1 (low) and K2+K3 (high: K2 supplies power, K3 shorts the star point). Low and high are interlocked in the same way as a reversing circuit, and it is common practice always to start at low speed first.

A5 Pole-changing speeds

$$n_{s,low} = \frac{120f}{2p} \qquad n_{s,high} = \frac{120f}{p} = 2\,n_{s,low}$$

Fans and pumps use the “variable torque” type (Y/YY); machinery uses the “constant torque” (Δ/YY) or “constant power” type. The nameplate states the type and the terminals (1U 1V 1W for low speed, 2U 2V 2W for high speed). A separate overload is needed for each speed because the rated currents differ.

## Phase and voltage protection relays Basic

A phase monitoring relay measures all three phases and has an output contact wired in series in the control circuit, dropping out the contactor on:

| Fault | Result without a relay | Typical setting |

| Phase loss | Motor runs on two phases at ~1.7 × current, overheats and burns out; cannot restart | Instant detection |

| Phase reversal | Pump or compressor runs backwards and is damaged; lifts/hoists become dangerous | Checked at power-up |

| Under/overvoltage | Insufficient torque, high current, or stressed insulation | ±10–15 %, delay 2–10 s |

| Unbalance | Rotor overheating (see S4–S5) | 5–10 % |

Automatic restart after a power failure: a circuit using a float switch or pressure switch in Auto mode will start by itself when power returns. That is acceptable for a water pump but not for a machine with people working near it. Assess the risk according to IEC 60204-1 and fit a warning sign “May start automatically without warning” on the machine. Where a building has several motors, give them different restart delays so their starting currents do not add up when power returns.

## Frequently asked questions

Why does a float-switch pump keep switching on and off rapidly?
The distance between the float's on and off levels (the differential) is too small for the flow rate. Use formula A2 to find the volume needed between the two levels, or use a two-level float or two-level electrodes. A pump that starts more often than allowed overheats and wears out its contactor quickly.

How does Hand-Off-Auto differ from Local-Remote?
Hand-Off-Auto selects whether the motor runs by hand (bypassing the automatic system), stops, or is commanded by an automatic device (a float switch or PLC). Local-Remote selects where commands come from, such as the push-buttons at the machine or the control room. Neither may bypass the protective devices or the emergency stop.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

The distance between the float's on and off levels (the differential) is too small for the flow rate. Use formula A2 to find the volume needed between the two levels, or use a two-level float or two-level electrodes. A pump that starts more often than allowed overheats and wears out its contactor quickly.

**How does Hand-Off-Auto differ from Local-Remote?**
Hand-Off-Auto selects whether the motor runs by hand (bypassing the automatic system), stops, or is commanded by an automatic device (a float switch or PLC). Local-Remote selects where commands come from, such as the push-buttons at the machine or the control room. Neither may bypass the protective devices or the emergency stop.

---

# Magnetic Contactors, Overload Relays, Motor Protection Breakers and Control Devices: AC-3, Trip Classes, Timers, Push-Buttons and Pilot Lights

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/control-devices/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: Every device in a motor control panel: how a magnetic contactor is built (coil, main and auxiliary contacts), utilization categories AC-1, AC-3, AC-3e and AC-4 to IEC 60947-4-1, a kW-at-400 V sizing table, overload relays and trip classes 10, 20 and 30, motor protection circuit breakers (MPCB), aM fuses, Type 1 and Type 2 coordination, timers, push-button and pilot-light colours to IEC 60204-1, and control transformers.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.4 · AC Motor Control · Contactors & Overloads

# Magnetic Contactors, Overload Relays, Motor Protection Breakers and Control Devices: AC-3, Trip Classes, Timers, Push-Buttons and Pilot Lights

Every motor circuit is built from the same set of devices: a short-circuit protective device, a switching device, an overload protective device and the command devices. This page explains how each one works, what the ratings printed on it mean, and how to choose it so that it lasts on a 400 V 50 Hz system.

In 30 seconds

- Order of duties: short circuit (MPCB/MCCB/fuse) → switching (contactor) → overload (overload relay)

- Choose a contactor by its AC-3 rating at 400 V ≥ motor current, not by its AC-1 current

- Set the overload to the motor In (star–delta: 0.58 In) · class 10 in general · 20/30 for high-inertia loads

- Type 2: after a short circuit the contactor can still be used (light, easily separated contact welding is allowed)

## The magnetic contactor Basic

A contactor is an electromagnetically operated switch. When the coil (A1–A2) is energised, the iron core pulls in the armature, which is fixed to the contact bridge. The main contacts (NO) close the power circuit, while the auxiliary NO contacts close and the NC contacts open. When the coil is de-energised, a spring pushes everything back. The advantages: the 400 V power circuit is separated from the control circuit, it can switch millions of times, and it can be commanded remotely or from a PLC.

Figure 1 · The coil is wound on the centre leg of the E-shaped core; the shading rings sit on the outer legs because AC flux passes through zero 100 times a second — if a ring cracks the contactor buzzes and chatters.

Figure 2 · Standard IEC 60947 terminal numbers: main contacts odd on the line side, even on the load side, coil A1 (top) A2 (bottom); auxiliary contacts use two digits — the tens digit is the position, the units digit the function (1-2 NC · 3-4 NO · 5-6 / 7-8 special function, e.g. timed) — NEMA uses L1 L2 L3 → T1 T2 T3 instead.

### The coil: AC or DC

- AC coil (e.g. 230 VAC 50 Hz): at pick-up it draws an inrush current 6–10 times its holding current, because the air gap is large and the impedance is low

- DC coil (e.g. 24 VDC): silent, constant current, suits transistor PLC outputs; it needs a diode or varistor across it to limit the voltage spike at switch-off

- Coil voltage range to IEC 60947-4-1: picks up reliably at 85–110 % Uc and drops out at 20–75 % Uc (AC) — a deep momentary voltage dip can stop a whole production line

D1 Coil operating range

$$0.85\,U_c \le U_{pick\text{-}up} \le 1.1\,U_c \qquad U_{drop\text{-}out} \approx (0.2\text{–}0.75)\,U_c$$

## Utilization categories AC-1, AC-3, AC-4 Intermediate

How hard it is to break a circuit depends on the current that has to be interrupted, so IEC 60947-4-1 rates contactors by utilization category. One and the same contactor has a different rating in each category.

| Category | Application | What the contacts must do |

| AC-1 | Resistive loads, heaters (cos φ ≥ 0.95) | Make and break rated current — the easiest duty, the highest current rating |

| AC-2 | Wound-rotor (slip-ring) motors | Make 2.5 Ie, break 2.5 Ie |

| AC-3 | Squirrel-cage motors: starting, and switching off while running | Make the starting current ~8 Ie but break only the running current ~1 Ie |

| AC-3e | High-efficiency IE3/IE4 motors | As AC-3 but withstands a higher inrush current |

| AC-4 | Inching (jogging) and plugging (reversing while running) | Frequently break the starting current ~6–8 Ie — the heaviest duty |

| AC-15 / DC-13 | Auxiliary contacts switching AC / DC coils | Break small electromagnetic loads |

D2 Contactor selection

$$I_e(\text{AC-3},\,400\ \text{V}) \ge I_n \qquad \text{for AC-4 duty derate to about } 0.3\text{–}0.5\,I_e(\text{AC-3})$$

AC-3 contactor sizes at 400 V and approximate motor power (typical catalogue values)

| Ie AC-3 (A) | 9 | 12 | 18 | 25 | 32 | 38–40 | 50 | 65 | 80 | 95 | 115 | 150 |

| kW at 400 V | 4 | 5.5 | 7.5 | 11 | 15 | 18.5 | 22 | 30 | 37 | 45 | 55 | 75 |

## Overload relays and trip classes Intermediate

An overload relay models the heating of the motor winding. A thermal (bimetal) relay uses strips of two different metals that bend as current flows through a heater; an electronic relay measures current with CTs and calculates. When the threshold is reached, contact 95–96 (NC) opens to de-energise the contactor coil and 97–98 (NO) closes to signal an alarm. The overload relay does not break the power circuit itself — it tells the contactor to break it.

Figure 3 · Trip time falls as current rises. The class gives the maximum trip time at 7.2 times the setting (roughly the starting current) — loads with a long run-up need a higher class.

D3 Overload setting

$$I_r = I_n \;(\text{DOL, reversing, soft starter}) \qquad I_r = \frac{I_n}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.58\,I_n \;(\text{star–delta, in the phase-current path})$$

D4 Trip class check

$$t_{trip}(7.2\,I_r) \le \text{class [s]} \qquad t_{start}

| Class | Trip time at 7.2 Ir | Suitable for |

| 10A | 2–10 s | Submersible pump motors, hermetic compressors with poor cooling |

| 10 | 4–10 s | General duty: pumps, small fans, conveyors (run-up < 5 s) |

| 20 | 6–20 s | Large fans, mixers, crushers (run-up 5–10 s) |

| 30 | 9–30 s | Very high-inertia loads: grinding mills, centrifuges |

Features worth having: ambient temperature compensation (−20…+60 °C), phase-loss sensitivity (differential), manual/automatic reset (use manual for general duty so that the machine does not restart by itself after a trip), and a test button.

## Short-circuit protection: MPCB, MCCB, fuses Intermediate

A short-circuit current of several thousand amperes must be cleared within a few milliseconds. The device doing this must have a breaking capacity no lower than the prospective short-circuit current at the point of installation, and it must not trip falsely during starting.

D5 Breaking capacity

$$I_{cu} \ge I_{k,max}\ \text{at the point of installation} \qquad I_{k} \approx \frac{S_{tr}}{\sqrt3\,V_L\,u_k} \;(\text{at the transformer terminals})$$

D6 No nuisance trip at start

$$I_{m} > (1.5\text{–}2)\,I_{st} \approx (10\text{–}13)\,I_n \qquad (\text{allowing for the asymmetric first half-cycle inrush})$$

| Device | Advantages | Things to know |

| MPCB (e.g. 13–18 A range) | Short-circuit + overload + isolation in one device, adjustable, auxiliary contact signals a trip | Magnetic trip fixed at ~13 × the top of the range · Icu varies by model |

| Motor-type MCCB (magnetic only) | High breaking capacity, used for large motors | Needs a separate overload relay |

| aM fuse | Very good current limiting, withstands starting current | Short-circuit protection only, needs an overload relay · replace all three phases |

| gG fuse | General purpose | Must be a larger size to withstand the starting current |

### Type 1 and Type 2 coordination (IEC 60947-4-1)

Type 1: under a short circuit there is no danger to people or the enclosure, but the contactor and overload relay may be damaged and need replacing · Type 2: after a short circuit the devices remain usable; light contact welding that is easily separated is allowed. Where the line must be back in production quickly, use Type 2, which manufacturers test as a set and publish as coordination tables — use one manufacturer's table for the whole combination.

## Timers and auxiliary relays Basic

- On-delay: coil energised → time runs → contacts change state · coil de-energised → reset immediately — used in star–delta starters and sequential starting

- Off-delay: coil energised → contacts change immediately · coil de-energised → they hold for a set time — used for cooling fans that run on after the machine stops

- Dedicated star–delta timer: separate Y and Δ contacts with a fixed built-in dead time of ~50–100 ms — recommended over a general-purpose timer

- Common terminal numbers: common 15 · delayed NC 16 · delayed NO 18 (or 55-56 / 67-68 on add-on blocks)

## Push-buttons and pilot lights (IEC 60204-1) Basic

| Device | Colour to IEC 60204-1 | Notes |

| START / ON | White (preferred), grey, black, green | Never red |

| STOP / OFF | Black (preferred), grey, white · red allowed | Never green · avoid red if near an E-stop |

| Emergency stop | Red on a yellow background, mushroom head, latching | Contacts with positive opening operation |

| Red light | Emergency, hazardous condition | Immediate action required |

| Yellow light | Abnormal, approaching a critical condition (e.g. tripped) | Investigate |

| Blue light | Action required (e.g. waiting for reset) | — |

| Green light | Normal condition | — |

| White light | Neutral status (e.g. supply on) | — |

Many factories in the region still follow the old convention of green = “motor running” and red = “power available/stopped”. Follow the plant's own standard consistently, and state the meaning on a label on the panel door.

## Control circuit supply Intermediate

Small panels often use 230 VAC taken from L–N through a fuse. IEC 60204-1 requires machine control circuits to be fed through a transformer with separate windings (except for a machine with a single motor starter and no more than two control devices), to lower the voltage and limit the effect of an earth fault. Systems with a PLC usually use 24 VDC from a power supply.

D7 Control transformer sizing

$$S_{tr} \ge \sum S_{hold} + S_{inrush,\,max} \qquad \text{check voltage dip at pick-up} \le 5\text{–}10\,\%$$

Example D-1

### Select the devices for a 7.5 kW 400 V 14.6 A motor, direct-on-line

- D2: AC-3 contactor ≥ 14.6 A → 18 A (rated 7.5 kW at 400 V)

- MPCB 13–18 A range, set Ir = 14.6 A (D3), class 10 · magnetic trip about 13 × 18 = 234 A > peak inrush ~ 2 × 95 = 190 A (D6)

- D5: if a 1000 kVA, uk 6 % transformer is close by, $I_k \approx 1000/(\sqrt3 \times 0.4 \times 0.06) = 24$ kA → use an MPCB model with Icu ≥ 25 kA, or an upstream limiter/fuse according to the manufacturer's table

- D7: three contactors, each holding 8 VA and pulling in at 70 VA → $S \ge 3(8) + 70 = 94$ VA → a 100 VA transformer

## Symbols for all these devices

Figure 4 · The IEC 60617 symbols used in every diagram in this series. How to read drawings in detail is covered in Symbols · Reading diagrams. · NEMA symbols are on the symbols and diagram-reading page

## Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a contactor and a relay?
The principle is the same: a coil pulls in the contacts. A contactor, however, has main contacts designed to break motor current, arc chutes, and ratings by utilization category such as AC-3. A control relay switches small currents in the control circuit (AC-15/DC-13) and is not used to switch a motor directly.

Can an MPCB replace an overload relay?
Yes. An MPCB (motor protection circuit breaker) combines an adjustable thermal overload element and a magnetic short-circuit trip in one device, so it is used with a contactor without a separate overload relay. The exception is a star–delta starter, where the protective device must sit in the phase-current path.

Does the START button have to be green?
IEC 60204-1 allows START/ON buttons in white, grey, black or green, recommends white, and forbids red. STOP/OFF buttons are black, grey or white (black preferred); red is allowed but should not be placed near an emergency-stop button. The emergency stop itself must be red on a yellow background. In practice, panels in Thailand and the region often use a green START and a red STOP, which is still within the accepted range.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# Motor Circuit Design and Installation: Device Selection, Cable Size, Starting Voltage Drop, Control Panels, Testing and a Troubleshooting Table

Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: A 10-step motor circuit design procedure for 400 V 50 Hz systems: deriving power from the load, choosing the motor and starting method, contactor, overload relay, circuit-breaker and breaking capacity, cable size by current and voltage drop (EIT wiring code of Thailand and IEC 60364), earth-fault current at the cable end, IEC 61439 control panels, IP ratings, panel heat and fans, insulation resistance testing, commissioning, maintenance, and a table of fault symptoms with causes.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.13 · AC Motor Control · Design, Installation & Troubleshooting

# Motor Circuit Design and Installation: Device Selection, Cable Size, Starting Voltage Drop, Control Panels, Testing and a Troubleshooting Table

This page brings every previous chapter together into one design job, from the load to commissioning, with what to check on site and a troubleshooting table compiled from the most common symptoms. Every number in the examples can be calculated from the formulas on the page.

In 30 seconds

- Design in order: load → motor → starting method → devices → cable → panel → test

- The cable must pass three checks: current rating, voltage drop (running ≤ 3–5 %, starting ≤ 10–15 %) and earth-fault current at the cable end

- Panel heat: $\Delta T = P/(kA)$ — a drive almost always means a fan is needed

- Before energising: megger ≥ 1 MΩ, check tightness, check phase sequence, test the control circuit on its own

## The 10-step design procedure Basic

Figure 1 · The sequence can loop back — for example, a high starting voltage drop (step 7) may force a change of starting method (step 3)

K1 Shaft power of a pump or a drive

$$P_{pump} = \frac{\rho g Q H}{\eta_p} \qquad P = T\,\omega = \frac{T\,n}{9550}\ \text{(kW)}$$

K2 Motor size margin

$$P_{motor} \ge (1.10\text{–}1.15)\,P_{load,max} \;\rightarrow\; \text{next standard size}$$

## Cable size, voltage drop and fault current at the cable end Intermediate

K3 Cable ampacity after derating

$$I_z\,k_{temp}\,k_{group} \ge I_n \qquad I_z \ge I_r\ (\text{overload protection setting})$$

K4 Running voltage drop

$$\Delta V\% = \frac{\sqrt3\,I_n\,L\,(R\cos\varphi + X\sin\varphi)}{V_L}\times100 \le 3\text{–}5\,\% \qquad R = \frac{\rho}{A},\ \rho_{Cu,70^\circ C} \approx 0.0225\ \Omega\,\text{mm}^2/\text{m}$$

K5 Starting voltage drop

$$\Delta V_{st}\% \approx \Delta V_{tr}\% + \frac{\sqrt3\,I_{st}\,L\,(R\cdot0.3 + X\cdot0.95)}{V_L}\times100 \le 10\text{–}15\,\%$$

K6 Earth fault at the cable end (TN system)

$$I_{f} = \frac{U_0}{Z_s} \ge I_a \qquad Z_s \approx Z_{src} + (1 + m)\,\frac{\rho L}{A_{ph}}\ \ (m = A_{ph}/A_{PE})$$

$U_0$ = 230 V · $I_a$ = the current that makes the protective device disconnect within the time required by the standard (for fixed motor circuits in a TN system usually 5 s; use the magnetic trip value of the MPCB/breaker for instantaneous disconnection). Take Ik and disconnection times from the installation standard that applies in the country concerned.

Example K-1

### A 15 kW 4-pole 400 V pump 50 m from the panel, 315 kVA transformer with uk 4 %, direct-on-line start

- M6: $I_n = 15{,}000/(\sqrt3 \times 400 \times 0.921 \times 0.84) = 28.0$ A · $I_{st} = 7 \times 28 = 196$ A

- L2 (at the transformer): $S_{sc} = 315/0.04 = 7.9$ MVA · $S_{st} = \sqrt3(400)(196) = 136$ kVA → $\Delta U \approx 1.7\,\%$

- K3: 6 mm² cable $I_z \approx 36$ A × 0.87 = 31.3 A ≥ 28 A ✓

- K4: $R = 0.0225/6 = 3.75$ mΩ/m → $\Delta V = \sqrt3(28)(50)(0.00375 \times 0.84 + 0.00008 \times 0.54) = 7.7$ V = 1.9 % ✓

- K5: $\sqrt3(196)(50)(0.00375 \times 0.3 + 0.00008 \times 0.95) = 20.4$ V = 5.1 % + 1.7 % = 6.8 % ✓ → direct-on-line starting is acceptable

- Devices: 32 A AC-3 contactor · 24–32 A MPCB set to 28 A · 6 mm² PE

## Control panels: layout, IP rating and heat Intermediate

Figure 2 · Arrange devices along the energy flow from top to bottom, with wiring ducts between rows and the terminal rail at the bottom near the cable entry

- Low-voltage assemblies are designed and verified to IEC 61439 (the panel builder must verify temperature-rise limits, clearances and the busbar short-circuit rating)

- IP54 for general factory areas, IP55/65 for wash-down or outdoor areas (IEC 60529) — a cut-out for a fan must use a fan-and-filter unit with the same IP rating as the enclosure

- Leave 20–30 % spare space · keep the clearances in the drive manual (100–200 mm above and below for airflow)

K7 Enclosure temperature rise and fan airflow

$$\Delta T = \frac{P_{loss}}{k\,A_e}\ \ (k \approx 5.5\ \text{W/m}^2\text{K painted steel}) \qquad \dot V\,[\text{m}^3/\text{h}] \approx \frac{3.1\,P_{loss}\,[\text{W}]}{\Delta T_{allow}}$$

Example K-2

### A wall-mounted 600 × 800 × 300 mm enclosure containing a 15 kW drive (losses ~2.5 %)

- $P_{loss} \approx 0.025 \times 15{,}000 + 40 = 415$ W (including contactors and the power supply)

- Effective cooling surface (not counting the back against the wall) $A_e \approx 0.6(0.8) + 0.6(0.3) + 2(0.8)(0.3) = 1.14$ m²

- K7: sealed $\Delta T = 415/(5.5 \times 1.14) = 66$ K — in a 35 °C plant room the inside would exceed 100 °C ✗

- Use a fan: allow 10 K above ambient → $\dot V = 3.1(415)/10 = 129$ m³/h → choose a fan-filter unit ≥ 160 m³/h (allowing for a clogged filter)

## Pre-commissioning tests Basic

K8 Insulation resistance acceptance

$$R_{iso} \ge 1\ \text{M}\Omega\ @\ 500\ \text{V DC (IEC 60204-1)} \qquad R_{40^\circ C} \ge 5\ \text{M}\Omega\ \text{windings}

- Visual inspection: devices match the drawings, cable sizes, wire numbers, all covers fitted, no wire offcuts left in the panel

- Tightness: every power terminal torqued to the specified value (paint-mark after tightening)

- Earth continuity: measure the PE resistance from the motor frame to the panel earth bar

- Insulation resistance: disconnect drives, soft starters and electronics first, then test the cable and motor at 500 V DC (K8)

- Control circuit: isolate the power circuit (switch the MPCBs off), supply control power only, and test the sequence, interlocks, timers and emergency stop

- Direction of rotation: uncouple if possible, bump-start briefly and check the direction (a pump run backwards for long can be damaged)

- Live run: measure three-phase currents, voltage, temperature and vibration, compare with the nameplate and record them as the baseline

## Troubleshooting table

| Symptom | Possible causes | What to check |

| Press START and the contactor does not pull in | Blown control fuse · overload still tripped · STOP/E-stop latched · loose wire | Measure voltage point by point from the L rail along the drawing |

| Pulls in while pressed but drops out on release | Self-holding contact (13-14) not wired or faulty | Measure across 13-14 while energised, check the wire in parallel with the START button |

| Contactor hums loudly | Low coil voltage · dirty pole faces · broken shading ring | Measure coil voltage while energised, clean the pole faces |

| Motor hums but does not turn | Lost phase · jammed load · wrongly connected in Y for a heavily loaded 400/690 V motor | Measure three-phase voltage at the motor terminals, turn the shaft by hand (isolate first) |

| Overload trips after a few minutes' running | Genuine overload · wrong setting · low or unbalanced voltage · failed bearing | Measure current against the nameplate, measure voltage, listen to the bearings |

| MPCB trips instantly at start | Short circuit · failed insulation · magnetic setting too low · star–delta changeover timing wrong | Megger, measure winding resistance, note when in the sequence it trips |

| Motor abnormally hot but does not trip | Blocked fan/fins · low-speed running on a VFD · harmonics · high ambient temperature | Measure frame temperature, clean, check the operating frequency |

| Contactor contacts burn out quickly | Undersized · frequent inching (AC-4) · coil not pulling in firmly | Compare the rating with the duty, check operations per hour |

## Preventive maintenance

- Monthly: listen, check temperatures, clean panel fan filters, check pilot lamps

- Every 6 months: infrared thermal scan under load (to find loose connections), measure three-phase currents

- Yearly: re-torque power terminals, inspect contactor contacts, measure insulation resistance and record the trend, test emergency stops

- By running hours: grease bearings as stated on the motor plate, replace the drive cooling fan (often every 3–5 years) and the DC-bus capacitors per the manual

## Frequently asked questions

What is the minimum acceptable insulation resistance for a motor?
For the electrical equipment of machines, IEC 60204-1 requires at least 1 MΩ at 500 V DC between conductors and earth. For low-voltage motor windings, IEEE 43 recommends a minimum of 5 MΩ (corrected to 40 °C), and you should watch the trend against previous readings — a steadily falling value matters more than a single reading.

Can I size a motor cable from current alone?
No. Three things must be checked: the current rating after derating for installation method and temperature, the voltage drop both while running and while starting, and that the earth-fault current at the cable end is high enough for the protective device to disconnect within the required time. Long cables are usually sized by voltage drop, not by current.

Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# Reading Motor Control Diagrams: IEC 60617 Symbols vs NEMA, IEC 81346 Reference Designations, Terminal Numbers, Wire Numbers and Cross-References

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/diagrams-symbols/
Updated: 2026-10-15
Summary: How to read motor control circuit diagrams in the European (IEC), American (NEMA) and Japanese styles: power circuit versus control circuit, symbols for contacts, coils, timers and overload relays, the device letter codes -Q -K -F -S -P -M of IEC 81346, terminal numbers 1/L1 2/T1 A1 A2 13 14 21 22 95 96, wire numbers, terminal strips, cross-page references, and turning relay circuits into Boolean algebra. Adds IEC and ANSI/NEMA single-line diagrams, NEMA/JIC ladder diagrams, the NEMA starter size table and an IEC-to-NEMA device-code comparison.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.5 · AC Motor Control · Symbols & Reading Diagrams

# Reading Motor Control Diagrams: IEC 60617 Symbols vs NEMA, IEC 81346 Reference Designations, Terminal Numbers, Wire Numbers and Cross-References

A circuit diagram is the common language of the designer, the panel builder and the maintenance technician. If you read it fluently you will wire it right the first time and find faults from the drawing without tearing the panel apart. This page teaches you to read drawings in the IEC convention used throughout this series, and compares them with the American style found on imported machines.

In 30 seconds

- A drawing has two parts: the power circuit (400 V to the motor) and the control circuit (230 VAC/24 VDC to the coils)

- Contacts are always drawn in the normal state (de-energised, not actuated)

- Series = AND · parallel = OR · NC = NOT — you can read a control circuit as logic straight away

- Device designation + terminal number, e.g. “-K1:13”, identifies a connection point uniquely in the whole panel

- A single-line diagram shows the whole system · NEMA drawings are read as left-to-right ladders with rung numbers under the coil

## Power circuit and control circuit Basic

The power circuit (main circuit) is drawn as three lines L1 L2 L3 running down from the top through the breaker, contactor and overload relay to the motor; you read it top to bottom, following the flow of energy. The control circuit is drawn between an upper rail (L or +24 V) and a lower rail (N or 0 V). Each vertical branch is called a “path” or “current path” and has a column number at the top. Symbols belonging to the same device (e.g. coil -K1 and contact -K1 13-14) may sit in different columns or on different pages; they are tied together by the device designation.

Power circuit: read top → bottom

Control circuit: L rail → devices → coil → N rail

### What an IEC 60204-1 control schematic contains

- Column numbers 1 2 3 … above the L1 rail locate every device, with a function text (e.g. “hold-in”) under the N rail

- The box under a coil is the contact cross-reference (contact mirror): its NO / NC rows give the column of each contact of that coil; “PWR” = the power poles sit in the power circuit

- Coils on the N rail with all contacts on the L side: an earth fault between a contact and the coil cannot pick the coil up (IEC 60204-1 clause 9.4.3)

- Fuse -F3 protects the control circuit · overload contact -F2 95-96 (NC) is in series with the coil · 97-98 (NO) signals the trip

- IEC 60204-1 lamp codes GN green = normal/running · YE yellow = abnormal (trip) · RD red = danger/emergency · BU blue = action required · WH white = general status

- Power circuit: green-yellow dash-dot = PE conductor bonded to the motor frame · short dashes between poles = mechanical coupling · the overload is a bimetal element per phase linked to contact 95-96

## The single-line (one-line) diagram Intermediate

A single-line diagram is the “map” of an electrical system: one line stands for all three phases (three oblique strokes show three conductors) and the sheet shows sources, transformers, busbars, feeders, protective devices, starters and motors with their ratings — but no control circuits, terminal numbers or internal wiring. It is used to check protection coordination, calculate fault levels and plan extensions.

Figure 2 · Single-line diagram with IEC 60617 symbols: 22/0.4 kV Dyn11 transformer → ACB → MDB busbar → DOL feeder (MPCB + contactor + overload), soft-starter and VFD feeders (figures are illustrative)

### Read it top to bottom

- Source and transformer — voltage, frequency, rating (kVA), uk %, vector group (Dyn11) and neutral earthing (TN-S)

- Main breaker (ACB) — rated current and breaking capacity Icu, which must exceed the prospective fault current at the bus

- CT and meters — the circle around the line is the current transformer feeding an ammeter or power meter

- Busbar — the thick line: 3N~ 400/230 V · every feeder branches from it

- Motor feeders — breaker/MPCB → starter (contactor + overload, soft starter or VFD) → cable (size, cores, shield) → motor (kW, current)

Figure 3 · American one-line diagram (ANSI/IEEE 315): breakers are boxes on the line, ANSI/IEEE C37.2 device numbers (52 = AC circuit breaker, 49 = thermal overload), NEMA size 1 starter and FLA taken from NEC Table 430.250

| Drawing | Shows | Used for |

| Single-line | The whole system, one line per three phases, with ratings | Protection coordination, fault levels, expansion |

| Power circuit (multi-line) | Every conductor of one feeder: L1 L2 L3 PE, terminal numbers, motor leads | Panel wiring, phase rotation |

| Control schematic | Coils, contacts, buttons, sensors between rails L–N (IEC) or X1–X2 (NEMA) | Control logic, fault finding |

### What a good single-line diagram must show

- Voltage, frequency, system earthing (TN-S, TN-C-S, TT, IT) and the fault level at the bus (kA)

- Type, rating and Icu of every breaker · fuses · protection-relay settings

- Cable size, cores, material and length (for voltage drop and fault checks)

- Motors: kW or hp, rated current, starting method and device codes that match the control schematic (-Q1 -K1 -F2 -M1 or DISC M OL MTR)

- The symbol standard used (IEC 60617/81346 or ANSI/IEEE 315/NEMA), stated in the drawing legend

## IEC 60617 symbols Basic

Figure 1 · A dashed line from a contact shows a mechanical link, e.g. a push-button (the square-bracket shape), a float, a pressure switch, or the thermal element of an overload relay.

### Drawing rules you must know

- Contacts are drawn in the “de-energised, not actuated” state — a limit switch that is normally held operated carries a note

- An NO contact is drawn with its blade tilted to the left; an NC contact has a short bar across at the contact point

- The half-circle on a timer contact shows the direction of the delay (like a parachute)

- A solid dot (●) is a junction; lines that cross without a dot are not connected

- A fuse is a rectangle with the conductor running through it · a contactor pole has a small bow at the contact · a circuit-breaker has a cross at the blade tip · an isolator has a bar across the blade tip

- Dashed lines are mechanical links between poles or devices — the three poles of a contactor, a breaker’s trip unit, or the mechanical interlock between coils -K1 and -K2

## Device designations and terminal numbers Intermediate

| Traditional code (used in this series) | New IEC 81346-2 (examples) | Device |

| -Q | -QA | MPCB, isolating switch (and power contactors in the new edition) |

| -K | -QA (contactor) · -KF (relay, timer, PLC) | Contactors, relays, timers |

| -F | -FC | Fuses, overload relays, protective devices |

| -S | -SF | Push-buttons, selector switches (operated by a person) |

| -B | -BG -BP -BL | Sensors, limit switches, pressure switches, floats |

| -P / -H | -PF -PG | Pilot lights, meters |

| -M | -MA | Motors |

| -X | -XD | Terminal strips |

| -T | -TA | Transformers, power supplies (the new edition uses T for energy conversion) |

A terminal number is always read together with the designation: “-K1:A1” is the coil terminal of contactor K1, “-X1:5” is terminal 5 of terminal strip X1. Wire numbers on drawings are often based on page and column number (e.g. wire 2.4 is a wire on page 2, column 4), which makes it practical to trace wires inside the panel.

### Cross-reference tables

Under each coil on an IEC drawing there is usually a small table showing where its contacts are, for example

-K1
1-2 │ 3.2 ← main contact, page 3 column 2
13-14 │ 4.3 ← NO used for self-holding, page 4 column 3
21-22 │ 4.6 ← NC used for interlocking, page 4 column 6
43-44 │ 4.8 ← NO for the run lamp

## Reading a control circuit as logic Intermediate

Current reaches a coil when there is at least one path on which every contact is closed, so the circuit can be written as Boolean algebra. This is the foundation of ladder programming in a PLC.

G1 Series = AND

$$K = A \cdot B$$

G2 Parallel = OR

$$K = A + B$$

G3 NC contact = NOT

$$K = \overline{A}$$

G4 Self-holding (seal-in)

$$K1 = \overline{S0}\cdot\overline{F2}\cdot(S1 + K1)$$

Example G-1

### Read the DOL circuit as an equation

- A single path from the L rail: F2 (95-96, NC) → S0 (NC) → [S1 (NO) in parallel with K1 13-14] → coil K1

- Replace each NC with NOT of “actuated”: $K1 = \overline{F2}\cdot\overline{S0}\cdot(S1 + K1)$ — identical to G4

- Check: press S1 → K1 = 1 · release S1 → the K1 term holds it · press S0 or F2 trips → K1 = 0, and it does not come back by itself when released

## American (NEMA/JIC) and Japanese drawings Intermediate

In North America motor drawings follow NEMA ICS 19 (designations and symbols), NEMA ICS 2 (contactors, starters and NEMA sizes), NFPA 79 / JIC (electrical equipment of industrial machinery) and the NEC (installation); symbols come from ANSI Y32.2 / IEEE 315. The sheet below is the symbol set used in this series’ ladder diagrams.

Figure 4 · NEMA/JIC symbols: contacts are parallel bars, NO ┤ ├ and NC ┤/├ · coils and lamps are circles with letters · overload heaters are zig-zags · power poles are two short bars across the line

| Item | IEC (Europe · Thailand · ASEAN) | NEMA / JIC (North America) |

| Drawing direction | Rails top and bottom, vertical circuits · columns 1 2 3 | Rails left and right (X1 · X2), horizontal rungs like a ladder · rung numbers 1 2 3 |

| NO / NC contact | Tilted blade / blade with a bar | Two parallel bars ─┤ ├─ / with a diagonal ─┤/├─ |

| Coil | Rectangle A1–A2 | Circle with letters M, CR, TR (no terminal numbers) |

| Device codes | -K1 -S1 -F2 -P1 -M1 | M · CR · TR · OL · PB · FU · PL · MTR |

| Power-pole terminals | 1/L1 2/T1 3/L2 4/T2 5/L3 6/T3 | L1 L2 L3 → T1 T2 T3 |

| Six-lead motor terminals | U1 V1 W1 U2 V2 W2 | T1 T2 T3 T4 T5 T6 (U1=T1 V1=T2 W1=T3 U2=T4 V2=T5 W2=T6) |

| Overload | Relay -F2 95-96 at the head of the coil circuit | OL heaters in the power circuit · OL contact (NC) next to the coil, near rail X2 |

| Control voltage | 230 VAC / 24 VDC | 120 VAC from a control transformer (X2 grounded) / 24 VDC |

| Cross-reference | Box under the coil gives the NO/NC columns | Rung numbers under the coil · underlined = NC |

| Wire numbers / colours | By sheet and column · green-yellow = PE | One number per node · NFPA 79: black = power, red = AC control, white = grounded (X2), green = ground |

| Starter sizing | Rating by utilisation category AC-3 (kW, A) | NEMA size 00–9 by hp at that voltage (table below) |

### Reading a NEMA ladder

- Read left to right: buttons and contacts on the left, loads on the right — coil M sits at the far right with OL, next to the grounded rail X2 (the same idea as IEC’s “coil on N”)

- Rung numbers outside rail X1 · wire numbers on the lines: one number per electrical node

- Numbers under a coil list the rungs that carry its contacts — underlined = NC, e.g. “1 2 3” = NO on rungs 1 and 2, NC on rung 3

- Contacts carry no terminal numbers such as 13-14: they are identified by device name (M, CR1, TR) · timer contacts state their type NOTC / NCTO (on-delay) or NOTO / NCTC (off-delay)

- Full examples with the power circuit: direct on line · reversing · wye–delta

### IEC ↔ NEMA device codes

| Device | IEC | NEMA / JIC |

| Breaker / MPCB | -Q1 | CB · MCP · DISC |

| Contactor / starter | -K1 (-QA1) | M · F · R · 1M 2M 1S |

| Control relay · timer | -K2 · -K4T | CR · TR |

| Overload | -F2 (95-96) | OL |

| Fuse | -F1 -F3 | FU |

| START / STOP buttons | -S1 / -S0 | START / STOP (PB) |

| Limit · pressure · float | -B1 -B2 -B3 | LS · PS · FS |

| Pilot light | -P1 (GN, RD) | PL (G, R, A, W) |

| Control transformer | -T1 | CT / CPT (H1–H4, X1–X2) |

| Motor | -M1 (U1 V1 W1) | MTR (T1 T2 T3) |

### NEMA starter sizes (ICS 2)

| NEMA size | Continuous (A) | Max hp at 230 V | Max hp at 460 V |

| 00 | 9 | 1.5 | 2 |

| 0 | 18 | 3 | 5 |

| 1 | 27 | 7.5 | 10 |

| 2 | 45 | 15 | 25 |

| 3 | 90 | 30 | 50 |

| 4 | 135 | 50 | 100 |

| 5 | 270 | 100 | 200 |

The hp figures are maxima for full-voltage, non-plugging duty — check the manufacturer’s catalogue and NEMA ICS 2 before selecting. A NEMA size is chosen from the hp, not the measured current, whereas an IEC contactor is chosen from current and utilisation category AC-3.

Current Japanese drawings use JIS C 0617, which matches IEC 60617, but older machines still carry the former symbols. Ladder diagrams in every brand of PLC are drawn horizontally, much like NEMA.

## Reading a drawing to find a fault

- Start at the motor/load with the problem and find its device designation in the power circuit (e.g. -K3)

- Find coil -K3 in the control circuit, then work down from the L rail one device at a time

- Measure the voltage to the N rail point by point; the first point with “no voltage” lies after the device that is open

- Use the cross-reference table to see which device the open contact (e.g. -K2 21-22) belongs to, and follow it from there

## Frequently asked questions

In which state are contacts shown on a diagram?
In the normal state: no coil energised, no button pressed and no force on any sensor (de-energised, unactuated). NO contacts are therefore drawn open and NC contacts closed, even though in real operation a contactor may be pulled in almost all the time.

Why do some drawings use K for contactors and others Q?
The traditional IEC/DIN convention uses K for contactors and relays. The newer IEC 81346-2 places power contactors in class Q (switching of energy flow), e.g. -QA1, and control relays in class K, e.g. -KF1. Both styles appear on real drawings, so check the designation key page of the drawing set.

How is a single-line diagram different from a power circuit?
A single-line diagram draws one line for all three phases and covers the whole system (source, transformer, busbar, feeders, protection, motors) with ratings. A power circuit shows every conductor and terminal number of one feeder and is used for panel wiring.

Why do NEMA drawings have no terminal numbers like 13-14 or 95-96?
NEMA/JIC identifies contacts by device name (M, CR, TR, OL) and by wire numbers on the lines instead of IEC 60947 auxiliary-contact numbers. Power poles are L1 L2 L3 → T1 T2 T3, and contact locations are read from the rung numbers under the coil (underlined = NC).

# Direct-On-Line (DOL) Motor Starter: Power Circuit, Self-Holding Control Circuit, Two-Location Control, Jogging and Step-by-Step Device Selection

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/dol-starter/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: The direct-on-line circuit for 400 V three-phase motors: power circuit with MPCB, contactor and overload relay; the self-holding (seal-in) control circuit; why the STOP button must be NC and wired in series; multi-location control; jog buttons; pilot lights; the sequence of operation; panel wiring; and a complete device-selection example for a 7.5 kW motor.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.6 · AC Motor Control · Direct-On-Line Starter

# Direct-On-Line (DOL) Motor Starter: Power Circuit, Self-Holding Control Circuit, Two-Location Control, Jogging and Step-by-Step Device Selection

DOL is the simplest and most common motor circuit, and the template for all the others: a reversing starter is two interlocked DOL starters, and a star–delta starter is a DOL starter with extra contactors and a timer. Understand this page in depth and the following pages become much easier.

In 30 seconds

- Power circuit: Q1 (short circuit) → K1 (switching) → F2 (overload) → motor

- Control circuit: F2 95-96 → STOP (NC) → [START (NO) ∥ K1 13-14] → coil K1

- All STOP buttons in series, all START buttons in parallel

- Self-holding gives no-volt release safety: after a power failure the motor does not restart by itself

- 7.5 kW motor: MPCB 13–18 A · 18 A AC-3 contactor · 2.5 mm² cable (≤ 60 m)

## Power circuit Basic

Figure 1 · DOL power circuit: three devices perform three different duties, and none may stand in for another (e.g. using the breaker to switch the motor on and off every day).

L1 DOL starting current

$$I_{st} = k_{st}\,I_n \qquad k_{st} = I_a/I_n \approx 6\text{–}8$$

L2 Voltage dip at the transformer

$$\Delta U\% \approx \frac{S_{st}}{S_{sc} + S_{st}}\times 100 \qquad S_{st} = \sqrt3\,V_L\,I_{st} \qquad S_{sc} = \frac{S_{tr}}{u_k}$$

L3 Cable voltage drop

$$\Delta V = \sqrt3\, I\, L\,(R\cos\varphi + X\sin\varphi) \qquad \cos\varphi_{start} \approx 0.3$$

## The self-holding control circuit Basic

Figure 2 · Column 1 drives the coil (STOP · START · K1) · column 2 is the hold-in contact · column 3 the run lamp (K1 43-44) · column 4 the trip lamp (F2 97-98) · the box under coil K1 gives the columns of its contacts

### Sequence of operation

- Normal state: F2 95-96 closed · S0 closed · S1 open · K1 13-14 open → coil not energised

- Press S1: current flows through S1 to coil K1 → K1 pulls in → main contacts connect the motor · 13-14 closes · 43-44 lights the run lamp

- Release S1: current still reaches the coil through 13-14, which is in parallel with S1 → self-holding

- Press S0: every path is broken → K1 drops out → 13-14 opens → releasing S0 does not bring it back

- Overload: F2 95-96 opens just like pressing STOP · 97-98 closes and the trip lamp lights · remove the cause, then reset

- Power failure: the coil loses supply, K1 drops out and the latch is lost → when power returns the motor does not start by itself

L4 Seal-in logic

$$K1_{\text{new}} = \overline{F2}\cdot\overline{S0}\cdot(S1 + K1_{\text{old}})$$

Why STOP must be NC: if you used an NO button wired as “press to break”, a loose wire or a dirty contact would mean pressing STOP does nothing. With an NC button wired in series, a broken wire stops the machine by itself — it fails safe. The same reasoning applies to overload contact 95-96 and to the emergency stop.

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

## NEMA/JIC version: the same circuit drawn the American way Intermediate

Machines from North America and plants designed to NFPA 79 / the NEC draw a DOL starter as a power circuit plus a control ladder on one sheet. This is the same circuit as figures 1–2 at 480 V 3Φ 60 Hz with 120 V control from a control transformer.

Figure 2a · NEMA/JIC direct-on-line starter: disconnect + fuses → starter M (L1 L2 L3 → T1 T2 T3) → OL heaters → motor · 480/120 V control transformer (X2 grounded) → ladder STOP – START ∥ M – coil M – OL

### Compared with the IEC figures 1–2

- Three-wire ladder: STOP (NC) – START (NO) in parallel with auxiliary contact M (NO) – coil M – OL (NC) — the same logic as IEC, read left to right

- OL sits next to the coil near grounded rail X2 (IEC puts the overload contact at the head of the circuit); the OL heaters are in the power circuit

- Numbers under the coil “1 2 3”: M has NO contacts on rung 1 (hold-in) and rung 2 (RUN lamp) and an NC contact on rung 3 (OFF lamp)

- Control transformer: primary fuses FU1 FU2 on H1 H4, secondary fuse FU3 on X1 and X2 grounded — the same reason as IEC’s “coil on N”: an earth fault in the control wiring must not pick up the coil

- No terminal numbers 1-2, 13-14 or 95-96 — device names (M, OL) and wire numbers 1–6 take their place · NEMA starters are chosen by hp: a 10 hp 460 V motor (FLA 14 A) takes size 1 — see the table on the symbols page

## Multi-location control and jogging Intermediate

Machines often need to be controlled both at the panel and out on the floor. The rule is all STOP buttons in series (any one stops it) and all START buttons in parallel (any one starts it). A jog (inching) button runs the motor only while it is held, for positioning a conveyor or a tool. It is made with a combined NO+NC button: the NC part breaks the self-holding path and the NO part feeds the coil directly.

Figure 3 · Combined jog button: the NC contact must open before the NO contact closes (break-before-make), otherwise the motor stays latched after the button is released.

Frequent jogging is AC-4 duty: the contactor breaks the starting current every time, so derate the contactor or choose a larger size, and watch for motor overheating from frequent starts.

## Selecting the complete set of devices step by step Intermediate

Example L-1

### A 7.5 kW 400 V 14.6 A water pump, 60 m from the panel, fed by a 500 kVA uk 4 % transformer

- L1: $I_{st} = 6.5 \times 14.6 = 95$ A

- L2: $S_{st} = \sqrt3(400)(95) = 65.8$ kVA · $S_{sc} = 500/0.04 = 12.5$ MVA → $\Delta U = 65.8/(12{,}500 + 65.8) = 0.5\,\%$ at the transformer — direct-on-line starting is easily acceptable

- 18 A AC-3 contactor · MPCB 13–18 A range set to 14.6 A, class 10 (the pump runs up in < 2 s)

- L3 with 2.5 mm² cable (R = 0.0225/2.5 = 9 mΩ/m): while running $\Delta V = \sqrt3(14.6)(60)(0.009 \times 0.82 + 0.00008 \times 0.57) = 11.3$ V = 2.8 % ✓

- During starting $\Delta V = \sqrt3(95)(60)(0.009 \times 0.3 + 0.00008 \times 0.95) = 27.4$ V = 6.9 % — together with the transformer dip still below 10 % ✓

- Control circuit 230 VAC through a 2 A fuse · START/STOP buttons · run/trip lamps

## Wiring inside the panel: good practice

- Power-circuit wire colours to the applicable standard (in Thailand, per the EIT (Engineering Institute of Thailand) wiring code: L1 brown, L2 black, L3 grey, N blue, PE green-yellow); use a distinct colour for control wiring, e.g. red (AC) and dark blue (DC)

- Fit wire-number markers on both ends as per the drawing, and crimp a lug or ferrule on every stranded conductor

- Connect door-mounted push-buttons through terminal strip -X1, not directly from devices inside the panel, so the door can be removed for service

- Test the control circuit before connecting the motor: isolate the power circuit, press START/STOP and check that the contactors and lamps operate in the right sequence

- Test the overload relay with its TEST button while running: the motor must stop and the trip lamp must light

## Frequently asked questions

Why use a self-holding auxiliary contact instead of a maintained switch?
For safety: when the power fails and returns, a self-holding circuit does not restart the motor by itself (no-volt release), because the contactor drops out when the supply is lost and someone has to press START again. With a maintained switch the motor would start the moment power returns, which is dangerous for anyone working on the machine (IEC 60204-1 requires protection against unexpected restarting).

How large a motor can be started direct-on-line?
There is no single number. It depends on the strength of the supply (transformer size, cable length) and the utility's requirements. The general rule is that the voltage dip at the main switchboard during starting should not exceed 10–15 % and must not disturb other equipment. Check it with the voltage-drop calculator on this page, and check the local utility's connection requirements.

# Three-Phase Motor Reversing Circuit: Swapping Two Phases, Electrical, Mechanical and Push-Button Interlocks, and Automatic Reversing with Limit Switches

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/forward-reverse/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: The forward–reverse circuit for a 400 V three-phase motor: why swapping L1 and L3 reverses the motor, the two-contactor power circuit, three layers of interlocking (NC contacts, double push-buttons and a mechanical interlock), reversing through STOP versus instant reversal, plugging and AC-4 duty, roller shutters, electric hoists, conveyors and limit switches.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.7 · AC Motor Control · Forward–Reverse

# Three-Phase Motor Reversing Circuit: Swapping Two Phases, Electrical, Mechanical and Push-Button Interlocks, and Automatic Reversing with Limit Switches

Roller shutters, electric hoists, two-way conveyors and lathes all need to reverse. This circuit is two DOL starters connected to one motor. The hard part is not making the motor turn the other way — it is guaranteeing that the two contactors can never close at the same time, because that is a phase-to-phase short circuit.

In 30 seconds

- K1 connects L1-L2-L3 straight through · K2 swaps L1 and L3 → the phase sequence reverses and so does the rotating field

- K1 + K2 closed together = a short circuit between L1 and L3

- Three layers of interlocking: NC auxiliary of the opposite contactor · NO+NC double push-buttons · mechanical interlock

- Instant reversal while running (plugging) draws more than the starting current and needs AC-4 contactors — stop first

## Power circuit: swapping two phases Basic

Figure 1 · The supply sides of K1 and K2 are connected in parallel. On the output side of K2, lines L1 and L3 are swapped before joining the output of K1 · ▽ is the symbol for a mechanical interlock

R1 Phase swap

$$\text{K1: } (L1, L2, L3)\to(U1, V1, W1) \qquad \text{K2: } (L3, L2, L1)\to(U1, V1, W1)$$

R2 Fault if both close

$$I_{k2} = \frac{V_{L1L3}}{2 Z_{src}} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} I_{k3} \approx 0.87\,I_{k3}$$

## Control circuit with three layers of interlocking Intermediate

Figure 2 · Each side is a DOL self-holding circuit, but with two NC contacts from the opposite side in its path: the other direction's push-button and the other contactor's auxiliary contact

| Layer | Made with | Prevents | Weak spot if it is the only layer |

| 1 Electrical (auxiliary) | K2 21-22 in series with the K1 coil and K1 21-22 in series with the K2 coil | Commanding the second contactor while the first is closed | Main contacts weld but the NC auxiliary can still reclose |

| 2 Push-button | Double buttons: pressing S1 first opens the NC in the K2 side | Pressing both buttons at once · forces reversal through a release first | No help if a contactor sticks |

| 3 Mechanical | A mechanical lever between the paired contactors | Both closing physically, even with a wrong control circuit | The contactor pair must be mounted as the manufacturer specifies |

R3 Interlocked logic

$$K1 = \overline{S0}\,\overline{F2}\,(S1 + K1)\,\overline{S2}\,\overline{K2} \qquad K2 = \overline{S0}\,\overline{F2}\,(S2 + K2)\,\overline{S1}\,\overline{K1}$$

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

In the simulator, press forward and then immediately press reverse: the interlock will refuse. Then tick “No stop-before-reverse” and reverse while the motor is running. Watch the current shoot above the starting current and the speed pass through zero.

## NEMA/JIC version: the reversing starter Intermediate

A NEMA reversing starter is two contactors, F (forward) and R (reverse), on one base with a factory-fitted mechanical interlock (M.I.). R swaps L1 and L3 just like K2 in the IEC drawing.

Figure 1a · NEMA/JIC reversing starter: power circuit (F straight · R swapping L1↔L3 · OL · motor T1 T2 T3) and the STOP / FWD / REV ladder with its interlocks

- Three interlock layers, as in IEC: NC contacts of F and R in the opposite rung · FWD/REV buttons whose NC half is in series with the other side · M.I. on the starter

- Numbers under the coils: F shows “1 2” — NO on rung 1 (hold-in) and NC on rung 2 (the interlock of R) · R shows “1 2” the other way round

- One STOP serves both rungs · a single OL sits next to rail X2 · reversing from running (plugging) needs a zero-speed relay or an off-delay timer

## Reversing while running (plugging) Advanced

If the motor is running forward at nearly full speed and the phases are swapped instantly, the rotating field reverses but the rotor is still turning the original way. The slip relative to the new field is therefore close to 2.

R4 Slip during plugging

$$s = \frac{-n_s - n}{-n_s} = 1 + \frac{n}{n_s} \approx 2 \quad (n \approx n_s)$$

At s ≈ 2 the current is slightly higher than at starting and the torque acts as a brake. All the kinetic energy of the load turns into heat in the rotor (about 3 times that of a single start). The contactors must be rated AC-4, and there must be a way to cut the supply when the speed reaches zero (a zero-speed switch); otherwise the motor will accelerate in the reverse direction.

R5 Rotor heat per operation (load with no torque)

$$E_{start} = \tfrac12 J\omega_s^2 \qquad E_{plug\,(\omega_s \to 0)} = \tfrac32 J\omega_s^2 \qquad E_{reverse\,(\omega_s \to -\omega_s)} = 4\cdot\tfrac12 J\omega_s^2$$

Example R-1

### A conveyor reversed while running, total J = 0.4 kg·m², 4-pole motor

- $\omega_s = 2\pi(1500)/60 = 157$ rad/s · kinetic energy $\tfrac12(0.4)(157^2) = 4.93$ kJ

- R5: a full reversal (forward → full speed in reverse) puts ≈ 4 × 4.93 = 19.7 kJ of heat into the rotor, compared with 4.9 kJ for a normal start

- If it reverses every 30 s, the motor heats up four times faster than with normal starts → stop before reversing, or use an inverter that decelerates under control

## Automatic reversing with limit switches Intermediate

Roller shutters and sliding tables must stop at the end of travel. Put an NC end-of-travel limit switch in series with the coil for that direction (-B1 in the forward circuit, -B2 in the reverse circuit). When the limit is hit, that direction's circuit opens while the opposite direction can still be commanded. For automatic back-and-forth travel, wire an NO contact of the same limit switch in parallel with the opposite direction's push-button.

- Use limit switches with positive-opening contacts (IEC 60947-5-1) for any safety-related position

- Add an over-travel limit beyond the normal limit and wire it into the main stop circuit, in case the first limit fails

- Electric hoists: never rely on auxiliary contacts alone — fit upper and lower limits and a mechanical brake

## Frequently asked questions

Is an electrical interlock on its own enough?
No. If the main contacts of one contactor weld, or the contactor sticks mechanically, its NC auxiliary contact may still be closed even though the main contacts are still made, so the other contactor can pull in and short two phases. A mechanical interlock between the two contactors physically stops them closing together. Manufacturers sell reversing contactor sets that include both.

Can I reverse the motor while it is running?
Technically yes (plugging), but the current is higher than the starting current, the torque shocks the shaft and gearbox, and the contactors must be rated AC-4. In most applications you should force the operator to press STOP and wait for the motor to stop first, or use a timer to delay the reversal.

Mod

Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# Three-Phase Induction Motor Principles for Industry: Rotating Field, Slip, Torque–Speed Curve, Starting Current and the Nameplate

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/induction-motor/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: How a three-phase induction motor works: the rotating magnetic field n_s = 120f/p, slip, the equivalent circuit, the torque–speed curve, starting current of 6–8 times rated, torque proportional to V², IE2 IE3 IE4 efficiency classes to IEC 60034-30-1, reading the nameplate (IP, IC, insulation class, S1 duty) and calculating rated current from kW for a 400 V 50 Hz system.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.1 · AC Motor Control · Induction Motor

# Three-Phase Induction Motor Principles for Industry: Rotating Field, Slip, Torque–Speed Curve, Starting Current and the Nameplate

Before choosing a contactor or designing a starter you need to know what the motor “wants” from the circuit: how much current it draws when starting, how much torque it gives, and what a voltage dip does to it. This page goes from the physics to the numbers on the nameplate, using the same 7.5 kW 4-pole 400 V 50 Hz motor throughout the course.

In 30 seconds

- Three-phase currents 120° apart create a magnetic field rotating at $n_s = 120f/p$

- The rotor turns slightly slower: slip $s$ is 1–5 % at rated load · rated torque $T = 9550P/n$

- At start ($s = 1$) current is 6–8 In but torque only 1.5–2.5 Tn

- Torque varies with the square of voltage: a 10 % voltage dip loses 19 % of torque

- kW on the nameplate = mechanical shaft power · rated current $I_n = P/(\sqrt3 V \eta \cos\varphi)$ ≈ 2 A/kW at 400 V

## Construction Basic

The squirrel-cage induction motor, the most common motor in factories, has two parts: the stator, a laminated iron core carrying three windings placed 120 electrical degrees apart, and the rotor, made of aluminium or copper bars cast into short-circuiting end rings at both ends. There are no brushes and no commutator, so it is rugged and needs little maintenance. The usual type is TEFC (Totally Enclosed Fan Cooled, code IC411), with a fan on the shaft blowing air over the cooling fins.

Figure 1 · Parts of a TEFC motor: all six stator winding leads come out to the terminal box, which is where we choose star or delta

## The rotating field and synchronous speed Basic

When three-phase currents displaced 120° in time are fed into windings displaced 120° in space, the vector sum of the three fields has a constant magnitude of 1.5 times the peak field of one phase and rotates around the stator at constant speed. This is the heart of the three-phase AC motor: rotation without any moving parts.

Figure 2 · At times t1, t2, t3 each phase current is different, but the resultant vector keeps the same length and turns 60° each time ωt advances 60°

M1 Synchronous speed

$$n_s = \frac{120\, f}{p}\ \ \text{rpm} \qquad (p = \text{number of poles})$$

| Number of poles p | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |

| n_s at 50 Hz | 3000 | 1500 | 1000 | 750 |

| Approx. rated n | 2900–2970 | 1440–1480 | 950–985 | 700–740 |

| Typical use | High-head pumps, small fans | General purpose (most common) | Large fans, crushers | Conveyors, hoists |

## Slip and torque Intermediate

The rotating field sweeps across the rotor bars and induces voltage and current in the rotor (Faraday's law). Because this current sits in a magnetic field it feels a force $F = BIL$ that drags the rotor round after the field. But if the rotor caught up with the field exactly, the flux cutting would vanish and the torque would be zero, so the rotor always turns slower — hence the name “asynchronous motor”.

M2 Slip

$$s = \frac{n_s - n}{n_s} \qquad n = n_s(1 - s)$$

M3 Rotor frequency

$$f_r = s\, f$$

M4 Torque from power and speed

$$T = \frac{P}{\omega} = \frac{60\,P}{2\pi n} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; T\,[\text{N}{\cdot}\text{m}] = \frac{9550\, P\,[\text{kW}]}{n\,[\text{rpm}]}$$

Example M-1

### A 7.5 kW 4-pole 50 Hz motor, nameplate 1470 rpm

- M1: $n_s = 120(50)/4 = 1500$ rpm

- M2: $s = (1500 - 1470)/1500 = 0.02 = 2\,\%$ · M3: $f_r = 0.02 \times 50 = 1$ Hz (the rotor current reverses very slowly)

- M4: $T_n = 9550(7.5)/1470 = 48.7$ N·m — the value to compare with the load torque and the starting torque

## Equivalent circuit and power flow Advanced

An induction motor is a transformer whose secondary (the rotor) can rotate. Referring the rotor quantities to the stator side gives the per-phase circuit of Figure 3. The rotor resistance appears as $R_2'/s$, which splits into the rotor copper loss $R_2'$ and a “load resistor” $R_2'(1-s)/s$ representing the mechanical power.

Figure 3 · Per-phase equivalent circuit (Y basis): at start s = 1 and the circuit impedance is only R₁ + R₂′ + jX — which is why the current is several times rated

M5 Power split in the rotor

$$P_{ag} = 3 I_2'^2 \frac{R_2'}{s} \qquad P_{cu2} = s\,P_{ag} \qquad P_{mech} = (1 - s)\,P_{ag} \qquad T = \frac{P_{ag}}{\omega_s}$$

The key practical result: rotor loss = slip × air-gap power. A motor running at high slip (low voltage, overload, wrongly connected in star) heats up immediately, and reducing speed by increasing slip is wasteful — unlike lowering the frequency with a VFD, where the slip stays small.

Example M-2

### Power flowing through the rotor of a 7.5 kW motor at s = 2 %

- Mechanical power including friction and fan ≈ 7.5 + 0.1 = 7.6 kW

- M5: $P_{ag} = P_{mech}/(1-s) = 7.6/0.98 = 7.76$ kW · $P_{cu2} = 0.02(7.76) = 0.155$ kW

- If the motor is forced to run at s = 10 % with the same torque, $P_{cu2}$ rises to about 0.78 kW — five times the rotor heating.

## The torque–speed curve and starting current Intermediate

The curves in Figure 4 are computed from the equivalent circuit of the example motor (double-cage rotor, tuned to typical catalogue data). The points to know:

- Locked-rotor torque Ts ≈ 2.2 Tn at n = 0 — must comfortably exceed the load's breakaway torque

- Breakdown (pull-out) torque Tk ≈ 3 Tn at about 85–90 % speed — if the load exceeds this the motor stalls

- Operating region to the right of the breakdown point, where the curve is almost a straight line and torque is proportional to slip

- Starting current ≈ 6.5 In, hardly falling until the speed reaches 80 % — so the whole run-up is a high-current period

Figure 4 · Orange = motor torque, blue = current (right axis), green = pump load, dashed = constant-torque load. Where the motor curve crosses the load curve is the operating point.

M6 Rated current

$$I_n = \frac{P_{out}}{\sqrt{3}\,V_L\,\eta\,\cos\varphi} \qquad P_{in} = \frac{P_{out}}{\eta}$$

M7 Starting current

$$I_{st} = \left(\frac{I_a}{I_n}\right) I_n \qquad \frac{I_a}{I_n} \approx 6\text{–}8$$

M8 Torque versus voltage

$$T(s) \propto V^2 \qquad \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^2 \qquad I(s) \propto V$$

Example M-3

### Rated current, starting current and the effect of a voltage dip

- M6: $I_n = 7500/(\sqrt3 \times 400 \times 0.904 \times 0.82) = 7500/513.6 = 14.6$ A — matches the nameplate

- $P_{in} = 7.5/0.904 = 8.30$ kW · $S = \sqrt3(400)(14.6) = 10.1$ kVA · $Q = \sqrt{10.1^2 - 8.30^2} = 5.8$ kvar

- M7: $I_{st} = 6.5 \times 14.6 = 95$ A when started direct-on-line

- M8: if the voltage dips to 90 % during starting, the starting torque is $2.2 \times 0.9^2 = 1.78$ Tn and the current $95 \times 0.9 = 86$ A

## Reading the motor nameplate Basic

Figure 5 · Example nameplate: the two voltage lines “400 V Δ / 690 V Y” say that on a 400 V system it must be connected in delta, and that it can be star–delta started

| Field | Meaning | Used for |

| 400 V Δ 14.6 A / 690 V Y 8.4 A | Rated voltage and current for each connection | Choosing the terminal connection, setting the overload |

| 7.5 kW · 1470 r/min · 50 Hz | Mechanical shaft power, speed at rated load | Finding rated torque and slip |

| cos φ 0.82 · IE3 90.4 % | Power factor and efficiency at rated load | Calculating current, kVA, energy cost, PF correction |

| IP55 | Dust (5) and water-jet (5) protection to IEC 60034-5 | Matching the location (IP55 general use, IP56/66 wash-down) |

| IC411 | Cooled by a shaft-mounted fan (TEFC) | Take care at low speed on a VFD |

| Ins.cl. F · ΔT B | Insulation rated 155 °C, but actual temperature rise within class B (130 °C) | A margin for insulation life |

| S1 · Ta 40 °C | Continuous duty, ambient up to 40 °C · altitude up to 1000 m | Plant rooms hotter than 40 °C require derating |

| Ia/In 6.5 · Ta/Tn 2.2 · Tk/Tn 3.0 | Ratios of starting current, starting torque and breakdown torque | Calculating starting current, voltage dip and ability to accelerate |

## Efficiency classes IE1–IE4 and why to choose IE3 or better Intermediate

IEC 60034-30-1 defines efficiency classes IE1 (standard), IE2 (high), IE3 (premium) and IE4 (super premium). Many countries set minimum energy performance standards (MEPS) at IE2 or IE3. The electricity cost over a motor's life is usually tens of times its purchase price, so a difference of only a few percent in efficiency pays off.

| 4-pole 50 Hz | IE1 | IE2 | IE3 | IE4 |

| 7.5 kW | 86.0 % | 88.7 % | 90.4 % | 92.6 % |

| 11 kW | 87.6 % | 89.8 % | 91.4 % | 93.3 % |

Example M-4

### Replacing IE1 with IE3 on a 7.5 kW pump running 6,000 h/year at 4.5 THB/kWh

- $P_{in,IE1} = 7.5/0.860 = 8.72$ kW · $P_{in,IE3} = 7.5/0.904 = 8.30$ kW

- Saving 0.42 kW × 6000 h = 2,520 kWh/year ≈ 11,300 THB/year

- Caution: IE3/IE4 motors have a higher inrush current at start, which is why IEC 60947-4-1 introduced the AC-3e utilisation category for contactors.

## What an electrician must remember on site

- Check the nameplate before every connection: the voltage and connection (Δ/Y) must match the 400 V system

- The no-load current of a 4-pole motor is about 30–50 % of In — that does not mean the motor is faulty

- Measure the current in all three phases; if they differ by more than ~10 %, check for voltage unbalance, contactor contacts and loose terminals

- A normally running motor too hot to touch (60–80 °C on the frame) is normal for class F; measure with a thermometer instead of by hand

## Frequently asked questions

Why does an induction motor turn slower than synchronous speed?
Torque comes from currents induced in the rotor, which requires the rotating field to cut the rotor conductors. If the rotor turned exactly as fast as the field there would be no flux cutting, no current and no torque, so it must always be slower. The difference is the slip, about 1–5 % at rated load.

Why doesn't the high starting current burn out the motor?
The current is high only for the few seconds of acceleration, and the heat accumulated (I²t) is still less than the insulation can take. If the rotor is locked or accelerates too slowly (very high inertia, low voltage), the heating becomes so high that an overload relay of a suitable class must trip first.

Is the power on the nameplate electrical or mechanical?
It is the mechanical power at the shaft (output), per IEC 60034-1. The electrical power drawn from the supply is larger, P/η; for example a 7.5 kW motor with 90.4 % efficiency draws 8.3 kW.

Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile
