# Star and Delta Motor Connections: the U1 V1 W1 / W2 U2 V2 Terminal Box, 230/400 V vs 400/690 V Motors and Reversing

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/motor-connections/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: Connect a three-phase motor in star (Y) or delta (Δ) correctly: winding voltage, line versus phase current, placing the copper links in the U1 V1 W1 W2 U2 V2 terminal box to IEC 60034-8, choosing the connection from a 230/400 V or 400/690 V nameplate, which motors can be star–delta started, reversing rotation, and the mistakes that burn motors out.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.3 · AC Motor Control · Star & Delta Connections

# Star and Delta Motor Connections: the U1 V1 W1 / W2 U2 V2 Terminal Box, 230/400 V vs 400/690 V Motors and Reversing

The mistake that most often burns out a new motor is not in the control circuit — it is connecting the terminals the wrong way. This page explains that star and delta differ in the voltage across each winding, and how to read the nameplate so you choose the right connection for a 400 V system every time.

In 30 seconds

- Y: each winding gets $V_L/\sqrt3$ = 230 V · Δ: each winding gets $V_L$ = 400 V

- A winding is designed for one voltage only — the connection must give it that voltage

- Nameplate 230/400 V Δ/Y → on 400 V connect Y · nameplate 400/690 V Δ/Y → on 400 V connect Δ

- Star–delta starting is only possible for motors that run in Δ at 400 V (400/690 V nameplate)

- To reverse rotation: swap any two phases

## The six-terminal box Basic

A three-phase motor has three windings, each with a start and an end. Under IEC 60034-8 the starts are called U1 V1 W1 and the ends U2 V2 W2 (older motors use U-X, V-Y, W-Z). In the terminal box the top row is U1 V1 W1 and the bottom row is ordered W2 U2 V2. You select Y or Δ by placing copper links.

Figure 1 · Star: one horizontal link joins W2-U2-V2 to form the star point · Delta: three vertical links U1–W2, V1–U2, W1–V2

## How star and delta differ Intermediate

C1 Star (Y)

$$V_{ph} = \frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}} \qquad I_L = I_{ph}$$

C2 Delta (Δ)

$$V_{ph} = V_L \qquad I_L = \sqrt{3}\, I_{ph}$$

C3 Power in either connection

$$P = 3\,V_{ph}\,I_{ph}\cos\varphi = \sqrt{3}\,V_L\,I_L\cos\varphi$$

C4 Same windings, same supply: Y vs Δ

$$\frac{V_{ph,Y}}{V_{ph,\Delta}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{I_{L,Y}}{I_{L,\Delta}} = \frac{1}{3} \qquad \frac{T_Y}{T_\Delta} = \frac{1}{3}$$

Where the 1/3 in C4 comes from: the winding voltage falls by √3, so the winding current falls by √3; in Y the line current equals the winding current, while in Δ the line current is √3 times the winding current. Together that gives $1/(\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3) = 1/3$. Torque varies with the square of the winding voltage, $(1/\sqrt3)^2 = 1/3$ — this is the basis of the star–delta starter.

Example C-1

### A 7.5 kW motor, nameplate 400 V Δ 14.6 A, connected in delta at 400 V

- C2: the winding current is $I_{ph} = 14.6/\sqrt3 = 8.43$ A at a winding voltage of 400 V.

- If it is connected in Y for starting, each winding gets 230 V: the starting line current is $95/3 = 32$ A (instead of 95 A) and the starting torque is $2.2/3 = 0.73$ Tn.

- The nameplate line 690 V Y 8.4 A confirms this: on a 690 V system in Y, line current = winding current = 8.4 A and each winding still gets 400 V.

## Choosing the connection from the nameplate Basic

The nameplate gives two voltages. The lower one is the line voltage when connected in Δ, the higher one the line voltage when connected in Y; both give the windings the same voltage. The working rule: find the line whose voltage matches the supply, and connect as the symbol on that line says.

Figure 2 · Decision chart for a 400 V 50 Hz system

| Nameplate | Winding voltage | Connection on 400 V | Star–delta possible? | Found on |

| 230/400 V Δ/Y | 230 V | Y | No | Small motors, about ≤ 3 kW (can run from a single-phase 230 V-input VFD when connected in Δ) |

| 400/690 V Δ/Y | 400 V | Δ | Yes | About ≥ 4 kW |

| 400 V Y (3 terminals) | 230 V | Connected at the factory | No | Submersible pumps, hermetic compressors |

| 380 V Δ (old nameplate) | 380 V | Δ | Yes | Older or imported motors |

Danger: some electricians remember “big motors are connected in delta” and connect a large 230/400 V motor in delta. The windings then get 73 % too much voltage and burn out within minutes. Size is not the criterion — only the nameplate is.

Example C-2

### A 2.2 kW pump, nameplate 230/400 V Δ/Y 8.0/4.6 A — where can it be used?

- Three-phase 400 V system: connect Y, line current 4.6 A, set the overload to 4.6 A, and start it direct-on-line or with a soft starter.

- A house with single-phase 230 V: use a VFD with single-phase input and 3-phase 230 V output, and connect the motor in Δ. The drive output current is 8.0 A.

- Never use star–delta on a 400 V system, because in the Δ stage the windings would get 400 V.

## What happens with a wrong connection Intermediate

| Case | Winding voltage | Symptoms | Result |

| 230/400 V connected Δ at 400 V | 173 % | Loud hum, no-load current above In, heats quickly | Insulation breakdown, burn-out |

| 400/690 V connected Y at 400 V | 58 % | Runs normally at no load; under load the speed drops and current is high | Overload trips, or overheating if set wrong |

| One winding reversed (U1–U2 swapped) | Unbalanced | Vibration, noise, very unequal currents | Overheating, no useful torque |

| Star–delta starter but the links were left in | — | Short circuit when the Y or Δ contactor closes | Breaker trips, arcing in the terminal box |

## Direction of rotation and reversing Basic

IEC 60034-8: with L1 L2 L3 connected to U1 V1 W1 in that order, the motor turns clockwise when viewed from the shaft end. Swap any two phases and the phase sequence seen by the motor reverses, the rotating field reverses and the motor turns the other way — the principle of the reversing circuit.

C5 Direction of rotation

$$L1\!\to\!U1,\ L2\!\to\!V1,\ L3\!\to\!W1 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{CW (viewed from shaft end)} \qquad \text{swap 2 lines} \Rightarrow \text{CCW}$$

With star–delta, both the winding starts (U1 V1 W1) and the winding ends (W2 U2 V2) must be swapped consistently. If only one set is swapped, the Y stage turns backwards but the Δ stage is wired wrongly (some windings get the wrong voltage or none at all) and a high current flows at changeover. The correct method is to swap two phases upstream, before they enter the starter.

## Checks before energising

- Read both nameplate lines and note the voltage and connection that match the supply

- Measure the resistance of all three windings with a milliohmmeter (they should differ by no more than about 2 %)

- Measure winding-to-frame insulation resistance with a 500 V DC megger (details in Design · testing)

- Tighten terminal nuts to the specified torque, use correctly sized lugs, and seal the terminal box to maintain its IP rating

- Connect the motor frame earth to the PE terminal in the terminal box

## Frequently asked questions

What happens if a 230/400 V motor is connected in delta on a 400 V supply?
Each winding gets 400 V although it was designed for 230 V (√3 = 1.73 times too much). The iron saturates and the magnetising current is several times normal even at no load. The overload may trip, or, if it is set wrong, the motor burns out within a short time.

Can a 400/690 V motor be connected in star on a 400 V supply?
It will run, but each winding gets only 230 V and the torque at every speed falls to 1/3. With more than about 1/3 of rated load the slip becomes high, the winding current exceeds its rating and the motor overheats. Star is only acceptable as the starting stage of a star–delta starter.

Why are the bottom terminals ordered W2 U2 V2 rather than U2 V2 W2?
Shifting the bottom row by one position (W2 under U1, U2 under V1, V2 under W1) lets the delta links sit straight up and down: U1–W2, V1–U2, W1–V2. Each link joins the end of one winding to the start of the next, which is exactly the delta connection.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# Motor Starter Simulator: DOL, Reversing, Star–Delta, Soft Starter and VFD

Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: A free in-browser starting simulator for a 7.5 kW 400 V 50 Hz induction motor: press START and STOP and watch contactors pull in, timers count down, the control-circuit state and real-time plots of current, speed and torque, all from a double-cage equivalent-circuit model and the equation of motion. Change between pump, conveyor and fan loads, set timers and dead time, inject phase-loss and overload faults, and work through 6 worksheets.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.14 · AC Motor Control · Starter Simulator

# Motor Starter Simulator: DOL, Reversing, Star–Delta, Soft Starter and VFD

A virtual lab for trying things you cannot or should not do on a real machine: starting a heavy load in star–delta, setting the timer too short, letting a phase drop out, or reversing while the motor is still turning. Every number comes from the same motor model used throughout the course.

How to use it

- Pick a starting method from the tabs · press START/STOP like real push-buttons (you can hold them)

- Left: the power circuit — energised contactors turn green, live conductors turn red — plus the control-circuit state step by step

- Right: meters and a plot of the last 20 seconds · below: load, settings and faults

## Simulator

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

## The model behind it

Every 1 ms the program computes the slip from the present speed, solves the per-phase equivalent circuit (R₁, X₁, Xm and a double-cage rotor) at the voltage and frequency the motor is receiving at that instant to get current and torque, and then integrates $J\,d\omega/dt = T_m - T_L$. The overload uses a first-order thermal model $d\theta/dt = ((I/I_r)^2 - \theta)/\tau$ and trips when $\theta \ge 1.2^2$, which gives a class 10 curve. During star–delta, current and torque in the Y stage are 1/3 of their delta values, as in formulas Y1–Y2.

## Six worksheets

### 1 · Direct-on-line starting current
DOL with a pump load of 0.7 Tn: record the peak current, the time for the speed to reach 1400 rpm and the running current, and compare with Ia/In on the nameplate.
Expect: ~90 A (6.5 In), run-up in under 1 s

### 2 · Normal star–delta start
Load 0.7 Tn, timer 6 s: record the current in the Y stage and the surge at changeover, as multiples of In, and the ratio to DOL.
Expect: Y stage ≈ 1/3 of DOL

### 3 · Timer too short
Set the timer to 0.5 s and repeat worksheet 2. How much does the changeover surge change? Explain it with the plot on the star–delta page.

### 4 · Heavy load with star–delta
Change to a conveyor at 1.0 Tn. What speed does the motor reach in the Y stage, and why? Try a soft starter limited to 3 In and a VFD on the same load. Which method suits it?

### 5 · Phase loss
Run DOL at 0.7 Tn, then tick “phase loss”. Watch the current, the speed and the time until the overload trips. Then stop and try to restart with the phase still missing.
Expect: no start, current stays high

### 6 · Reversing while turning
On the reversing tab, tick “no interlock via STOP”. Run forward to full speed, then press reverse. Record the peak current and the time to pass through zero speed, and calculate the energy with R5.

## Frequently asked questions

How accurate is this simulator?
The model is the per-phase equivalent circuit of a 7.5 kW 4-pole double-cage motor, tuned to typical catalogue data (In ≈ 14 A, Ia/In ≈ 6.5, Ta/Tn ≈ 2.2, Tk/Tn ≈ 3.0). It computes the steady state at each speed and combines it with the equation of motion, so it is good for learning trends and comparing methods. It does not model detailed electrical transients (except the current surge at the changeover, which is approximated).

## FAQ

**How accurate is this simulator?**
The model is the per-phase equivalent circuit of a 7.5 kW 4-pole double-cage motor, tuned to typical catalogue data (In ≈ 14 A, Ia/In ≈ 6.5, Ta/Tn ≈ 2.2, Tk/Tn ≈ 3.0). It computes the steady state at each speed and combines it with the equation of motion, so it is good for learning trends and comparing methods. It does not model detailed electrical transients (except the current surge at the changeover, which is approximated).

# Soft Starters, Autotransformers and Motor Starting Methods Compared: Current, Torque, Voltage Dip and Cost

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/soft-starters/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: How a soft starter works: anti-parallel thyristors, firing-angle control, voltage ramp, current limit, torque control, bypass contactor and soft stop against water hammer in pumps. Autotransformer starting, the current and torque formula for each method, and a comparison of DOL, star–delta, soft starter and VFD with a voltage-dip calculator.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.9 · AC Motor Control · Soft Starters & Autotransformers

# Soft Starters, Autotransformers and Motor Starting Methods Compared: Current, Torque, Voltage Dip and Cost

Every method that lowers the voltage at start-up obeys the same rule: current falls in proportion to voltage, but torque falls with the square of voltage. This page uses that rule to compare starting methods with numbers, and explains the soft starter, now a favourite choice for modern pump installations.

In 30 seconds

- Reduce the voltage by a factor $k$ → current × $k$, torque × $k^2$

- Soft starter: thyristors chop the waveform, ramp the voltage, limit current to 2–4 In, then bypass

- Autotransformer at tap $a$: motor current × $a$, line current × $a^2$, torque × $a^2$

- Soft stop reduces water hammer in pump pipework — something star–delta cannot do

## The rule of reduced-voltage starting Intermediate

T1 Reduced-voltage starting

$$\frac{V}{V_n} = k \;\Rightarrow\; I_{st} = k\,I_{st,DOL} \qquad T_{st} = k^2\,T_{st,DOL}$$

T2 Torque at a current limit

$$T_{st} = T_{st,DOL}\left(\frac{I_{lim}}{I_{st,DOL}}\right)^2$$

Example T-1

### Motor with Ia/In = 6.5, Ta/Tn = 2.2, current limit set to 3 In

- $k = 3/6.5 = 0.46$ → initial voltage about 46 %

- T2: $T_{st} = 2.2(0.46)^2 = 0.47$ Tn — enough for a centrifugal pump (~0.15 Tn) but not for a loaded conveyor (~1.0–1.5 Tn)

- Compare star–delta: current $6.5/3 = 2.2$ In but torque $2.2/3 = 0.73$ Tn — lower current yet higher torque, because the winding voltage falls only by $1/\sqrt3$ while the line current falls to 1/3 (it behaves like an autotransformer with $a = 0.58$, see Example T-2)

## How a soft starter works Intermediate

Each phase has two thyristors (SCRs) connected in anti-parallel. The controller fires the thyristors at an angle α after the voltage zero crossing, so the motor receives only the tail end of each half-cycle. As α is steadily reduced, the rms voltage at the motor steadily rises. When full voltage is reached an internal bypass contactor closes and the thyristors stop conducting, so there is no heat loss in them during normal running.

Figure 1 · Motor voltage waveform during the ramp: from narrow slices of the wave (large α) to the full wave, then bypass

T3 RMS voltage vs firing angle (resistive approximation)

$$\frac{V_{rms}}{V} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{\alpha}{\pi} + \frac{\sin 2\alpha}{2\pi}}$$

Formula T3 applies to a resistive load and is meant to show the trend. A motor is an inductive load whose current lags, so the conduction interval is longer than this. A real soft starter measures the current and adjusts α by feedback.

### Common starting modes

- Voltage ramp: starts at an initial voltage (30–60 %) and rises linearly over a set time (5–30 s)

- Current limit: adjusts the voltage so the current never exceeds k·In (2–4 In) throughout acceleration

- Torque control: makes the torque rise smoothly so speed rises almost linearly; well suited to pumps and conveyors

- Kick start: applies a short burst of high voltage at the start to overcome static friction

- Soft stop / pump stop: lowers the voltage slowly when stopping so the water in the pipe decelerates without slamming the check valve (water hammer)

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

### Connection and precautions

- Upstream short-circuit protection is required: a circuit-breaker for Type 1 or semiconductor fuses for Type 2 coordination, per the manufacturer's tables

- Never connect power-factor correction capacitors between the soft starter and the motor — connect them on the supply side and switch them out during the ramp

- Set the motor rated current, overload class and number of starts per hour as specified by the manufacturer (the thyristors heat up during starting)

- A line-side contactor or disconnect switch is needed for isolation during maintenance (blocked thyristors do not count as isolation)

## Autotransformer starting Advanced

A three-phase autotransformer has taps such as 50 %, 65 % and 80 %. The motor receives $aV$ and the motor current falls by a factor $a$, but because the transformer also transforms current, the current in the supply lines falls by $a^2$ — a better reduction in line current than a resistor starter or a soft starter at the same torque. It is used for large motors such as raw-water pumps and large compressors (often built as a Korndorfer starter with closed-transition changeover).

T4 Autotransformer starter at tap $a$

$$I_{motor} = a\,I_{st,DOL} \qquad I_{line} = a^2\,I_{st,DOL} \qquad T_{st} = a^2\,T_{st,DOL}$$

Example T-2

### 65 % tap with a motor of Ia/In = 7, Ta/Tn = 2.3

- $a^2 = 0.4225$ → line current $0.4225 \times 7 = 2.96$ In · torque $0.4225 \times 2.3 = 0.97$ Tn

- Compare a soft starter at the same line current of 2.96 In: T2 → only $2.3(2.96/7)^2 = 0.41$ Tn

- The autotransformer gives almost twice the torque at the same line current, at the price of size, weight and cost

## Comparing every method Intermediate

Figure 2 · Starting current and torque of an example motor (Ia/In 6.5 · Ta/Tn 2.15)

T5 Supply dip for any method

$$\Delta U\% \approx \frac{\sqrt3\,V_L\,I_{line,st}}{S_{tr}/u_k + \sqrt3\,V_L\,I_{line,st}}\times 100$$

| Criterion | DOL | Star–delta | Autotransformer | Soft starter | VFD |

| Line current | 6–8 In | 2–2.7 In | 2–4 In | 2–4 In | ≤ 1.5 In |

| Starting torque | Highest | 1/3 | a² | (I/Is)² | High, controllable |

| Smoothness | Jerk | Two jerks | Moderate | Smooth | Smoothest |

| Soft stop | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ (controlled) |

| Cables to motor | 3 | 6 | 3 | 3 (inside delta: 6) | 3, shielded |

| Harmonics | — | — | — | During ramp only | Continuous |

| Relative cost | 1 | 1.5–2 | 3–5 | 2–3 | 3–6 |

## Frequently asked questions

Can a soft starter control speed?
No. A soft starter reduces the voltage but the frequency stays at 50 Hz, so under normal load the motor always runs close to rated speed. Reducing the voltage under load only raises the slip and heats the motor. If you need speed control you must use a variable-frequency drive (VFD).

What is an inside-delta soft starter connection?
Some models place the thyristors in series with each winding inside the delta, so they carry only 0.58 In and a smaller soft starter can be used. However, six cables must be run to the motor, as with star–delta, and the connection must follow the manufacturer's diagram exactly.

Mod

Summary: Design and wire a star–delta (Y-Δ) starter for 400/690 V motors on a 400 V 50 Hz supply, step by step: why current and torque fall to 1/3, the KM1 KM2 KM3 power circuit, overload position and the 0.58 In setting, contactor sizing, the control circuit with interlocks, timer and dead time, the current surge at changeover, the delta-side phase sequence, six-lead cabling, closed-transition star–delta and a troubleshooting table.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.8 · AC Motor Control · Star–Delta Starter

# Star–Delta Starter in Detail: Power Circuit, Control Circuit, 0.58 In Contactor Sizing, Overload Setting, Timer and Changeover Timing

Star–delta is the most popular way to reduce starting current in the region, because it uses ordinary devices and no electronics. It is also the circuit that is wired wrongly most often. This page goes through everything that has to be right: which motors can use it, where the overload goes, contactor sizes, the wiring sequence, the timer, and what really happens during the changeover.

In 30 seconds

- Only for motors with a 400/690 V Δ/Y nameplate · remove the links in the terminal box and run 6 leads

- Star stage: KM1 + KM2 · run stage: KM1 + KM3 · KM2 and KM3 must never close together

- Current and torque in star = 1/3 of a direct-on-line start

- KM1 = KM3 ≥ 0.58 In · KM2 ≥ 0.33 In · overload in the phase-current path set to 0.58 In

- Change to delta at 85–90 % speed · with a 50–100 ms dead time

## Principle: start with 1/√3 of the winding voltage Basic

Take a motor that normally runs in delta on 400 V. If its windings are connected in star for starting, each winding receives only 230 V, so the line current drops to 1/3 and the torque drops to 1/3 (derived in C4). When the motor has accelerated close to full speed, it is switched to delta to get full torque.

Y1 Starting current in star

$$I_{L,Y} = \frac{I_{L,\Delta}}{3} = \frac{k_{st}\,I_n}{3}$$

Y2 Starting torque in star

$$T_Y(n) = \frac{T_\Delta(n)}{3} \qquad T_{st,Y} = \frac{T_a/T_n}{3}\,T_n \approx 0.7\text{–}0.8\,T_n$$

Figure 1 · Computed curves for the example motor: in star (solid lines) the current starts at 2.2 In and the torque at 0.72 Tn. On changing to delta at ~1330 rpm the current jumps up along the yellow line

Important limitation: the torque in star is only ~0.7 Tn, so star–delta suits loads that start light (centrifugal pumps, fans, compressors with an unloading system). If the load needs high starting torque — a fully loaded conveyor, a crusher with material left inside — the motor cannot accelerate in star and then surges almost as much as a direct-on-line start at changeover. You lose time and gain no current reduction.

## Power circuit and overload position Intermediate

Figure 2 · (The drawing uses the codes -K1 -K2 -K3, corresponding to KM1 KM2 KM3 in the text.) KM1 (main) feeds U1 V1 W1 through F2 · KM3 (delta) connects W2 U2 V2 back to L1 L2 L3 · KM2 (star) shorts W2 U2 V2 together

| Contactor | Function | Closed during | Current carried |

| KM1 main | Feeds the winding starts U1 V1 W1 | Star + run | Phase current $I_n/\sqrt3$ (when running) |

| KM2 star | Shorts the winding ends W2 U2 V2 to form the star point | Star only | $k_{st}I_n/3$ for a short time; breaks only the current after acceleration |

| KM3 delta | Connects each winding end to the next phase | Run only | Phase current $I_n/\sqrt3$ |

Y3 Main and delta contactors

$$I_e(\text{KM1}) = I_e(\text{KM3}) \ge \frac{I_n}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.58\,I_n \quad (\text{AC-3})$$

Y4 Star contactor

$$I_e(\text{KM2}) \ge \frac{I_n}{3} \approx 0.33\,I_n \quad (\text{AC-3})$$

Y5 Overload setting (in the phase-current path)

$$I_r = \frac{I_n}{\sqrt3} \approx 0.58\,I_n$$

Why F2 goes after KM1: this position carries the winding current in both the star and run stages, so the relay protects the windings most directly. If the overload is placed before the split to KM1 and KM3 (in the line-current path), it must be set to In and the relay has to be larger. Some manufacturers place F2 after KM3 instead — always check the position on the drawing before setting it. If an MPCB is used ahead of the starter (line current), set the MPCB to In and use a separate overload in the phase-current path, or let the MPCB provide all the overload protection according to the manufacturer's tables.

### Delta-side wiring sequence

The standard arrangement wires KM3 to give the same result as the links in the terminal box: L1→W2, L2→U2, L3→V2 (winding U1–U2 receives the L1–L2 voltage). The direction of rotation in Y and in Δ then matches automatically. Some manufacturers recommend the “lagging” connection L1→V2, L2→W2, L3→U2, which brings the new winding voltage closer in phase to the residual voltage in the motor and so reduces the surge at changeover. Both turn the same way and both are correct. The key point is never to swap leads at will — swapping the wrong pair short-circuits some windings or gives them the wrong voltage.

## Control circuit: sequence and interlocks Intermediate

Figure 3 · KM2 closes before KM1 (through KM2 13-14), so no power reaches the motor until the star point is made. KM1 holds itself in through 43-44 · KM2 and KM3 are interlocked with each other through 21-22, and should also have a mechanical interlock

- Press S1 → K4T starts timing, and KM2 (star) closes through K4T 15-16 (delayed NC) and KM3 21-22

- KM2 13-14 closes → KM1 closes → the motor is energised in star · KM1 13-14 holds in the START button · 43-44 holds in its own coil

- When time t has elapsed: K4T 15-16 opens → KM2 drops out → KM2 21-22 recloses

- K4T 17-18 closes (a dedicated Y-Δ timer adds a further 50–100 ms delay) → KM3 closes → delta

- Press S0 or an overload trip → everything drops out and the timer resets

Figure 4 · The dead time between KM2 opening and KM3 closing is needed so that the arc in KM2's arc chute is fully extinguished first

Y6 Changeover dead time

$$t_{dead} \approx 40\text{–}100\ \text{ms} \;>\; t_{arc,KM2} + t_{close,KM3}\ \text{margin}$$

## NEMA/JIC version: the wye–delta starter and motor leads T1–T6 Intermediate

North America calls star–delta “wye–delta” (open transition = the motor is briefly disconnected at the change-over). The same three contactors are used, but motor leads are T1–T6 and the control is a ladder.

Figure 3a · NEMA wye–delta: 1M (line) feeds T1 T2 T3 through the OL heaters · 2M (delta) connects L1→T6, L2→T4, L3→T5 · 1S (wye) shorts T4 T5 T6 · timer TR changes over

| IEC | NEMA | Role |

| -K1 | 1M | Line (main) contactor |

| -K2 | 1S | Star (wye), shorts T4 T5 T6 |

| -K3 | 2M | Delta (run) |

| -K4T | TR | Timer: contacts NCTO (15-16) and NOTC (17-18) |

| U1 V1 W1 / U2 V2 W2 | T1 T2 T3 / T4 T5 T6 | Delta: T1–T6 · T2–T4 · T3–T5 (IEC: U1–W2 · V1–U2 · W1–V2) |

The names 1M / 2M / 1S vary by manufacturer (some swap the roles of 1M and 2M) — follow the machine’s own drawing · get the delta-side phasing right: wrong T4/T5/T6 order gives a change-over surge worse than a direct start · closed-transition starters add resistors so the supply is never interrupted.

## Setting the timer and the current at changeover Advanced

The run-up time depends on the inertia and the accelerating torque (motor torque minus load torque), from Newton's second law for rotation.

Y7 Acceleration time

$$J\frac{d\omega}{dt} = T_m - T_L \;\Rightarrow\; t_{acc} \approx \frac{J\,\Delta\omega}{\overline{T_m - T_L}}$$

Y8 Condition before changing to delta

$$T_Y(n) > T_L(n)\ \ \forall\, n During the dead time the motor has no supply, but flux remains in the rotor, producing a residual voltage at the terminals whose frequency falls with the speed. When KM3 connects, if the phase of this residual voltage does not match the supply, a momentary surge is added on top of the normal current at that speed. The lower the changeover speed, the higher the normal delta current at that speed (see Figure 1).

Example Y-1

### 37 kW pump, 400 V Δ, In = 66 A, Ia/In = 7, Ta/Tn = 2.3 — design the star–delta starter

- Y1: direct-on-line $7 \times 66 = 462$ A → in star $462/3 = 154$ A

- Y3: KM1 = KM3 ≥ $0.58 \times 66 = 38.3$ A → 40 A AC-3 · Y4: KM2 ≥ $0.33 \times 66 = 21.8$ A → 25 A AC-3

- Y5: overload (after KM1) set to 38.3 A → a 30–40 A class 10 relay

- Y2: starting torque in star $2.3/3 = 0.77$ Tn > pump breakaway torque ~0.15 Tn ✓

- Six leads from the panel to the motor, each carrying the phase current of 38.3 A → size the cable for 38.3 A, not 66 A (see Y9)

Example Y-2

### Estimate the timer setting for the 37 kW pump

- $T_n = 9550(37)/1480 = 239$ N·m · motor + pump inertia $J \approx 0.3 + 0.6 = 0.9$ kg·m²

- Average torque in star ~0.8 Tn · average pump torque over 0–90 % speed ~0.35 Tn → accelerating torque ~0.45 Tn = 108 N·m

- Y7: $\Delta\omega = 0.9 \times 155 = 140$ rad/s → $t \approx 0.9(140)/108 = 1.2$ s

- Set the timer to 3 s (allowing for voltage dip and wear), then confirm with a clamp meter that the current in star has settled before the changeover

## Try it in the simulator

Try three scenarios: (1) load 0.7 Tn, timer 6 s — a smooth changeover · (2) cut the timer to 0.5 s — the current at changeover rises sharply · (3) a conveyor load of 1.0 Tn — the motor cannot accelerate in star, then surges almost as much as DOL

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

## Six leads to the motor Intermediate

Y9 Cable sizing for six leads

$$I_z \ge \frac{I_n}{\sqrt3} \ \text{per conductor} \qquad \Delta V \text{ from the phase current and the actual length}$$

- Two sets of conductors must be run (U1 V1 W1 and W2 U2 V2), which raises cable cost over long distances — one reason new installations are moving to soft starters or VFDs

- Both sets must run in the same conduit or tray to avoid induced heating in metal conduit

- Mark the cable ends to match the motor terminals at both ends — a mistake here connects the delta in the wrong pattern

## Closed-transition star–delta Advanced

The closed-transition version adds a fourth contactor and three resistors. Before KM2 opens, the fourth contactor connects the windings to the supply through the resistors, so the motor is never disconnected during the changeover and the surge is much smaller. It suits large motors and high-inertia loads, but it is more complex and more expensive. Today this kind of duty is usually handled by a soft starter instead.

## Star–delta troubleshooting table

| Symptom | Possible causes | Check / fix |

| Breaker trips the moment it changes to delta | KM2/KM3 overlap · links not removed · wrong delta wiring sequence | Check the dead time, interlocks, terminal box and the W2 U2 V2 lead numbers |

| Motor turns slowly in star and does not come up to speed | Starting load too heavy · voltage dip · a 230/400 V motor connected | Measure the current in star, check the nameplate, reduce the load at starting or change the starting method |

| Very high surge at changeover | Timer too short · dead time too long (motor slows down a lot) | Set the timer from the actual speed; use a dedicated Y-Δ timer |

| Overload trips during normal running | Set to 0.58 In but the relay is in the line-current path (or the other way round) | Check the F2 position on the drawing and set it to match |

| Motor reverses direction when it changes to delta | Phases swapped on only the winding-start set or only the winding-end set | Wire the W2 U2 V2 set as drawn; swap phases only at the supply |

| KM2 chatters or hums during starting | Coil voltage dips under the high starting current · cracked shading ring | Measure the coil voltage during starting; check the control transformer size |

## Frequently asked questions

Why are the contactors in a star–delta starter smaller than the motor rating?
Because the main contactor (KM1) and the delta contactor (KM3) each carry the winding phase current, which is In/√3 = 0.58 In. The star contactor (KM2) carries current only during starting, 1/3 of the direct-on-line starting current, and breaks a low current, so ≥ 0.33 In is enough. Example: a 66 A motor uses 40 A + 40 A + 25 A.

How many seconds should the star–delta timer be set to?
Set it to change to delta when the motor reaches about 85–90 % of speed, which you can see as the current falling and settling during the star stage. Small pumps and fans often use 3–8 s; high-inertia loads may need 10–20 s. The best method is to clamp a meter on the line and watch the current in star, then set the timer slightly longer than the point where the current settles. Too short and the surge is almost as large as a direct-on-line start; too long and the motor runs in star for no reason.

The motor runs in star, then the breaker trips when it changes to delta. Why?
Common causes: no dead time or too short a dead time, so KM2 and KM3 overlap through the arc; a wrong delta-side wiring sequence that connects the windings in the wrong pattern; a timer so short that the motor has not accelerated; or the copper links in the terminal box were not removed.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# The 230/400 V 50 Hz Low-Voltage Supply in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Myanmar, Malaysia and Singapore for Motor Control

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/supply-systems/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: The three-phase four-wire 230/400 V 50 Hz supply under IEC 60038 and the voltages actually found in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Myanmar, Malaysia and Singapore: phase versus line voltage, ±10 % tolerance, TN-C-S and TT earthing, phase sequence, voltage unbalance and motor derating, and running 60 Hz motors on a 50 Hz supply.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.2 · AC Motor Control · 230/400 V 50 Hz Supply

# The 230/400 V 50 Hz Low-Voltage Supply in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Myanmar, Malaysia and Singapore for Motor Control

Motors and control gear are designed for one particular voltage and frequency. If you understand the supply on site — its real voltage, its earthing system and its power quality — you can choose the terminal connection and set the devices correctly from the start. This page collects what you need to know for seven countries that share the same kind of supply.

In 30 seconds

- Three-phase four-wire: phase voltage 230 V (L–N), line voltage 400 V (L–L) = √3 × 230

- Every country here uses 50 Hz · real voltages lie between 220/380 and 240/415 V

- Three-phase motors connect to L1 L2 L3 + PE, no N · 230 V control circuits use L–N

- 1 % voltage unbalance causes 6–10 % current unbalance → the motor must be derated

## The three-phase four-wire system Basic

The utility's distribution transformer (e.g. 22 kV/400 V or 33 kV/400 V) has its low-voltage side connected in Y with the neutral point earthed, giving conductors L1, L2, L3 and N. Between a phase conductor and neutral is the phase voltage, 230 V; between two phase conductors is the line voltage, 400 V.

Figure 1 · Three phase voltages 120° apart (325 V peak) and the line voltage v₁₂ = v₁ − v₂ (565 V peak), leading by 30°

S1 Line and phase voltage

$$V_L = \sqrt{3}\,V_{ph} \qquad 230 \times \sqrt3 = 398 \approx 400\ \text{V} \qquad V_{peak} = \sqrt2\, V_{rms}$$

S2 Three-phase power

$$P = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L \cos\varphi \qquad S = \sqrt{3}\,V_L I_L$$

## Voltage and frequency by country Basic

IEC 60038 sets the nominal value 230/400 V for 50 Hz systems, and countries in the region have been moving to it from 220/380 V or 240/415 V. Equipment rated “380–415 V 50 Hz” (the normal rating for IEC contactors, drives and motors) can be used in all of them.

| Country | Nominal value | Still found on site | Frequency | Things to know |

| Thailand | 230/400 V | 220/380 V in older systems | 50 Hz | Metropolitan Electricity Authority (MEA) and Provincial Electricity Authority (PEA) · installations to the Engineering Institute of Thailand (EIT) wiring code |

| Laos | 230/400 V | 220/380 V | 50 Hz | Grid interconnected with Thailand at many points; Thai equipment can be used |

| Cambodia | 230/400 V | 220/380 V | 50 Hz | Voltage varies a lot by area; measure before installing |

| Vietnam | 220/380 V | — | 50 Hz | A 400 V motor gets 5 % below its nameplate: starting torque ~10 % lower, full-load current slightly higher |

| Myanmar | 230/400 V | Large voltage swings | 50 Hz | Under/overvoltage and phase-loss protection relays recommended |

| Malaysia | 230/400 V | 240/415 V (before 2008) | 50 Hz | Older 415 V-rated motors and transformers are still compatible |

| Singapore | 230/400 V | — | 50 Hz | Installation to SS 638 (based on IEC 60364) |

This table is an overview for learning. The guaranteed voltage and its tolerance (e.g. +10 %/−6 % or ±10 %) are set by each country's utility and may be revised. Always check the local supplier's documents.

Example S-1

### A 400 V motor on 380 V and 415 V supplies

- 380 V is 95 % of the nameplate → torque at every point on the curve falls to $0.95^2 = 0.90$ (M8).

- At constant load the slip rises by about $1/0.90$ and full-load current increases by roughly 3–5 % → keep the overload set to the nameplate current; do not raise it.

- 415 V is 104 %: flux is higher and no-load current increases, but it is still within zone A of IEC 60034-1 (±5 %), so the motor runs normally.

## Earthing systems: TN-C-S and TT Intermediate

The earthing system tells you by which path the motor's metal frame is “earthed”, and that decides whether a fault current to the frame is large enough to trip the breaker. In Thailand the utility earths the neutral at the transformer and the customer joins N and PE at a single point in the main switchboard (TN-C-S). Other countries use both TN and TT, depending on the supplier and the type of installation.

Figure 2 · TN-C-S: a single PEN conductor runs from the transformer to the main switchboard; after the switchboard N and PE are separated and must never be joined again. The motor frame is always connected to PE.

| System | Path of an earth-fault current | Disconnecting device | Watch out for |

| TN-C-S / TN-S | Through PE back to the transformer; low impedance, high current | Breaker/fuse/MPCB disconnects quickly | Cable length must not be so long that the fault current is too small · never re-join N and PE after the split point |

| TT | Through the customer's earth electrode and the soil; low current | RCD (residual-current device) | A breaker alone often cannot disconnect in time · drives need a suitable RCD type |

## Phase sequence and direction of rotation Basic

The phase sequence L1→L2→L3 (some sites use R-S-T or A-B-C) sets the direction of the rotating field. With L1-L2-L3 connected to U1-V1-W1 in that order, an IEC motor turns clockwise viewed from the shaft end (IEC 60034-8). Before coupling to a pump or compressor that must not run backwards, check the phase sequence with a phase-rotation meter or bump the motor briefly uncoupled.

S3 Reversing rotation

$$(L1, L2, L3) \to (L3, L2, L1) \;\Rightarrow\; n_s \to -n_s$$

## Voltage unbalance and motor derating Advanced

When the three phase voltages are unequal, a negative-sequence voltage appears, which produces a field rotating “backwards”. The motor's negative-sequence impedance is very low (close to its starting impedance), so even a small voltage unbalance causes a large current unbalance and rotor heating.

S4 Voltage unbalance (NEMA working definition)

$$\%VU = \frac{\max |V_{L} - \bar V_L|}{\bar V_L} \times 100 \qquad \bar V_L = \frac{V_{12} + V_{23} + V_{31}}{3}$$

S5 Current unbalance estimate

$$\%I_{unb} \approx \frac{I_{st}}{I_n}\,\%VU \approx (6\text{–}10)\,\%VU$$

| %VU | 1 % | 2 % | 3 % | 4 % | 5 % |

| Derating factor (approx., per NEMA MG 1) | 0.98 | 0.95 | 0.88 | 0.82 | 0.75 |

Example S-2

### Measured 402 V · 396 V · 389 V

- Average $(402 + 396 + 389)/3 = 395.7$ V · largest deviation $|389 - 395.7| = 6.7$ V

- S4: $\%VU = 6.7/395.7 = 1.7\,\%$ → S5: current unbalance of about 10–17 %

- Derating factor ≈ 0.96 · find the cause first — poorly distributed single-phase loads, loose connections or a transformer problem — before upsizing the motor.

## 60 Hz motors on a 50 Hz supply Intermediate

Machines imported from North America, and some from Japan or Korea, may have 60 Hz motors. Core flux varies as $V/f$, so that ratio must be kept close to its original value.

S6 60 Hz motor on 50 Hz

$$\Phi \propto \frac{V}{f} \qquad V_{50} = V_{60}\cdot\frac{50}{60} \qquad n_{50} = \frac{5}{6} n_{60} \qquad P_{50} \approx \frac{5}{6} P_{60}$$

| 60 Hz nameplate | Suitable voltage at 50 Hz | Usable on a 400 V system? |

| 460 V 60 Hz | 383 V | Yes (380–400 V), speed −17 %, power −17 % |

| 380 V 60 Hz (some Japanese/Korean models) | 317 V | Not advisable: 400 V is 26 % too high, flux saturates, overheating |

| 230 V 60 Hz | 192 V | No — needs a transformer or a VFD |

The most flexible solution is a VFD: you can set the base frequency and base voltage directly to the 60 Hz nameplate (see VFD principles).

## Power-quality problems that affect motors

- Phase loss (single phasing): one fuse blows or a contact burns. A running motor keeps running with ~1.7 times the current in the two remaining phases and cannot restart → use an overload with phase-loss detection or a phase-protection relay.

- Voltage sags: AC contactors may drop out when the coil voltage falls below ~60 %, stopping a whole line — think about safe automatic restart.

- Harmonics: from drives and electronic loads; they add heating in direct-on-line motors and put PF-correction capacitors at risk of resonance (see True PF and harmonics (Thai)).

## Frequently asked questions

Is there a difference between 220 V and 230 V mains?
It is the same system with its nominal value changed under IEC 60038 from 220/380 V to 230/400 V. Equipment designed to IEC works on both because they fall within the ±10 % tolerance. The real voltage on site is usually between 215 and 240 V.

Can a 60 Hz motor from the USA run on 50 Hz?
Yes, if the voltage is reduced in proportion to frequency (keeping V/f the same). A 460 V 60 Hz motor, for example, can run at 380–400 V 50 Hz, with speed and power reduced to 5/6. A 230 V 60 Hz motor would need 190 V at 50 Hz, which our systems do not provide; fed with 230 V 50 Hz its flux is 20 % too high and it overheats.

Does a three-phase motor need the N conductor?
No. A three-phase motor is connected to L1, L2, L3 and the PE earth only. The N conductor is used for 230 V control circuits or single-phase loads.

Summary: A 12-step VFD commissioning procedure that works for any brand: nameplate data, auto-tune, acceleration and deceleration times, command sources, preset speeds from digital inputs, 0–10 V and 4–20 mA analog inputs, constant-pressure water pumps with the drive's built-in PID, conveyors, fans, the affinity laws Q ∝ n, H ∝ n², P ∝ n³, calculating energy savings and payback, temperature derating in hot and humid climates, bypass, and common fault codes.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.12 · AC Motor Control · VFD Setup & Applications

# VFD Setup and Applications: Basic Parameters, Multi-Step Speeds, 0–10 V / 4–20 mA, Constant-Pressure PID Pumps and Energy Savings from the Affinity Laws

Every drive manufacturer names its parameters differently, but what has to be set is the same on every brand. This page gives a commissioning sequence that works in general, the most common applications, and how to prove with numbers whether a VFD is worth the money.

In 30 seconds

- Enter the full nameplate data, then auto-tune before doing anything else

- Ramp times too short → OC/OV trips · too long → sluggish response

- Analog: $f = f_{min} + (f_{max} - f_{min})\cdot\frac{x - x_0}{x_1 - x_0}$

- Pumps and fans: $P \propto n^3$ — cut speed by 20 % and power falls to ~51 % (with no static head)

- Hot, humid climate: check the temperature inside the panel and derate per the manual

## The 12-step setup Basic

- Reset to factory defaults (when reusing a drive that has been used before)

- Motor data: voltage, current, power, frequency, speed and cos φ from the nameplate (for the Y/Δ connection actually used)

- Auto-tune: static (stationary) if the load cannot be uncoupled, rotating if it can

- Control mode: V/f for pumps and fans or several motors · vector for high torque at low speed

- Minimum and maximum frequency: e.g. 20–50 Hz for a pump (below that the water will not rise)

- Acceleration and deceleration times: start at 5–10 s and adjust (see P1)

- Stop method: ramp (decelerate over time) or coast (free-wheel) — large fans usually coast

- Command source: keypad / terminals (DI) / communication (Modbus) · speed source: keypad / AI / preset / bus

- Digital inputs: RUN FWD, RUN REV, reset, preset speed, external fault

- Analog input: type (0–10 V or 4–20 mA) and scaling (see P2)

- Outputs: fault/run relays to pilot lamps or the PLC · AO showing frequency or current

- Test: run uncoupled, check the direction of rotation (it can be reversed by a parameter), apply load, measure current, record every setting

Parameter names with the same function (examples of terms manufacturers use)

| Function | Terms found in manuals |

| Motor rated current | Motor rated current · Rated motor current · Nominal current |

| Acceleration / deceleration time | Acceleration time · Ramp-up time · Accel 1 / Decel 1 |

| Run command source | Run command source · Control place · Operation mode |

| Frequency source | Frequency reference · Speed setpoint source |

| Switching frequency | Carrier frequency · PWM frequency · Switching frequency |

P1 Minimum ramp time without tripping

$$t_{acc,min} \approx \frac{J\,\omega_n}{T_{lim} - \overline{T_L}} \qquad T_{lim} \approx 1.5\,T_n\ \ (\text{set by the drive current limit})$$

P2 Analog reference scaling

$$f = f_{min} + (f_{max} - f_{min})\,\frac{x - x_0}{x_1 - x_0} \qquad x: 0\text{–}10\ \text{V or } 4\text{–}20\ \text{mA}$$

Example P-1

### A PLC sends 12 mA to a pump set for a 20–50 Hz range

- P2: $f = 20 + 30\,(12 - 4)/(20 - 4) = 20 + 15 = 35$ Hz

- If the 4–20 mA wire breaks, the signal becomes 0 mA — set the drive to detect “signal loss” (< 2–3 mA) and then stop or run at a fallback speed, instead of interpreting it as 20 Hz

## Multi-step speeds from digital inputs Basic

Two or three digital inputs select preset speeds in binary. This suits conveyors or mixers that need only a few speeds, and they can be commanded from a selector switch or a PLC without any analog signal.

| DI3 | DI4 | Resulting speed | Example value |

| 0 | 0 | Main reference (keypad/AI) | 50 Hz |

| 1 | 0 | Preset 1 | 15 Hz (jog/positioning) |

| 0 | 1 | Preset 2 | 30 Hz |

| 1 | 1 | Preset 3 | 45 Hz |

## Constant-pressure water pumping with the drive's PID Intermediate

A building booster water system uses a 4–20 mA pressure transmitter wired to the drive's AI. You set the target (e.g. 3.5 bar) and the drive computes PID and adjusts the frequency to hold the pressure constant even as water demand changes. Functions you should set:

- Sleep / wake-up: when there is no demand, the frequency falls to a low value; after it stays there longer than a set time the drive stops the pump, and it restarts when the pressure drops a set amount below the target

- Dry-run protection: abnormally low current or power at high frequency = the pump is running dry; stop and raise an alarm

- Pipe fill: fill the pipework slowly at start-up to prevent water hammer

- Multi-pump: many drives can start a second pump (DOL or another drive) when demand exceeds one pump

PID theory and tuning are in Control systems: PID (Thai), and an example of a PLC commanding a VFD is in PLC analog, PID and VFD.

## The affinity laws and energy savings Intermediate

Figure 1 · Left: the affinity laws · Right: at 80 % flow, throttling with a valve still uses about 90 % power, while a VFD uses about 55 %

P3 Affinity law — flow

$$\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

P4 Affinity law — head

$$\frac{H_2}{H_1} = \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^2$$

P5 Affinity law — power

$$\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^3$$

P6 System with static head

$$H_{sys} = H_{st} + kQ^2 \qquad \frac{n}{n_1} \approx \sqrt{h_0 + (1 - h_0)q^2} \quad (h_0 = H_{st}/H_1,\ q = Q/Q_1)$$

P7 Energy saved per year

$$\Delta E = (P_{throttle} - P_{VFD})\,h \qquad \text{money} = \Delta E \times \text{tariff per kWh}$$

P8 Simple payback

$$t_{payback} = \frac{\text{installed VFD cost}}{\text{savings per year}}$$

Example P-2

### A 30 kW ventilation fan runs 6,000 h/year at an average 75 % flow; electricity costs 4.5 baht/kWh

- Damper throttling: $P \approx 30(0.55 + 0.45 \times 0.75) = 26.6$ kW

- VFD (P5, no static head): $30 \times 0.75^3 / 0.97 + 0.6 = 13.6$ kW (including drive losses)

- P7: $\Delta E = (26.6 - 13.6)(6000) = 78{,}000$ kWh/year ≈ 351,000 baht/year

- P8: installed drive 180,000 baht → payback ~0.5 year

## Installing in a hot, humid climate Intermediate

- Most drives are rated at 40 °C ambient (some at 50 °C); above that, derate by about 1–2.5 %/°C per the manual — the inside of a panel standing in the tropical sun can exceed 50 °C

- Above 1000 m altitude, derate ~1 % per 100 m

- High humidity and condensation: fit anti-condensation heaters in panels that stand idle for long periods, and choose conformally coated boards (3C2/3C3)

- Cooling: drive losses are ~2–3 % of rated power and must be included when sizing the panel fan (see K7)

## Bypass and multiple motors Advanced

Critical duties (a fire pump must never rely on a VFD as its only path; main wastewater pumps) may need a bypass: contactor KM-VFD (on the drive output) and KM-BYP (from the mains straight to the motor), interlocked both electrically and mechanically, switching over only when the drive has stopped and the motor is de-energised, and with an overload relay for the bypass path. One drive can run several motors at once in V/f mode, provided the drive is sized ≥ 1.1 × the sum of the motor currents and each motor has its own overload relay.

## Common fault codes

| Code (typical) | Meaning | Cause / remedy |

| OC / Overcurrent | Instantaneous overcurrent | Accelerating too fast, shorted motor cable, no auto-tune, boost too high |

| OV / DC overvoltage | DC bus too high | Decelerating too fast, overhauling load, high supply voltage → increase decel time or fit a braking resistor |

| UV / Undervoltage | DC bus too low | Supply dip, lost input phase, blown input fuse |

| OH / Overtemperature | Heatsink too hot | Failed drive fan, hot panel, clogged with dust, high switching frequency |

| OL / Motor overload | Motor thermal model full | Overload, long running at low speed and high torque, wrong motor current setting |

| GF / Earth fault | Earth leakage on the output | Deteriorated cable or motor insulation, moisture in the terminal box |

| PHL / Input phase loss | Input phase missing or unbalanced | Check fuses, terminals and the three-phase voltages |

## Frequently asked questions

How much energy do I save by running a pump at half speed?
By the affinity laws, in a system with no static head the power falls to (0.5)³ = 12.5 %, a saving of almost 88 %. A real system that must lift water to a height has to keep a certain minimum speed to overcome the static head, so it saves much less. Use the system curve, or the calculator on this page, which accepts a static-head fraction.

My VFD trips on OC (overcurrent) during acceleration. How do I fix it?
Increase the acceleration time, check that the motor current and power are entered correctly and that auto-tune has been done, check the motor cable for short circuits or earth leakage, and see whether the load is mechanically jammed. If the load genuinely has high inertia, you may need a drive with a heavy-duty rating.

# Variable-Frequency Drives (VFDs) for Motors: Rectifier, DC Bus, IGBT PWM, V/f and Vector Control, and Correct Wiring

URL: https://modsengineeringmath.com/learn/en/motor-control/vfd/
Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: How a variable-frequency drive works for 400 V 50 Hz motors: six-diode rectifier, 540–565 V DC bus, IGBT PWM inverter, constant V/f control, voltage boost, field weakening, sensorless vector control, input and output wiring, shielded cable and EMC, cable length and dv/dt, Type B RCDs, braking resistors, single-phase-in three-phase-out drives, and what must never be connected on the output.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 21.11 · AC Motor Control · VFD Principles

# Variable-Frequency Drives (VFDs) for Motors: Rectifier, DC Bus, IGBT PWM, V/f and Vector Control, and Correct Wiring

A contactor can only switch a motor on or off. A VFD creates a new three-phase supply whose frequency and voltage are both adjustable, so the motor can run at any speed with controlled current. This page explains what is inside the box, why V/f must be held constant, and the wiring rules that let a drive run for years without disturbing other systems.

In 30 seconds

- AC 400 V → rectifier → DC bus ≈ 540–565 V → IGBT PWM → AC 0–400 V, 0–50 Hz (or higher)

- Hold V/f = 8 V/Hz to keep the flux constant → full torque at every speed below 50 Hz

- Above 50 Hz the voltage stays constant, the flux falls and torque falls as 1/f

- Output side: no capacitors, never switch a contactor while running, shielded cable earthed 360°

- A single-phase 230 V supply can drive a 230/400 V motor connected in Δ

## Inside a VFD Basic

Figure 1 · Three parts: the rectifier (AC → DC), the DC bus with its capacitors (energy storage) and the IGBT inverter (DC → AC at adjustable frequency)

V1 DC bus voltage

$$V_{dc} \approx 1.35\,V_L = 540\ \text{V (loaded)} \qquad V_{dc,0} = \sqrt2\,V_L = 566\ \text{V (no load)}$$

Six IGBTs switch at 2–16 kHz to produce voltage pulses whose width varies sinusoidally (PWM). The motor, being an inductance, filters out the pulses, so the current is nearly sinusoidal. A higher switching frequency makes the motor quieter but heats the IGBTs more (derating is required).

V2 Maximum output voltage

$$V_{LL,rms} = 0.612\,m\,V_{dc}\ (\text{SPWM}, m \le 1) \qquad V_{LL,max} \approx 0.707\,V_{dc}\ (\text{SVPWM})$$

With $V_{dc}$ = 540 V the maximum SVPWM output voltage is ≈ 382 V, slightly below 400 V, so drives use over-modulation near base frequency. If the supply is low (e.g. 380 V), the motor at 50 Hz receives less than its nameplate voltage and the current at full load is slightly higher.

## V/f control Intermediate

The flux in the iron core is proportional to $V/f$. If the frequency is reduced without reducing the voltage, the core saturates and the current soars; if the voltage is reduced too much, the flux weakens and torque is lost. The drive therefore holds the ratio constant up to the base frequency (from the motor nameplate). At low frequency the voltage drop across R₁ becomes a large fraction, so the voltage is raised slightly (boost).

Figure 2 · Below 50 Hz: constant torque, power rises with speed · Above 50 Hz: constant voltage, constant power, torque falls as 1/f

V3 Constant V/f

$$V(f) = V_n\frac{f}{f_n} + V_{boost}\left(1 - \frac{f}{f_n}\right) \qquad \frac{V_n}{f_n} = \frac{400}{50} = 8\ \text{V/Hz}$$

V4 Speed with a VFD

$$n = \frac{120 f}{p} - \Delta n \qquad \Delta n \approx s_n\,n_{s,n}\ \ (\text{constant at rated torque})$$

V5 Field weakening (f > f_n)

$$T_{cont} \approx T_n\,\frac{f_n}{f} \qquad T_{max} \approx T_{max,n}\left(\frac{f_n}{f}\right)^2 \qquad P \approx P_n$$

Example V-1

### A 7.5 kW, 4-pole, 1470 rpm motor at 30 Hz and 60 Hz

- V3 (ignoring boost): 30 Hz → $V = 8 \times 30 = 240$ V · 60 Hz → voltage held at 400 V

- V4: rated speed drop $\Delta n = 1500 - 1470 = 30$ rpm → 30 Hz: $n = 900 - 30 = 870$ rpm · 60 Hz: $n \approx 1800 - 35 \approx 1765$ rpm (in field weakening the slip at rated power rises slightly)

- V5: at 60 Hz the continuous torque ≈ $48.7 \times 50/60 = 40.6$ N·m; power is still ~7.5 kW, but the maximum torque falls to $(5/6)^2 = 69\,\%$

- At 30 Hz the full 48.7 N·m is available electrically, but the shaft-mounted fan turns at 60 % speed and cools less; with a constant-torque load the motor must be derated

### V/f versus sensorless vector control

V/f simply commands a voltage and frequency without knowing what the motor is doing. It suits pumps and fans and can drive several motors in parallel. Vector control (FOC) estimates flux and torque from the measured currents and controls the flux-producing and torque-producing currents separately, giving high torque at low speed (150 % at 1 Hz) and fast response — suited to conveyors, mixers and hoists. It requires auto-tuning so the drive can measure the motor parameters before use, and works with one motor per drive.

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

## Wiring Basic

Figure 3 · Terminal names differ between brands but the functions are the same: R S T (L1 L2 L3) input, U V W output, digital inputs, analog inputs, fault relay and braking-resistor terminals

### Power-side rules

- Feed the input through the MCCB or fuses specified in the manual (gG/gR fuses protect IGBTs/diodes better). An input contactor (if fitted) is for isolation, not for run/stop (use the digital inputs), because the DC bus capacitors charge every time power is applied

- No separate overload is needed: the drive protects the motor with a thermal model once the nameplate current is entered correctly (except where several motors share one drive — then each motor needs its own overload)

- Use symmetrical shielded motor cable with the shield bonded to earth 360° at the clamps at both ends; the motor PE conductor returns to the drive's PE terminal

- Keep motor cables at least 20–30 cm from signal cables; where they must cross, cross at right angles

- For cables longer than the manual allows (often about 50–100 m for shielded cable), use an output reactor, dv/dt filter or sine filter

Never on the U V W output: no power-factor correction capacitors or snubbers · never open or close a contactor while the drive is delivering output · never apply mains to U V W (e.g. a bypass without an interlock) · never insulation-test with a megger while the cable is still connected to the drive

### The DC bus is dangerous even after switch-off

The DC bus capacitors hold a charge of 540–565 V for several minutes after power is removed. The manual specifies a waiting time (often 5–15 minutes), and you must confirm by measuring at the DC+ and DC− terminals before touching anything.

## EMC, leakage current and RCDs Intermediate

The steep voltage edges of PWM (thousands of volts per microsecond) drive high-frequency current through the capacitance of the cable and motor to earth and radiate interference. An input EMC filter prevents interference from flowing back into the supply, but increases the earth leakage current.

- Three-phase drives can produce smooth DC leakage current, so a Type B RCD is required · single-phase drives use Type F or Type B

- On an IT system (unearthed), the Y capacitors of the internal filter must be disconnected as described in the manual

- Bearing currents from common-mode voltage cause fluting of the bearings in large motors; use insulated bearings or a shaft earthing brush

## Braking and braking resistors Advanced

When the drive is told to decelerate faster than the load would coast to a stop, the motor becomes a generator and energy flows back into the DC bus. A diode rectifier cannot return it to the mains, so the bus voltage rises until the drive trips on “DC overvoltage”. Remedies: lengthen the deceleration time, use a braking resistor via a brake chopper, or use a regenerative (AFE) drive.

V6 Braking resistor

$$E = \tfrac12 J(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) \qquad P_{peak} \approx \frac{J\,\omega_1\,\Delta\omega}{t_{dec}} \qquad R \le \frac{V_{br}^2}{P_{peak}},\ R \ge R_{min}$$

Example V-2

### A fan with J = 2.2 kg·m² decelerated from 1470 rpm to 0 in 10 s

- $\omega_1 = 2\pi(1470)/60 = 154$ rad/s · $E = \tfrac12(2.2)(154^2) = 26.1$ kJ (some is lost to air drag, so this is the worst case)

- V6: $P_{peak} \approx 2.2(154)(154)/10 = 5.2$ kW

- The chopper operates at $V_{br} \approx 760$ V (typical for a 400 V drive) → $R \le 760^2/5{,}200 = 111\ \Omega$, and it must not be less than the $R_{min}$ in the manual · The average power depends on how often braking occurs; it is not 5.2 kW continuously

## Single-phase-in, three-phase-out drives Basic

Homes, farms and shops that have only a single-phase 230 V supply can use a drive with a single-phase input (L N terminals) and a three-phase 230 V output to run three-phase motors up to about 2.2–3 kW. The motor must be a 230/400 V type connected in Δ so that each winding receives 230 V. The advantages are higher starting torque than a single-phase capacitor motor, adjustable speed and low starting current. The limitation is that the input current is peaky (low true power factor), so the input breaker must be chosen according to the manual.

## Frequently asked questions

Can I put a contactor between the VFD and the motor?
Only for isolation or bypass, and it may be opened or closed only when the drive is not delivering output (command a stop and wait for the output to switch off first). Opening the output while current flows causes voltage spikes that destroy the IGBTs and the contacts, and closing it while the drive is running causes a current surge that trips the drive.

Why does the residual-current device trip when a VFD is installed?
The EMC filter and the capacitance of the shielded cable cause high-frequency leakage current to earth, and DC leakage is also possible. Use an RCD designed for drives (Type B for three-phase drives, Type F for single-phase drives), rated 30 mA only where needed for personal protection, or 100–300 mA for fire protection, following the manufacturer's recommendations.

Can a VFD be used with an old motor?
Usually yes, but fast IGBT switching produces high peak voltages at the motor terminals when the cable is long, and the insulation of an old motor may not withstand them. Keep the cable short, use a dv/dt filter or sine filter for long runs, and check cooling when running at low speed.

Mod

Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# PLC Automation

A PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) replaces panels of hundreds of relays with a program you can edit. This course runs from how a PLC scans, through wiring PNP/NPN sensors correctly, writing ladder logic, timers and counters, to motor control, star–delta, sequential systems, analog and PID, and commanding VFDs. Every example can be tried straight away in the simulator on the page. There are formulas with citable IDs and worked examples.

In 30 seconds

- A PLC repeats three things every few milliseconds: read inputs → run the program → write outputs

- Ladder: series = AND · parallel = OR · NC = NOT · a self-holding rung works like a contactor

- A PNP sensor pairs with a sinking input (COM to 0 V) · NPN pairs with sourcing

- STOP and emergency-stop buttons are wired NC, and critical interlocks must stay in hardware

- IEC 61131-3 timers TON, TOF, TP and counters CTU, CTD work on every brand

## Learning path by level

## Try it: a star–delta PLC in your browser

Press START (I0.1) and watch the green power flow through the ladder. Timer T1 counts 6 seconds, K2 (star) drops out, there is an 80 ms dead time, then K3 (delta) pulls in. Choose another example from the menu, or open “Edit the program” to write your own. The full simulator with worksheets is at Ladder simulator.

JavaScript is needed for the simulator

## Key equations used throughout

H1 Worst-case response

$$t_{resp,max} \approx t_{in} + 2\,t_{scan} + t_{out}$$

H2 Latch rung

$$Q = \overline{\text{STOP}}\cdot(\text{START} + Q) \;\;\equiv\;\; \text{STOP wired NC → NO contact in the program}$$

H3 On-delay timer

$$Q_{TON} = IN \wedge (ET \ge PT) \qquad ET \le PT$$

H4 Analog scaling

$$y = y_{min} + (x - x_{min})\,\frac{y_{max} - y_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}$$

## Frequently asked questions

What should I know before learning PLCs?
You should understand contactor control circuits (self-holding, interlocks, timers), because ladder logic is designed to read like a relay circuit, and basic 24 VDC and 230 VAC electrics so you can wire I/O correctly. All of this is covered in the motor-control course on this site.

Which PLC brand should I start with?
The principles are the same for every brand because they follow IEC 61131. Choose a brand used in the factories or schools near you, and one with free software and a simulator. In this region Mitsubishi, Omron, Siemens, Delta, Schneider, Rockwell and Keyence are common.

How is a PLC different from an Arduino or a microcontroller?
A PLC is designed for the factory environment: noise-immune, isolated 24 VDC I/O, a predictable scan, self-diagnostics, standardised languages, modules that can be serviced and replaced in use, and certification to industrial standards. A microcontroller is more flexible and cheaper, but the user has to build all that robustness themselves.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 22.8 · PLC · Analog, PID & VFD

# Analog, PID and Drive Control with a PLC: 4–20 mA Scaling, the PID Block, a Constant-Pressure Pump and Modbus RTU

The real world is not just 0 and 1: pressure, level, temperature and motor speed are continuous quantities. This page goes from the raw number in an analog module to a pressure-control loop that commands a drive — the most common job in buildings and factories.

In 30 seconds

- Scaling: $y = y_{min} + (x - x_{min})(y_{max} - y_{min})/(x_{max} - x_{min})$, computed in REAL

- Below 3.6 mA or above 21 mA is a fault, not a measurement

- PID: $u = K_p\left(e + \frac{1}{T_i}\int e\,dt + T_d\frac{de}{dt}\right)$ · start tuning with PI

- Commanding a VFD: DI + AI is simplest · Modbus returns data (current, faults) over a single pair

## From raw counts to engineering units Basic

Figure 1 · A 0–10 bar, 4–20 mA pressure transmitter into an analog module that returns raw counts of 0–27648

P1 Linear scaling

$$y = y_{min} + (x - x_{min})\,\frac{y_{max} - y_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}}$$

P2 Resolution per raw count

$$\Delta y = \frac{y_{max} - y_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}} \qquad \text{e.g. } \frac{10\ \text{bar}}{27648} = 0.36\ \text{mbar}$$

P3 Signal validity (NAMUR NE 43)

$$3.8 \le I \le 20.5\ \text{mA: valid measurement} \qquad I \le 3.6 \text{ or } I \ge 21\ \text{mA → fault}$$

Example P-1

### Scaling a raw value of 13824 with INT gives zero

- Wrong: Bar := Raw / 27648 * 10; in INT → 13824/27648 = 0 (truncated) → 0 bar

- Also wrong: Raw * 10 / 27648 in INT → 27648 × 10 = 276480 overflows INT

- Right: Bar := INT_TO_REAL(Raw) * 10.0 / 27648.0; → 5.0 bar

- Check P3: Siemens modules return negative raw values when the current is below 4 mA (down to −4864 ≈ 1.185 mA), and with wire-break diagnostics enabled they report a special value (32767) — check both the raw range per P3 and the module's status bits.

## The PID block in a PLC Intermediate

Figure 2 · Constant-pressure loop: SP − PV = e → PID → frequency → VFD → pump → pressure → transmitter

P4 PID (standard form)

$$u(t) = K_p\left(e + \frac{1}{T_i}\int_0^t e\,d\tau + T_d\,\frac{de}{dt}\right) \qquad e = SP - PV$$

P5 Discrete PID (sample time $T_s$)

$$u_k = K_p\left(e_k + \frac{T_s}{T_i}\sum_{j=0}^{k} e_j - \frac{T_d}{T_s}(PV_k - PV_{k-1})\right)$$

The derivative term uses PV instead of e (derivative on measurement) so the output does not kick when SP changes, and anti-windup is needed: when the output hits its limit (e.g. 50 Hz), stop accumulating the integral. Most pump and fan loops use PI only (Td = 0) because pressure signals are noisy.

### Initial tuning for a constant-pressure pump

- Start with a small Kp (e.g. 0.5 of full scale), a long Ti (e.g. 5 s) and Td = 0

- Increase Kp until it starts to oscillate, then halve it

- Reduce Ti gradually until the value returns to setpoint quickly enough without oscillating (typically 1–5 s for water pressure)

- Test by actually opening and closing taps, watching both the dip and the overshoot

Try the effect of Kp, Ti and Td in the PID lab (Thai), and a pressure loop with a VFD pump in the virtual instrumentation lab (Thai).

## Commanding a drive from the PLC Intermediate

| Method | Wiring | Advantages | Limitations |

| Digital + preset speeds | Several DO → DI wires | Simple, noise-immune | Only a few speeds |

| Digital + analog | DO → RUN · AO → AI (4–20 mA) | Continuous adjustment, easy to understand | Feedback limited to what is wired (AO, relays) |

| Modbus RTU (RS-485) | One twisted pair, several drives | Read current, frequency and faults; set parameters | Communication settings needed; slower response with many stations |

| Industrial Ethernet | PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP, EtherCAT | Fast, lots of data, full diagnostics | Needs a module and network configuration |

P6 Frequency setpoint over Modbus

$$\text{Reg} = \frac{f}{0.01\ \text{Hz}} \quad (35.5\ \text{Hz} \to 3550) \qquad \text{or} \quad \text{Reg} = \frac{f}{f_{max}}\times \text{Scale}_{100\%}$$

Example register map (hypothetical, for learning — every brand differs; use the real manual)

| Register | Name | Read/write | Value |

| 40001 | Control word | W | Bit 0 = RUN · bit 1 = REV · bit 2 = RESET |

| 40002 | Frequency reference | W | 0.01 Hz |

| 40011 | Status word | R | Bit 0 = Ready · bit 1 = Running · bit 3 = Fault |

| 40012 | Output frequency | R | 0.01 Hz |

| 40013 | Output current | R | 0.1 A |

| 40014 | Fault code | R | Code per the manual |

RS-485 wiring, CRC-16 calculation and a frame builder are in Modbus RTU · TCP (Thai). Remember: set the “communication timeout” in the drive so it stops if the PLC is silent for longer than the set time — otherwise, if the communication cable breaks, the drive keeps running at the last frequency.

Example P-2

### The PLC sends 4–20 mA to a VFD ranged 20–50 Hz; 42 Hz is wanted

- Invert P1: $I = 4 + 16\,(42 - 20)/(50 - 20) = 4 + 11.73 = 15.73$ mA

- If the analog output is 0–27648 = 4–20 mA: raw value $= 27648 \times 11.73/16 = 20275$

- Set the drive to treat AI below 2 mA as a broken wire and choose the response (stop / fallback speed)

## Frequently asked questions

Is it better to run PID in the PLC or in the VFD?
For a single loop where the transmitter can be wired straight into the VFD, the drive's own PID is simple, responds quickly and keeps working even if the PLC fails. If several pumps must be coordinated, there are many conditions, or the loop must be logged and adjusted from SCADA, PID in the PLC is more flexible.

What value do I send over Modbus to command 35.5 Hz?
It depends on the register units in the drive manual. Many drives use 0.01 Hz units, so you send 3550. Some use a fraction of maximum frequency, e.g. 0–16384 or 0–10000 = 0–100 %. Always read the manual and test with a low value first.

Mod

Updated: 2026-10-14
Summary: The steps for testing and commissioning a PLC system: pre-energisation checks, point-by-point I/O testing, analog loop checks, the dangers of forcing bits, program backup and version control, stop categories 0, 1 and 2 per IEC 60204-1, emergency stop with a dual-channel safety relay, Performance Level (PL) per ISO 13849-1 and SIL per IEC 62061, light-curtain safety distances per ISO 13855, and a troubleshooting flow for when a machine will not run.

THภาษาไทยENEnglish

// Chapter 22.9 · PLC · Commissioning & Safety

# PLC Commissioning, Machine Safety and Troubleshooting: Loop Checks, Forcing, Emergency Stop, IEC 60204-1, ISO 13849 and Documentation

A program that passes in the simulator is not yet a machine ready for use. Commissioning is when accidents happen most often, because the wiring is incomplete, people are not yet familiar with the machine and the program is being edited live. This page gives a systematic procedure, the safety principles the standards require, and a disciplined way to find faults.

In 30 seconds

- Test in layers: wiring → supplies → I/O point by point → logic without power → live run

- Emergency stop = stop category 0 or 1 through safety devices, not through a standard PLC program

- The required level (PLr) comes from the risk assessment · light-curtain distance $S = K\,T + C$

- Every force needs a procedure, and none may remain at handover

## Testing and commissioning procedure Basic

- Before power-up: check the wiring against the drawings, PE continuity, power-cable insulation resistance (with electronics disconnected) and that terminals are tight

- Energise section by section: 24 VDC control power first, measure the voltage at every I/O group · power circuit still isolated

- Test inputs one at a time: press the real button / trigger the real sensor in the field, watch the bit change in the software, record it on the I/O check sheet

- Test outputs one at a time: with the power circuit still isolated, command each output (using test mode or a force under procedure) and check the right contactor, valve or lamp operates

- Analog loop check: inject 4 · 12 · 20 mA with a calibrator and read the engineering value in the PLC and on the HMI

- Safety tests: every emergency stop, safety gate and light curtain — check that power is really removed and that reset must be done manually

- Dry logic test: run the whole sequence with the power circuit isolated, simulating sensors

- Live run: one motor at a time, checking direction and current, then the whole sequence, both normal and abnormal cases (pull a sensor, trip an overload)

- Handover: no forces left, program backed up with comments, documentation: I/O list, as-built drawings, drive parameters

Forcing: before forcing an output that makes the machine move, warn everyone in the area, have someone standing at the emergency stop, and log it. Most software shows a warning symbol while a force is active — check it every time before leaving site.

## Stop categories and emergency stop (IEC 60204-1) Intermediate

K1 Stop categories

$$\text{Cat 0: remove power immediately} \qquad \text{Cat 1: controlled stop, then remove power} \qquad \text{Cat 2: controlled stop, power kept on}$$

An emergency stop must be category 0 or 1 only. Category 1 is used when cutting power immediately is more dangerous, e.g. a large centrifuge that must be braked by the drive before power is removed (using a time-delayed safety relay). The emergency-stop button is a red mushroom head on a yellow background, latches when pressed, has positively driven (direct-opening) contacts, and releasing it must not restart the machine by itself.

Figure 1 · The safety relay monitors both channels and cross-channel shorts; its safety contacts are in series with the PLC output, so it can always cut the coil — the PLC only reads the status

## Safety levels: PL and SIL Advanced

ISO 13849-1 assesses risk from three factors: severity of injury (S1 slight / S2 serious), frequency of exposure to the hazard (F1 seldom / F2 frequent) and possibility of avoiding it (P1 possible / P2 scarcely possible). This gives the required level PLr from a to e. The safety function is then designed (category structure B, 1, 2, 3, 4; component lifetime MTTFd; diagnostic coverage DC) so that PL ≥ PLr.

K2 PL / SIL by dangerous failure rate

$$\text{PL d} \approx \text{SIL 2}: 10^{-7} \le PFH_D

| Example function | Typical PLr | Common implementation |

| Emergency stop on a general machine | c–d | Dual-channel button + safety relay + two contactors in series with feedback |

| Safety gate on a cutting machine / press | d–e | Two gate switches or a coded switch + safety PLC |

| Light curtain in front of a press | d–e | Type 4 light curtain + mounting distance per K3 |

K3 Minimum safety distance (ISO 13855)

$$S = K\,T + C \qquad K = 2000\ \text{mm/s (if } S \le 500\ \text{mm)},\ 1600\ \text{mm/s (otherwise)} \qquad C = 8(d - 14)\ \text{mm},\ d \le 40\ \text{mm}$$

Example K-1

### A 14 mm resolution light curtain with a total stopping time of 120 ms

- Total time T = light-curtain response + safety relay + machine stopping time (measured) = 0.12 s

- $C = 8(14 - 14) = 0$ · $S = 2000(0.12) + 0 = 240$ mm ≤ 500 ✓ so K = 2000 applies

- Mount the light curtain at least 240 mm from the hazard point (the standard's minimum is 100 mm) and prevent reaching over the top or around the sides

## Troubleshooting when the machine will not run Intermediate

- Check the PLC status: RUN/STOP, ERR lamp, battery lamp, event log (diagnostic buffer)

- Check the HMI: alarm messages, the step it is stuck in (if written as a state machine)

- Work back from the output: an output that should be on but is not → open that rung online → find the contact that is “not green” → is it an input or an internal bit?

- If it is an input: look at the module LED → if off, measure the voltage at the terminal → check the sensor / wiring / sensor supply

- If the output bit is 1 but the device does not operate: output LED → output fuse → interposing relay → coil → hard-wired interlocks (auxiliary NC, 95-96, safety relay)

Golden rule: “change one thing at a time and record every change”, especially when editing the program online. Keep a copy before every edit and name the file with the date and the reason.

## Documentation to hand over

- As-built electrical drawings with the bill of materials

- I/O list (address, tag name, description, signal type, scaling range)

- Commented PLC and HMI programs as source files (not just an upload from the PLC), with passwords handed to the owner

- Parameter settings of every drive and smart device

- Signed I/O check sheets, loop checks and safety-function test results

- Operating manual and recovery procedure after an emergency stop

## Frequently asked questions

Why is forcing bits in a PLC dangerous?
A force sets a bit regardless of the program conditions or the real state of the input. The machine may move when nobody expects it, software interlocks are bypassed, and if the force is forgotten it stays in place until an accident happens. There should be a procedure: get permission, warn everyone in the area, log it, and check that no forces remain before handing over the machine.

Can I wire the emergency-stop button into the PLC and let the program cut the outputs?
Not with a standard PLC. An emergency stop needs a reliability level assessed to ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061, which general-purpose PLCs are not certified for. Use a safety relay or a safety PLC that removes power from the actuators directly, and bring its status into the PLC for display and for sequencing the restart.

Mod

Ajarn Mod · Teerawut Savangboon
Lecturer in Electrical Engineering, Dhonburi Rajabhat University, Samut Prakan · Profile

# PLC Programming Languages to IEC 61131-3: LD, FBD, ST, SFC and IL — One Program in Several Languages, Data Types and Choosing a Language
